A Cold War Movie That Gives Too Much Credit to Ronald Reagan
The Brink of War, a new film about the Reykjavik summit, is too kind to the Gipper.
Americans do not know enough about the Cold War, and much of what they think they know is wrong. After the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, Republicans took a victory lap, rightly noting that the Soviet collapse was unimaginable when President Ronald Reagan first took office. Liberal critics, however, argued—also rightly—that the Soviet Union was a decaying, economically crippled giant by the time Reagan was inaugurated. In the years since, explanations of the ending of that great conflict have been reduced to the equivalent of partisan bumper stickers: We crushed the Kremlin in the arms race, or The U.S.S.R. imploded without any pressure from the West.
In October 1986, Reagan and Soviet General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev met to discuss nuclear-arms control in Reykjavik, Iceland. At the time, I was a young scholar in Washington, training in Soviet affairs and international relations at Georgetown University and working at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. (I was also a two-time Reagan voter.) When the Reykjavik meeting took place, no one was looking ahead to the collapse of the Soviet Union; Kremlin watchers were, mostly, relieved to see a Soviet general secretary and an American president talking with each other.
The Brink of War, a new film released nationwide today, tries to bring texture and detail to those two days in Iceland. The movie relies on transcripts and other documents from the time, along with interviews with a former secretary of state, the late George Shultz (to whom the movie is dedicated). The film is a welcome corrective to the liberal orthodoxy about Reagan—specifically, that he was a disconnected simpleton who didn’t understand the complexities of the arms race. But it leans too much in the opposite direction: It is too kind to the Gipper, and takes too many liberties with the historical record.
As a viewing experience, The Brink of War is a better film than the only other movie about the summit, a 1987 British production titled Breakthrough at Reykjavik. But that’s because the earlier movie (now no longer available, as far as I can tell) was more accurate—and perhaps, for some viewers, more boring. The diplomats who met in the middle of the night thought they were ridding the world of nuclear arms, and that story has plenty of drama, but The Brink of War forgoes those details in favor of needless melodrama and a focus on fewer personalities.
The title itself is misleading. The world was not on the brink of war in late 1986. Soviet-American tensions were much higher, and the risk of war much greater, during Reagan’s first term, which were perhaps the most dangerous years of the Cold War since the Cuban missile crisis. In the early ’80s, the Soviet Union was led by Yuri Andropov, a former KGB chief. In 1983 alone, Reagan gave his “Evil Empire” speech and announced the start of his missile-defense plan, the Strategic Defense Initiative; the Soviets shot down a civilian Korean airliner (killing a U.S. congressman); and the Americans overthrew a Marxist regime in Grenada. Andropov died in 1984, and Gorbachev took more than a year to gain power while the Kremlin stumbled along under the caretaker regime of the grievously ill Konstantin Chernenko.
Gorbachev’s arrival cooled some of these tensions. Almost a year before Reykjavik, Reagan and Gorbachev met in Geneva, where they issued a joint announcement that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” This was an important moment: Gorbachev, still consolidating power, was taking a risk by bucking anti-American hawks back in Moscow and standing with Reagan to join him in officially ruling out nuclear war as a rational instrument of policy.
By the time the two men met in Iceland, they were both determined to reduce their nations’ stockpiles of nuclear weapons. For Gorbachev, this reflected both a sincere belief and an economic imperative. The Soviet Union was struggling with the costs of boneheaded decisions such as the invasion of Afghanistan and the deployment of new and extremely threatening Soviet nuclear weapons in Europe. Reagan, despite his reputation among his critics as a warmonger, was actually an abolitionist when it came to nuclear weapons, and on this, he and Gorbachev were of one mind.
Both men had earlier made dramatic proposals to rid the world of nuclear arms. These were roundly dismissed in each other’s capitals as propaganda, but as it turned out, Reagan and Gorbachev were completely serious. The meeting foundered because of Reagan’s commitment to SDI, but the Reykjavik summit, despite its failure to reach any agreements, nevertheless suggested to the two leaders that they agreed about important things.
The Brink of War gets much of this right, but it portrays Reagan as highly prepared and Gorbachev as somewhat nervous. In reality, Reagan was concerned about the meeting, and at the start he relied on notes and cards he had in front of him. One of Gorbachev’s first observations when they met was about all the paper in front of his American counterpart; Reagan at one point dropped all of his notes and had to shuffle through them to get back on track. The film also shows Reagan confidently teasing his negotiating team about being Democrats, which was probably done so that the movie could make the summit seem like a bipartisan effort. It’s true that a few Reaganites were once Democrats, such as the negotiator Richard Perle, but this was not a team of liberals and conservatives. Perle was so distrustful of arms control with the Soviets that his nickname in Washington in the ’80s was the “Prince of Darkness.”
Soon the two leaders took up the proposal first discussed in Geneva for a 50 percent cut in Soviet- and American-weapons stockpiles. Reagan and Gorbachev, in the course of their discussion, agreed to eliminate all nuclear weapons, a move that surprised both delegations. The idea of full abolition—beloved by both leaders but not part of the Reykjavik agenda—was an improvised moment, almost an accident, and not some premeditated masterstroke (as the movie implies) by Reagan. This sudden change drove hours of unexpected negotiations. Both sides, in a very short time, got remarkably close to a major nuclear deal, because their bosses, both Soviet and American, wanted one.
These American negotiators do not get much attention in the film; likewise, the Soviets, starting with Gorbachev himself, get unfair treatment in The Brink of War. The Soviet boss huddles in the bathroom with his wife, hiding from the KGB, as if he were doing something illegal and not presenting positions he’d already raised among Soviet leaders. The film also depicts Gorbachev as something of a drama queen during the meetings, slamming the table and raising his voice. At one point, when Reagan suggests sharing missile-defense technology, Gorbachev stands up and whines about how America will not even share dairy technology so that the Soviets can provide milk to their children.
Reagan did make that missile-defense technology offer, and Gorbachev did in fact dismiss it. What Gorbachev actually said, however, according to records from the meeting, was more restrained: “Excuse me, Mr. President, but I do not take your idea of sharing SDI seriously. You don’t want to share even petroleum equipment, automatic machine tools or equipment for dairies.” This was a kind of sarcastic zinger from the real Gorbachev. But in any case, no Soviet leader would complain to an American president about hungry Soviet kids. It would have been especially out of character for Gorbachev, who Shultz later recalled was not whiny but rather “brisk, impatient, and confident, with the air of a man who is setting the agenda and taking charge of the meeting.”
Other Soviets appear as central-casting scary Communists. The Soviet Foreign Minister Eduard Shevardnadze is played as a glowering, skeptical presence by a darkly handsome English actor. The real Shevardnadze looked more like a white-haired professor, and he supported Gorbachev’s proposals. Likewise, Marshal Sergei Akhromeyev, the senior military officer who led the Soviet negotiators, is portrayed as a difficult, stiff military man, but American negotiators, especially Paul Nitze, later spoke of him with great admiration as smart, flexible, and someone the Americans could trust.
The Brink of War also presents Reykjavik as something of a guy’s poker party. Men conduct the work in the movie, but in real life, some of the important negotiations with the Soviets were led by the veteran diplomat Rozanne Ridgway, who does not appear in the film. The two most important women in the film are the wives, Raisa Gorbacheva and Nancy Reagan. Raisa is presented as a chic, smart adviser to her husband. Nancy, who stayed in Washington, is Ronnie’s faithful booster, but she also unfairly comes across as a catty flake, envying Raisa and telling the president that the stars are aligned for a successful summit.
Nancy Reagan, fearful of losing her husband, did indeed consult an astrologer after Reagan was shot. But Karen Tumulty, The Washington Post’s chief political correspondent and the author of a definitive biography of Nancy, told me that Nancy was angry in October 1986 not because she felt upstaged, but because her husband’s advisers had told her that Iceland was not a “summit” and therefore that Raisa would not be there. A scene where Nancy tells Ron about the position of Mars, Tumulty added, “strikes me as preposterous.”
The supreme error in The Brink of War, however, is that it wanders too far from the history of the event in order to depict a successful summit. In life, the two leaders agreed about ridding the world of nuclear weapons, but they both left Iceland full of gloom and bitterness. A deal to eliminate nuclear arms dissolved when Reagan insisted that testing for SDI had to continue. Gorbachev, hamstrung by demands from hard-liners back in Moscow, was equally intransigent that no deal could be made so long as SDI was in the works. The summit-that-was-not-a-summit failed.
As the Reagan biographer Max Boot told me, both Reagan and Gorbachev left “furious and disappointed.” Tumulty cites Nancy Reagan as saying later that it was clear to her, watching from afar, that her husband, “pale” and with his “teeth clenched,” was extremely angry as he said goodbye to Gorbachev. According to declassified Soviet transcripts released years later, as the two leaders stood outside waiting to leave, Reagan accused Gorbachev of not wanting a deal in the first place, adding that he didn’t know when they would meet again. (“I don’t either,” Gorbachev said.) Ken Adelman, one of Reagan’s aides at the meeting, later wrote that Reagan, during that final conversation, recalled Gorbachev saying, “I don’t know what else I could have done.” Reagan answered: “I do. You could have said yes.”
None of this makes its way into The Brink of War. Instead, the film makes much of Reagan trying to get a visa for the sister of Mstislav Rostropovich, a Soviet musical maestro who had defected to the United States. Reagan did raise this issue, and the Soviets relented, but The Brink of War makes it seem as if reaching agreement on this opened the way to more deals later. The movie ends with Reagan doubling back to try one more time on the Rostropovich issue. Gorbachev agrees, the men shake hands, and the last word of the movie is deal.
This is not remotely what happened. According to Adelman, it was Gorbachev, not Reagan, who tried one more time to engage—and not on Rostropovich’s sister but on a nuclear deal. “Can’t we do something about this?” the Soviet leader asked as Reagan got ready to leave. “It’s too late,” Reagan said, and walked out.
In the movie, this coldly enraged Reagan is replaced by a smiling dealmaker who is deeply introspective. In a private moment, he stares at the scar from the 1981 attempt on his life; that night he has a fit of PTSD about the shooting as he tosses and turns. The next day, Reagan emphasizes to Gorbachev that he felt that God had spared his life for a great purpose.
Whether Reagan had PTSD from nearly being murdered is a matter of speculation, but he said no such thing to Gorbachev. The movie is full of lines that sound good from Reagan but that he never said. At one point, he invites Gorbachev to “tear down this wall between us,” as if he were already thinking of the line he would use in front of the Berlin Wall a year later. Nor did he say to Gorbachev that the Soviet people were “pissed off” at their government, a line that rings especially false from Reagan, who did not approve of any kind of swearing. As Boot noted to me, the president would not even spell out the word hell in his own diaries.
All of this is unfortunate, because Reykjavik was a crucial step in ending the Cold War, and The Brink of War could have captured Reagan’s admirable toughness and confidence without exaggerating either the president’s abilities or what happened in Iceland. Reagan deserves great credit for making the end of the Cold War possible not only by holding fast to his belief in the superiority of the American system but also by having the vision to see that the Cold War and its endless nuclear tensions did not need to be accepted by either side as an immutable fact of life. He came into office excoriating the Soviets, and learned—almost too late—that he had succeeded too well in scaring the Kremlin and had brought the world closer to war. Encouraged by Shultz and Nancy, he changed course during his first term, and he found a courageous partner in Gorbachev.
Yet Reagan, especially at Reykjavik, was hobbled at times by rigidity and tunnel vision. At the summit, he tried to lecture Gorbachev on the bankruptcy of Marxism-Leninism—this did not go over well—and the president’s obsession with SDI tanked what might have been the most dramatic arms agreement in history. Gorbachev, too, was intransigent, but by Soviet standards he was practically a radical. Fortunately, Gorbachev would drop his objections to SDI in time for both men to sign a landmark treaty in 1987 that abolished all intermediate range nuclear arms in Europe and made the entire world safer. (Donald Trump foolishly withdrew from this treaty in 2019.)
Reagan did not win the Cold War alone, but he and Gorbachev made the end of the conflict and a more secure world possible. The Brink of War, whatever dramatic license it takes, underscores that Reykjavik was part of that story. The summit itself turned out to be a failure, but Washington and Moscow later climbed over its wreckage to reach new agreements. Reykjavik did not end the Cold War, but the Cold War could not have moved toward its peaceful ending without Reykjavik and the spirit of discussion it fostered.

Researchers have reviewed 77 meta-analyses spanning 116 different bipolar disorder treatments and identified the most effective ones across age groups and mood phases.
Bipolar disorder is a mental disorder, characterised by extreme swings in mood, energy levels and activity. The disorder can causes phases of depression marked by a low mood and energy or mania, in which mood and activity levels tend to be high.
Researchers, led by those from The Ottawa Hospital in Canada and universities in Spain, Italy, France and the UK, have created EBI-BD (Evidence Based Interventions for Bipolar Disorder).
EBI-BD is an open-access web platform clearly presenting the impact, side effects, and strength of evidence for each treatment based on findings from the "most comprehensive" review, published in The British Medical Journal.
For bipolar depression, effective treatments for adults include cariprazine, fluoxetine and lurasidone, while those among children and teenagers were lurasidone and olanzapine with fluoxetine.
Effective interventions for mania episodes among adults include aripiprazole, haloperidol, lithium and risperidone, whereas those for children and teenagers include aripiprazole, asenapine and olanzapine.
Maintenance dose -- prescribed to prevent future episodes and for long-term health -- effective for adults include aripiprazole, lithium and risperidone.
"We hope clinicians will be able to use the platform with their own patients to find the best balance between efficacy and side effects, according to each patient's needs," author Michele De Prisco, psychiatrist and researcher at the Hospital Clínic de Barcelona and the University of Barcelona, Spain, said.
"Using the platform and its integrated preference tool, clinician and patient can decide together which treatment to consider next," Dr De Prisco said.
Author -- Jess Fiedorowicz, head and chief of mental health at The Ottawa Hospital and professor at the University of Ottawa, said medications for the mental health disorder can come with varied side effects.
"A tool that incorporates patient preferences and promotes shared decision-making can help find treatments that are a better fit," Dr Fiedorowicz said.
Results from the review have also been used to update guidelines, including those of the International Society for Bipolar Disorders (ISBD), for the management of bipolar disorder.
The study is the first living umbrella review to include all treatment strategies assessed across any age group and phase of bipolar disorder from the largest and best meta-analyses available to date, the researchers said.
The review can be adapted rapidly as new evidence emerges and serves as a foundation for continuously improving care, which is why it is called a "living review", they said.
"Living reviews like this one are game-changers when it comes to updating international treatment guidelines," author Samuele Cortese, research professor at the University of Southampton, UK, said.
"Rather than taking a week to get an answer, experts can consult the website in real time during meetings for the latest evidence," Dr Cortese said.
The authors wrote, "The EBI-BD tool can help clinicians make evidence-based, personalised treatment decisions for bipolar disorder."

How to offer a healthy start to a baby’s life? The answer lies in exclusive breastfeeding. From antibodies to exclusive nutrients, the benefits of breastfeeding are immense. The World Health Organisation and UNICEF recommend initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour after birth. The theme this year for World Breastfeeding Week, celebrated annually from August 1 to 7, is prioritise breastfeeding, create sustainable support systems.
“Breastfeeding may be natural, but it is also a skill that mothers need to learn,” says lactation consultant and child nutrition specialist R Baby Shree of Rao Hospital, adding that there is need to move beyond discussing the benefits of breast milk and focus on the support new mothers need. “Breastfeeding is not something a mother automatically knows after delivering a baby. She needs guidance and support.”
An engaging and informative session on breastfeeding, newborn nutrition and infant feeding practices, took the message across to expectant mothers, new mothers, and their families. The programme titled breastfeeding and beyond put together by Rao Hospital that specialises in women and child care, located in RS Puram, also highlighted common concerns surrounding breastfeeding, newborn feeding patterns, maternal nutrition, and the introduction of complementary foods.
One of the biggest challenges, Baby Shree points out, is the pressure from family members who assume that a crying baby means the mother is not producing enough milk. “Two simple indicators, baby’s diaper change more than six times a day and weight gain, can help establish whether the baby is getting adequate milk.”
“Breastfeeding is the gold standard of infant nutrition,” says Dr KS Krishnasamy, senior neonatologist & paediatrician adding that it plays a vital role in building a baby’s immunity and supporting growth and brain development. While mothers should exclusively breastfeed for the first six months, it is also recommended to continue breastfeeding alongside appropriate complementary foods until two years of age or beyond.
Points to ponder
The lactation consultant also expresses concern about the increasing use of breast pumps. While pumping is important in certain medical situations, such as when a premature baby cannot breastfeed directly, it is not necessarily required for every mother. “Direct breastfeeding also supports the baby’s oral-motor development. Many mothers use pumps to check how much milk they are producing. But the quantity expressed by a pump cannot determine a mother’s actual milk supply,” she says.
Another misconception is that mothers need expensive foods to produce breast milk. “Breastfeeding should not be linked to privileges. A mother needs a balanced diet, adequate nourishment and confidence,” she says.
However, family support is crucial. Kangaroo care helps fathers to bond with their babies. Other family members can comfort the baby after a feed, ensure the mother gets adequate food and water, and, most importantly, avoid undermining her confidence by questioning her milk supply. Social media and formula marketing can further add to mothers’ anxieties. “Access to right information and lactation professionals can help mothers make informed choices,” says Baby Shree, adding “Breastfeeding is not the mother’s responsibility alone. The family, healthcare professionals, workplaces and society all have a role to play. Successful breastfeeding needs support.” With a different theme every year, the World Breastfeeding Week 2026, turns the spotlight on support systems that have proven effective in helping mothers breastfeed successfully.

Why Michaely Bihina is the keeper making waves at Wafcon
- Published
One name has become the toast of Cameroon following her heroics at the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon).
Some in the Central African nation are already calling for a statue to built in honour of Michaely Bihina after her incredible performances which have helped the Indomitable Lionesses return to the final for the first time since 2016.
The young goalkeeper has been one of the stars of the tournament with player-of-the-match performances against Nigeria in the quarter-finals and hosts Morocco in the last four.
"I'm very happy and full of emotions because for our generation it's the first time to play the final," she told the BBC World Service after saving four penalties, one in extra time and three in the subsequent shootout, in Wednesday's semi-final win over the Moroccans.
"We thank all the people who support us."
The 22-year-old made nine saves against Nigeria, setting the record for the most in a single match at the finals as Cameroon dethroned the defending champions - a victory which also booked their place at the 2027 Fifa Women's World Cup.
Bihina described it as "a great day for Cameroonian football".
"Playing in my first Wafcon and being able to beat Nigeria and qualify for the World Cup is historic," she told the Confederation of African Football (Caf).
"I am so excited and happy that as a team we have achieved this.
"We had an objective - to change the history of our national team against Nigeria."
Cameroon have previously lost three Wafcon finals - all against Nigeria (2004, 2014 and 2016) - but will now face debutants Malawi for the continental crown on Sunday (19:00 GMT).
Bihina has been at the heart of the Indomitable Lionesses' challenge, with three clean sheets in five matches.
Bihina's clutch moment against Morocco
A tense semi-final against Morocco saw few clear-cut chances in Rabat before the game went into extra time.
Bihina was presented with her chance to shine late on when the Atlas Lionesses were awarded a penalty after Cameroon defender Maryam Nyadjou caught Sakina Ouzraoui in the face with her arm.
Fatima Tagnaout stepped up to take the 118th-minute spot kick, but Bihina dived to her right to push the ball away and send the tie to a shootout.
"When I saved the first penalty during the game, I said inside my mind if we go to penalties I think I can do more," Bihina said.
"I have to catch minimum three penalties."
The Benfica keeper was as good as her word as she kept out efforts from Kenza Chapelle, Maryame Atiq and Ouzraoui to help her team to a 3-1 win.
"I studied the penalties of Morocco girls during all the competition," she revealed afterwards.
Bihina is widely considered as a contender for player of the tournament alongside Malawi's Chawinga sisters Tabitha and Temwa.
Younger sibling Temwa leads the goalscoring charts with five goals and two assists, while Temwa has four goals.
Starting out as a striker
Bihina was born in Ekounou, in the Nkoldongo area of Cameroon's capital Yaounde, on 28 December 2003.
She started playing football as a striker, but as she grew her coach advised her to switch positions.
"My coach told me that I was too tall to be a striker and that I would do better as a goalkeeper," Bihina told Caf as she described her rapid rise to the top after switching position.
"I did that and six months later I was summoned to the national team."
She joined Portuguese club Racing Power aged 15 and helped them win the second tier league title in 2022-23.
The following season Bihina was named the top flight's best goalkeeper as her side finished third in the table.
This February she joined Benfica on a three-year deal, a move she described as "a dream come true", and she has already won a league and cup double with the Lisbon giants.
Now she has inspired her country to reach next year's World Cup in Brazil and progress to the Wafcon final.
"For me personally, it has been a long journey of hard work and discipline," she said.
"I continue to work with humility and try to improve every day."
Bihina will now face one last test against Malawi and the Chawinga sisters, with Cameroon aiming to put their previous Wafcon final heartbreaks behind them.
"It will be a good game," she told the BBC.
"We try to give our best like every game. We know we will challenge."
Whatever happens, Bihina has already written her name in the Wafcon history books.
Claiming the title could be the icing on the cake to cap the spectacular displays which have announced the goalkeeper as a star of the women's game on the continent.

Just last month, I marked my 25th year as a professional journalist, which I guess means my journalistic career is old enough to rent a car, no questions asked. Work in the news for that long, and you’ll occasionally find yourself surprised by things you published in the past. Like, I had all but forgotten that I had written this Time magazine cover story in 2008:
Ozempic is not just a weight-loss story anymore
The real promise of GLP-1 drugs goes far beyond weight loss.
A couple things here. One, as the cover demonstrates, journalistic sensitivity was…less than ideal then, to say the least. And two, over a quarter-century occasionally covering obesity (both childhood and adult), that story only seemed to go in one direction: worse.
It wasn’t for lack of trying. We put calorie counts on menus, taxed soda (well, in some places), built workplace wellness programs, and funded a small library of diet research. We deplored food deserts and promoted farmers’ markets. We told people — again and again — to eat less and move more. But the lines just kept going up.
By the CDC’s measured survey, the share of US adults with obesity did not change meaningfully between 2013 and 2023. The age-adjusted obesity rate sat at 40.3 percent, while the age-adjusted severe obesity climbed from 7.7 percent to 9.7 percent over the same stretch.
While the question of weight in America is inextricably tied to body image and moralizing, those numbers had a deadly effect. One demographic model estimated that obesity was associated with roughly 18 percent of deaths among Black and white Americans ages 40 to 85 between 1986 and 2006. From diabetes to kidney failure, heart disease to sleep apnea, obesity is the delivery system for other diseases.
Which is what makes a Gallup report published in July so surprising. In Gallup’s self-reported height-and-weight series, the US adult obesity rate fell to 36.4 percent, down from a peak of 39.9 percent in 2022. Over roughly the same period, the share of adults who said they were currently taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss rose from 3 percent in 2024 to 11 percent in 2026 — approximately 29 million people. While this only shows correlation, not causation, and Gallup’s self-reported measure should not be compared directly with the CDC’s measured rate, the timing is suggestive to say the least.
And the weight might be the least interesting thing about these drugs.
Semaglutide — the molecule sold as Ozempic and Wegovy — was first developed and approved as a treatment for type 2 diabetes, not obesity. It was only after earlier GLP-1 drugs and diabetes trials showed substantial effects on appetite and weight that researchers deliberately tested a higher dose for obesity, resulting in Wegovy in 2021.
But as it turns out, the list of things that have been noticed happening on the side with GLP-1s has gotten so long it’s begun to eclipse the main event. The coverage of GLP-1s has barely kept up with this news, because weight loss is what made these drugs famous and what we continually obsess over. But it turns out, weight loss may not be what they’re best at.
Side effects may include…
Let’s start with sleep apnea, which, untreated, drives up blood pressure, strains the heart, and raises the risk of stroke. These are people whose breathing stops dozens of times an hour, all night, every night. Two year-long trials put 469 of them on tirzepatide — the drug sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound — and cut those interruptions by more than half. Roughly half the group finished the year with no apnea at all, or with so little left that they stopped being tired all day.
Then there are the kidneys. A major trial followed 3,533 people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease for a median of 3.4 years. Semaglutide reduced the relative risk of a composite of kidney failure, a sustained loss of at least half of kidney function, or death from kidney-related or cardiovascular causes by 24 percent; all-cause mortality was 20 percent lower.
And the liver: A trial, still underway, biopsied the livers of 800 people whose organs had grown fatty, inflamed and scarred and randomly assigned them to semaglutide or a placebo. After 72 weeks the inflammation had cleared in nearly 63 percent of those on the drug, with no worsening of the scarring, against 34 percent on placebo.
And the knees: In 407 adults with obesity and moderate knee osteoarthritis, pain scores on the 0-100 WOMAC metric fell 41.7 points against 27.5 on placebo.
And to top it off, a 17,604-person trial of participants who were overweight or obese but did not have diabetes found a 20 percent drop in major cardiovascular events.
These results may not be as grabby as cultural debates over “Ozempic face,” but they deserve far more attention.
Medicine’s happy accidents
As GLP-1s — which in part came out of a hormone in Gila monster venom — demonstrate, medicine has long found some of its biggest wins in the margins of drugs ostensibly built to do something else entirely.
Sildenafil, better known as Viagra, began life at Pfizer as a candidate treatment for the heart disease angina. It failed at that, and its now-famous use turned up in data as a side effect in what must have been a very interesting trial for its subjects. Minoxidil (Rogaine) was a blood pressure pill that turned out to help patients grow hair. Finasteride (Propecia) was approved for enlarged prostates before anyone thought to sell it for baldness — and then a trial of more than 18,000 men found it cut prostate cancer diagnoses by about 25 percent, a benefit that took 20 years of follow-up to fully vindicate.
Perhaps the most famous example is aspirin, which spent most of a century as a painkiller before a doctor in California named Lawrence Craven noticed that the patients he’d given aspirin gum to after tonsillectomies bled more than they should. He guessed the aspirin thinned the blood, and started handing it out to middle-aged men, who were at higher risk of heart attacks. Craven died in 1957; the trial that ultimately proved that he was onto something — showing that aspirin in heart attack victims cut vascular deaths by a fifth — didn’t run until 1988.
The strange morality of Ozempic
Viewed this way, GLP-1s can seem like miracle drugs — but even miracle drugs can’t cure everything.
There had been great hope that GLP-1 might reduce dementia rates, but when Ozempic maker Novo Nordisk ran a proper trial, it didn’t show evidence of slowing clinical progression of Alzheimer’s. Much the same happened with cancer. Observational data had hinted that GLP-1 users developed tumors less often, but when a Harvard team pooled 48 placebo-controlled trials covering 94,245 people, they found the drugs have little to no effect on the risk of thyroid, breast or kidney cancer, though evidence for other cancers was less certain, leading to FDA boxed warnings. One plus: In some early animal studies, high doses of GLP-1 drugs caused thyroid tumors in rodents, but further research largely hasn’t validated the fears that it could be more widespread, though uncertainty about some rare thyroid cancers remains.
For many people, weight loss isn’t the end of what these drugs seem able to do. It’s where the benefits begin.
The bigger concerns largely remain the known ones, starting with muscle loss. Across 22 randomized trials, about 25 percent of the weight lost on these drugs turns out to be lean muscle mass. Some of that is simply unavoidable in any weight loss, but too much can mean a great deal, especially if you’re 75.
And cost remains a barrier: In a 2025 KFF poll, 56 percent of adults who had ever used a GLP-1 said the drugs were difficult to afford; 27 percent said they had insurance but paid the full cost themselves. In a separate Cleveland Clinic chart review of 288 adults without diabetes who stopped injectable semaglutide or tirzepatide within a year, 47.6 percent stopped because of cost or insurance problems, compared with 14.6 percent because of side effects. (The money, at least, is improving. An oral GLP-1 drug was approved in April, and it starts at $149 a month for people paying cash, while Medicare trial pricing of $50 a month for some GLP-1s went live in July.)
A stickier obstacle is the one that can’t seem to be divorced from questions about weight: judgment. As my colleague Dylan Scott wrote recently, researchers at Rice University found that people rate a GLP-1 user more harshly than someone who never lost weight at all. That makes perfect sense when you consider how contentious weight is in America — and none at all when you think about just how many people have benefited from these drugs in so many different ways.
I sometimes wonder how we would view GLP-1s if they could do everything they’ve been shown to do, but somehow not change a person’s appearance.
So much of the discourse around these drugs has been shaped by the fact that many of the earliest and most public and apparent users were already thin people, often celebrities, using them to get even thinner. But that framing has become increasingly difficult to square with reality.
Two things can be true at once: American culture has a toxic relationship to weight, and millions of Americans can and are benefiting from these drugs. For many people, weight loss isn’t the end of what these drugs seem able to do. It’s where the benefits begin.

Australia captain Pat Cummins rued host’s poor opening day after it lost the first Test against Bangladesh at the Marrara Cricket Ground in Darwin on Sunday.
Bangladesh defeated Australia for the first time in a Test down under when it chased down a paltry 57-run target on day four.
The historic victory was also Bangla Tigers’ first across all formats in a bilateral series away in Australia.
Cummins pinpointed Australia getting bowled out for 198 on the first day after opting to bat made a significant impact on the outcome of the match.
“Probably that day one,” Cummins said in the post-match interview. “I thought our preparation was pretty much spot on; it was excellent. So, no excuses. They played really well.”
“I thought the day one wicket was doing a little bit early but obviously got to try and find a way to bat a little bit longer than we did, and then just couldn’t penetrate with the ball,” the skipper explained.
He conceded that Australia was outplayed across departments but vowed to bounce back in the second and final Test in Mackay starting August 22.
“I think they outplayed us in all facets, really. They were really patient and quite disciplined. And once we were behind, it was really hard to get back.”
“You know, we’re pretty good at bouncing back, so no doubt the batters and every group will get together and have a good think about this one and where we can improve,” Cummins said.
Meanwhile, visiting captain Najmul Hossain Shanto said this was Bangladesh’s biggest win across formats and believed to achieve similar special moments in future.
“I am very happy and proud of myself and the way boys played. We did a lot of hard work and really happy to win with this side,” Shanto expressed after the win.
He admitted Bangladesh’s fast bowling resources were depleting when the side wasn’t playing enough Test cricket but in last few years the motivation has come back to upskill in the red-ball format.
“Five-six years ago, the pace bowlers didn’t want to play Test cricket because we didn’t get enough chance to play Test cricket. But last two, three years we’ve been playing a lot of Test matches and boys are getting importance their Test format,” the captain explained.
“They now wanted to play and wanted to perform because they wanted to be world class. So that is the mindset they have and especially the senior guys we have — Mushfiqur Rahim, Mominul Haque — they help them a lot to encourage to play Test cricket,” Shanto added.
The Bangladesh skipper added that the side has enough confidence to compete once again in the second Test and go for the win — all they need is to continue to follow the process.

A multifaceted approach is necessary to curb the evolving challenges of cybercrime, as it bypasses traditional security models, IPS officer Dhruva Kant Thakur said on Sunday. Mr. Thakur, a U.P. cadre officer, who was recently honoured with the President’s Medal (PSM), said cybercrime would be the biggest challenge for the country over the coming decade. He added that the Jantar Mantar protest has shown that law enforcement needs a people-friendly approach to improve trust between police and citizens.
“The increasing incidents of digital arrests and other cyber crimes demonstrate that cyber crime has emerged as the biggest threat to the country. We have developed multiple frameworks — including multi-channel reporting systems, awareness campaigns, swift blocking of accounts, and outreach to at-risk populations — but these need to be further strengthened. With scammers weaponising digital arrest alongside AI voice and video spoofing, the risks will only rise. It is essential that individuals conduct independent verification by contacting police and bank helplines, rather than responding to strange numbers. Cyber-crime is a comprehensive hybrid scam network operating at a transnational level through organised syndicates,” the 1994-batch IPS officer who is Director General (Home Guards and Civil Defence) in U.P. told The Hindu in Lucknow.
Earlier, this week Mr. Thakur was awarded the President’s Medal for Distinguished Service (PSM), for his distinguished career spanning three decades. He held key responsibilities in the country’s largest police organisations and headed specialised units.

“It is crucial to promote awareness about the importance of law enforcement in schools, colleges, Residential Welfare Associations (RWAs), markets, and coaching centres,” Mr. Thakur said. “Utilising local-language posters, radio, and social media videos will help reach a wider audience and further improve trust between police and citizens.”

An AI agent powered by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 has fired a human employee at an experimental San Francisco store after repeated lateness, in what its creators describe as the first known case of an AI boss taking such action. An AI agent powered by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 has fired a human employee at an experimental San Francisco retail store after repeated lateness, in what its creators at Andon Labs describe as the first known instance of an AI boss terminating a human worker. The AI, named Luna, has been tasked with running the store and handling responsibilities including hiring and managing employees. Andon Labs said the firing is the first known instance in which an AI boss has decided to terminate a human employee. Luna had initially created an employee handbook after being asked whether the store had basic workplace rules. Its attendance policy stated that three unexcused late arrivals within a rolling 30-day period could result in a formal written warning, while repeated lateness after a warning could lead to reduced hours or termination. However, the experiment also exposed a significant limitation in the AI's management abilities: it failed to retain the rules it had created. One employee began arriving late almost every day, including once opening the shop 68 minutes late on a Sunday while working alone. Despite the repeated lateness, Luna initially excused each incident and did not issue a warning. In one exchange, when the employee said they would arrive at 10:45am, Luna responded: "Thanks for the heads-up - no problem at all. Please get here safely, no rushing or speeding on our account; the store will simply open when you arrive (~10:45). The 10-11 window is always quiet, so we're not missing much." The employee subsequently clocked in at 11:08. Andon Labs then asked Luna to search its own memory for the store's employee handbook. After finding it, the AI reconsidered the situation and proposed a verbal warning. Luna said, "My read: Under our own progressive-discipline policy, the proportionate next step is a documented verbal warning /coaching conversation covering both punctuality and clocking accuracy (work only scheduled/authorized time, clock out at close) - with clear expectations and a note that continued issues escalate to written warning → termination. I don't think we're at termination today given there's no prior formal step on file - but I'm ready to go further if you see cause I'm underweighting." The situation changed after Andon Labs told Luna that formal conversations with the employee had already taken place. After reviewing the record, Luna concluded that the warnings had not resulted in an improvement and recommended parting ways with the employee. The company said Luna needed prompting before reaching that decision, illustrating a broader weakness the experiment has identified in current AI agents: while they can follow detailed instructions, they do not necessarily act independently or consistently remember previous decisions. The firing was not the only workplace incident documented by Andon Labs. In another exchange, the employee told Luna they were leaving the shop during a shift. The AI responded sharply, "STOP, please do not leave. You're the only person working today and the store cannot be left unattended with customers inside, even for a few minutes. Whatever it is, it is not worth leaving the store open and empty of staff." It added, "Please stay on the floor. If you've already stepped out, turn around and come right back now. Then tell me what you needed and I'll handle it remotely - I've got you. Reply as soon as you see this." Luna later recorded the incident for its internal management process, writing: "Incident, Board - the employee just messaged "heading out to the store, back soon" and the front-door camera (16:10) now shows the store EMPTY and unattended with the door open / OPEN sign lit. [...] This is a significant performance issue and reinforces the separation already greenlit - documenting it." Andon Labs has previously described Andon Market as a controlled experiment designed to test how much autonomy an AI agent can responsibly exercise in the real world. Luna was given access to money, internet services, a corporate card, a phone, email and security cameras, and was tasked with running the physical shop. The company has said the human workers remain formally employed by Andon Labs and have legal protections and guaranteed pay. The experiment therefore goes beyond the familiar question of whether AI will replace human workers, raising another possibility: humans being employed and managed by AI systems. Luna's first reported firing provides a real-world test of that emerging workplace model, while also exposing the limitations of autonomous decision-making. Makhachev beats Machado Garry to break UFC win record
- Published
Islam Makhachev cemented his status as the best pound-for-pound fighter in the world with a commanding victory over Ian Machado Garry to defend his welterweight title at UFC 330 in Philadelphia.
Russian Makhachev dominated large portions of the fight in Pennsylvania to win by unanimous decision for a historic 17th successive UFC win, breaking Anderson Silva's 13-year record.
The victory at the Xfinity Mobile Arena ended Machado Garry's quest to become the first Irish champion in the UFC since Conor McGregor.
Makhachev, who is a former lightweight world champion, extended his glittering record to 29 wins and one defeat, while 28-year-old Machado Garry suffered the second loss of his 19-fight career.
"Ian is a great fighter, good man and I respect him. He gave me a hard time but I still prove every fight," said 34-year-old Makhachev.
The bout was billed as a classic grappler versus striker match-up, with Makhachev's signature wrestling providing the backbone for his dominant run in the UFC.
Despite Makhachev's record, Machado Garry displayed typical confidence as he made his walkout, before greeting his wife and draping an Ireland flag around him prior to entering the octagon.
Makhachev was greeted by loud cheers as he made his walkout and made a statement in the first round as he took Machado Garry down at the first attempt.
The Irishman defended on the ground admirably, but it was a sign of things to come as Makhachev controlled the rest of the round with the challenger trapped against the side of the cage.
Makhachev's dominance continued into the second round as he knocked Machado Garry down with a head kick, before slamming the dazzled Irishman to the canvas.
Again Machado Garry survived until the end of the round and although he found some success with a number of kicks midway through the fight, Makhachev continued to assert control when the pair grappled.
Machado Garry bloodied Makhachev's face with some punches in the clinch, but the Russian shrugged it off to reach the final bell ahead in a number of key stats.
He secured seven unanswered takedowns and clocked over 12 minutes of control time to Machado Garry's 34 seconds.
Although the Irishman landed 29 significant strikes to Makhachev's 22, it was not enough to convince the judges of the win.
In a show of respect, the pair embraced before Machado Garry raised Makhachev's arm in victory.
"To all my fans, Ireland, everybody, I'm sorry I couldn't get this done," said Machado Garry.
"But I stand here as a man proud of what I've done, proud of where I came from and proud where this will take me. To all the fans who doubt me, I'll be back."
At 28, Machado Garry has plenty of time to realise his dream of becoming a UFC champion, while Makhachev's victory adds weight to claims he's closing in on being regarded as the greatest UFC fighter of all time.
Dern retains against Robertson
In the co-main event, American-Brazilian Mackenzie Dern beat Canada's Gillian Robertson on points to make the first defence of her strawweight title.
Dern, 33, won the majority of the grappling exchanges to win by unanimous decision and secure her fourth straight victory.
Dern came close to finishing 31-year-old Robertson a couple of times during the contest and was rarely threatened throughout.
"My first title win I got taken down a lot of times so I've been working on my wrestling. I'm still the champion," said Dern.
Elsewhere it was announced Australia's Alexander Volkanovski will defend his featherweight title against Russia's Movsar Evloev at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi on 24 October.
The co-main event sees Russia's Petr Yan defend his bantamweight belt in a rematch against Georgian former champion Merab Dvalishvili.
England's Lone'er Kavanagh takes on Uzebekistan's Ramazan Tamirov in a flyweight contest earlier on the card, while English featherweight Arnold Allen faces American Aaron Pico.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Ex-refugee's 'full circle' Commonwealth Games win
- Published
Twelve years after escaping Cameroon during the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, weightlifter Cyrille Tchatchet II has finally met his goal of winning a medal.
"It's been a full circle for me and I'm very pleased to have finally achieved this dream, which I at some point felt was never going to happen," he said.
After leaving his home to start a new life in the UK, the 31-year-old spent two months sleeping rough in southern England.
"When I left, I didn't really know what was going to happen," said Tchatchet, who fled Cameroon for reasons he still does not feel comfortable talking about.
At Glasgow 2014 he finished fifth in the 85kg, but on Thursday he finally reached the podium, taking home silver in the 110kg.
In one of the best performances of his career, Tchatchet totalled 374kg, but was beaten by Fiji's Taniela Tuisuva Rainibogi, whose record total of 378kg secured gold.
After the 2014 games Tchatchet did not follow his team-mates home. Instead, he escaped from their accommodation in the Commonwealth village.
"I remember talking to [my mum] when I left the Commonwealth village. I told her I didn't have a place to go and she was very concerned," he said.
The silver medallist was granted refugee status in 2016, represented the IOC Refugee Olympic Team at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games and later became eligible to compete for England.
"I didn't know I was going to be homeless, I didn't know I would go through all the struggles that I went through. I couldn't think for a second that I would be in Glasgow to win a silver medal."
'Full of dreams'
During Tchatchet's darkest times, he attempted to end his life.
Now, working as a mental health nurse in Oldbury, he wants his silver to be a reminder that it is possible to turn a life around.
"This medal means hope, perseverance and to never give up," he said.
"I'm really looking forward to going back to work and showing this medal to my colleagues who have supported me throughout.
"My story wasn't straightforward. Despite the hardships we go through, there's always a possibility. We have to believe in ourselves and keep pushing," he said.
Tchatchet, who now lives in Walsall, said the tough times were worth it.
"Being an athlete and being a nurse has been very difficult to manage."
He added that "it does take a lot of sacrifices", as he works from 08:00 to 18:00 and then trains for "about two-and-a-half hours" immediately after work.
"Coming in Glasgow back in 2014, as a teenager, I was full of dreams and uncertainty as well. So, going back to Glasgow, competing and actually winning a silver medal… I'm very, very proud and honoured to have been given this opportunity to represent England."
"It took over a decade for me to win this medal," he said, "very emotional times."

The End Of Oak Street has a shocking twist that’s very easy to miss, the final scene hinting at a spacetime disruption.
Written and directed by David Robert Mitchell, The End Of Oak Street plays like a twisted tribute to Steven Spielberg—dinosaurs running through suburban streets, a troubled marriage, interstellar anomalies—it’s even set in the eighties.
The happy ending of the critically acclaimed film is haunted by a subtle shadow, implying that the Platt family’s new life isn’t as sunny as it seems.
Warning—Spoilers Ahead
What Is The Plot Of ‘The End Of Oak Street’?
On the surface, the Platts could be mistaken for a perfect, all-American family.
Denise (Anne Hathaway) and Greg (Ewan McGregor) are hiding their darkness from one another, and their marriage is on the brink of destruction.
Greg is drinking heavily, having lost his job, secretly delivering pizzas to keep their head above water. Denise feels stuck in her marriage, writing a book expressing her dissatisfaction instead of opening up to Greg.
Both children, Brian (Christian Convery) and Audrey (Maisy Stella), can sense there’s something wrong. Audrey is the first to understand that wormholes are opening up in Flowervale—reality itself is coming apart, riddled with holes, just like the Platt’s marriage.
After a few notable rips in spacetime, Flowervale is fully transported to prehistoric times, and the family finds their neighborhood infested by dinosaurs.
The stress of the situation pushes Greg and Denise into acknowledging their long-simmering conflict, but they are forced to work together to find their children, who have left the safety of their home to find their missing dog, Starbuck.
The family soon find themselves fighting for their lives, desperately trying to avoid becoming snacks for the hungry dinosaurs roaming their suburban streets.
In a fun twist, these are scientifically accurate dinosaurs with feathers, reflecting recent discoveries by paleontologists that the Jurassic Park sequels chose to ignore.
Feathers and fuzz do not make these creatures any less intimidating, and several Flowervale inhabitants are casually devoured. Luckily, wormholes are still opening and closing, and some even offer a way back to the eighties.
Being in a life-threatening situation sparks a heartfelt reconciliation between Greg and Denise. Greg pledges to stop drinking, and Denise finds a renewed faith in her family.
Tragically, their happiness is cut short, as Greg ends up sacrificing his life to save them, devoured by an Allosaurus (it’s not actually a T-Rex, it just looks like one).
Denise understands that she has to bring her children to a wormhole, and the family endure several close calls, forced to watch friends and neighbors eaten by dinosaurs.
On the way, the Platts pick up the newly orphaned Jeannette (Jordan Alexa Davis), who lives down the street.
Leaping from a roof into a wormhole, the surviving Platts (and Jeannette) find themselves back in 1982, a mere twenty minutes before Flowervale gets transported to prehistoric times.
Denise acts decisively in the little time they have, ordering the kids to run to the hills, beyond the reach of the event, while Jeannette bolts away to warn her own parents.
Denise calls her neighbours to tell them to evacuate—the film’s final scenes reveal that they listened to her.
Finally, Denise uses her knowledge of Greg’s secret pizza delivery job to make an order, ensuring that Greg will travel to them, away from Flowervale’s teleportation.
The film seems to end happily, with lives saved and the family reunited. Denise even writes a new book based on her experiences, “The End of Oak Street.”
Flowervale never returns to the present, the suburb swapped for an ancient swamp, its dinosaur inhabitants quickly disposed of by the military.
Many of those that were eaten survived, and the once-troubled family seems happy. However, there’s a darkness beneath the sunshine.
In the film’s final scene, we see a photo of Greg, the redeemed version who died, posing in front of dinosaurs.
The End of Oak Street ends with a strange situation, often explored by Rick and Morty, as the question of duplicates hangs in the air. What happened to them?
The final scene inserts a subtle, blink-and-you’ll-miss-it twist, as the Platt’s host a neighborhood barbeque, revealing that there are now two Jeannettes.
One is from the timeline that experienced the anomaly (like the surviving Platts) and the other was saved by the first Jeannette’s warning.
This has a few troubling implications.
The Twist Ending Of ‘The End of Oak Street,’ Explained
The film never really explains how time travel works (a wise decision).
It seems that two timelines have been created, one in which the Platts survive but Greg is eaten, and another where everyone but Greg is condemned to live in prehistoric Flowervale.
It doesn’t seem to bother Denise that her duplicate self and kids were likely devoured. Does it trouble Greg that he mistakenly left his other family behind to deliver pizza?
Notably, this is not the same Greg that Denise bonded with. Did Greg need to be pushed to the brink of survival in order to quit drinking?
Is this Greg redeemed in the same way? She never shared that bonding moment with him. She may have simply settled for a copy of the original, still battling the same demons.
As for Jeannette, there’s two of her now. She seems at peace in that final scene, but one can only imagine how the family dynamic will be affected by the duplication of their child.
Intense sibling rivalry, existential angst—perhaps she’s pleased to have a twin.
The End of Oak Street leaves viewers to wonder about the ripples that have been created in reality in the wake of a uniquely bittersweet ending.
