Punjab/Srinagar, Aug 16: Three persons, including two residents of Srinagar, were killed while three others sustained injuries in a road accident in Bhogpur area of Jalandhar, Punjab, officials said.
Officials told news agency JKNS that, the accident occurred when a speeding Maruti Fronx collided with a roadside vendor before crashing into a tree, resulting in multiple casualties.
The roadside vendor, a Punjab resident, also died in the accident.
Officials said three other occupants of the vehicle, all residents of Srinagar, sustained injuries in the accident and were shifted to a nearby hospital for treatment.
Further details regarding the condition of the injured and circumstances leading to the accident are awaited.

Srinagar, Aug 16: Jammu and Kashmir BJP workers protested outside the Congress office here on Sunday over opposition party leader Sonia Gandhi allegedly objecting to the singing of the full version of "Vande Mataram" at an Independence Day event in Delhi.
Carrying BJP flags, the protesters raised slogans against Sonia Gandhi and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi. They also burnt effigies of the Congress leaders.
They were prevented from reaching the main gate of the Congress office by police personnel, who were deployed in numbers to maintain law and order.
The BJP on Saturday accused Sonia Gandhi of objecting to the singing of the full version of "Vande Mataram" at the Independence Day function at the Congress headquarters in Delhi.
The Congress, however, denied the charge, asserting that she was only asking for a chair for party chief Mallikarjun Kharge as he had been standing for a while.
Addressing a rally in Rajasthan's Chittorgarh on Sunday, Union Home Minister Amit Shah demanded that the Congress apologise to the people and Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, who wrote "Vande Mataram", for insulting the national song.

Gaza genocide: How Israel made horror a ritual of daily life
Life under genocide has its familiar daily rituals. A discerning eye detects latent horrors in the scenes that unfold in succession across screens.
Elsewhere, the scene itself disappears beneath rubble, entombing the bodies of thousands of Palestinians whose breath was cut off below, while their families remain unable to retrieve them.
In the Gaza Strip, modern brutality has made its terrible presence felt through atrocity after atrocity, in full view of the entire world.
These horrors were caused not by a natural disaster, but by the tsunami of modern genocide carried out by Israel using American and western weapons, munitions and technologies.
Genocide has taken possession of the defining features of everyday life in all their details, leaving its tragic imprint on the population in every sphere.

The fragments that follow are drawn from that reality.
The children of Gaza know no daily life without a menacing sound accompanying them day and night, without pause. This has been the case almost since the moment they first opened their eyes to the world.
Sonic terror
The sound that accompanies Gaza day and night is the buzzing of Israeli military drones, which circle overhead in swarms and tirelessly monitor every part of the Gaza Strip around the clock.
These drones acquired their local name from their disturbing acoustic effect: residents call them "zanana", an Arabic coinage derived from the buzzing sound they emit.
The world has come to know that there is no shelter in Gaza, and nowhere within it that is safe
Young children besieged in this narrow strip overlooking the flank of the Mediterranean Sea may find it difficult to imagine a world free of the noise, a noise that entrenches within them a constant sense of threat, of bombardment that may come at any moment.
In this way, the occupation seizes control of the soundscape and sends its inhabitants a message: they are being watched relentlessly and the next projectile may strike one of them here or there, killing or wounding that person together with everyone nearby.
This thunderous hovering is a mixture of auditory domination, sonic terror and psychological intimidation.
Every Palestinian in Gaza has personal experience of tragedies associated with these military drones in their various forms, through witnessing firsthand the bombardments that took the lives of relatives, neighbours and loved ones, whose bodies were torn apart while their memories remained.
Air strikes were unknown before the modern age. They began to develop during the First World War and gave rise to a preventive practice: warning sirens were sounded so people could take cover and seek refuge in shelters prepared for that purpose.
The genocidal campaign targeting the Palestinian people in Gaza since October 2023 has employed the most advanced instruments of warfare of its time, including squadrons of American-made warplanes and drones sharing the work of aerial bombardment.
Yet not a single warning siren has sounded in Gaza.
This is not the result of negligence or malfunction. The very idea of warning sirens has become absurd as bombardment has continued without interruption, making any warning a cruel joke.
More importantly, there is no shelter for residents to flee to, no possibility of protection from the exploding horrors falling from the sky.
The crowding of civilians into an underground shelter would itself pose a grave risk to their lives. Heavy munitions penetrate deep below the surface and leave vast craters, as has been seen in the heart of residential neighbourhoods, in refugee camps, around hospitals and near places of worship.
The primitive tools available cannot retrieve those trapped beneath the rubble.
The world has come to know that there is no shelter in Gaza, and nowhere within it that is safe.
Even United Nations schools in which displaced families sought refuge were turned into traps for repeated mass killings. The same was true of Muslim and Christian places of worship, which were crushed. Not even historic monasteries were spared.
Hospitals were reduced to ruins, ambulance crews were massacred, Red Cross facilities were not spared, and seven World Central Kitchen aid workers were killed when their convoy was struck in Deir al-Balah on 1 April 2024.
Art of survival
Daily life in Gaza means enduring without water taps and without any guaranteed, safe opportunity to quench one's thirst.
At the outset, the occupation army destroyed Gaza's water networks. On 9 October 2023, then Defence Minister Yoav Gallant announced a "complete siege" of the strip. Water supplies to its more than 2 million people were cut off.
With most homes destroyed and civilian infrastructure devastated, the ordinary household tap has almost disappeared. Only a few water points remain, where residents crowd to fill containers by rudimentary means. What once took seconds at a tap has become a prolonged daily journey, one with no guarantee of a safe return.
Follow Middle East Eye's live coverage of Israel's genocide in Gaza
Israeli strikes have repeatedly targeted Palestinian men and women of every age, including children, during their march of torment in search of water.
Palestinian families have had to divide these daily tasks among their members: one person must fetch whatever water can be found; others carry empty vessels in the hope of filling them with scarce food that falls far short of the nutritional needs of children and adults alike; still others endure the hardship of searching for flour and other necessities of life.
They may find nothing. They may return wounded by Israeli bullets, or with bodies reduced to pieces by the projectiles of what calls itself "the most moral army in the world".
When obtaining water requires such threatening and arduous effort, attempting to meet ordinary human needs, such as relieving oneself or bathing, must take place under degrading conditions, particularly for women and girls.
Palestinian women in Gaza deserve recognition for their mastery of the art of survival under these crushing circumstances.
They have had to take the lead in moving their families from the ruins of destroyed homes to an open space by the roadside or on the sands of the beach. They help erect tents from whatever materials are available, in a form of forced recycling.
In this punishing mode of life, everything our age knows about perfumes, cosmetics and skincare products must be forgotten. Women and girls must adapt to a reality in which even basic necessities like feminine hygiene supplies and ordinary toilets are unavailable.
Moreover, women of all ages bear an immense burden in circumstances where privacy has been reduced to an absolute minimum.
The kitchen as ordinary families know it has vanished entirely. Whatever food is available must be cooked over a stove made of clay or stone, which mothers are forced to fuel by burning materials harmful to health and the environment.
This method may itself ignite fires that consume the crowded tents of displaced families.
When a person in Gaza speaks, we may notice things they would not ordinarily disclose. They may have permanently lost some of their teeth, like vast numbers of residents upon whom the genocide has left its mark in this respect as well.
This occurred after the occupation army crushed dental clinics throughout the strip and destroyed, burned or put out of service hospitals that had previously treated dental patients. It also inflicted heavy casualties among medical personnel.
For a prolonged period, residents suffered under a ban on the entry of medicines, therapeutic supplies and medical equipment.
Simply obtaining toothpaste and a toothbrush from the market became an unattainable luxury.
This wretched reality has caused a collective deterioration in dental health, affecting every generation. This society of crumbling teeth is an eloquent image of the enforced deprivation imposed upon a population in a territory where a suffocating siege strangles daily life, stripping teeth from the pale faces of its people and, at times, leaving them with no food worth chewing.
Barefoot witnesses
The Israeli occupation army has forced most of the Gaza Strip's population into repeated displacement from one area to another, through sudden expulsion orders or intensified attacks.
Time and time again, residents have had to surge along rough roads torn up by bulldozers, or move between heaps of rubble and refuse towards some destination within the strip, carrying their belongings and the materials needed for rudimentary camping.
No sooner do they settle there than the army may compel them to flee once again towards another destination, and so the cycle continues.
Palestinians, young and old, have experienced displacement in conflicting directions: on foot, aboard carts pulled by horses or donkeys, or in whatever vehicles remain.
Among the scenes witnessed by the world were displaced people walking in worn-out sandals, or even barefoot, after their shoes had disintegrated during the long journey and no suitable replacements could be found.
Residents are forced to patch their shoes and repair frayed sandals.
As the occupation authorities have prevented the entry of the population's many basic necessities, acquiring a new pair of shoes, or even a simple pair of sandals, has become an unattainable aspiration for many.
The cruelty of everyday life in Gaza is revealed in many such scenes: children and adults lacking usable shoes as they endure long marches along the routes of displacement. Yet in this merciless reality, this is far from their greatest concern.
One of the most horrifying truths is that there is scarcely a child in Gaza who has not repeatedly seen torn human remains.
Some of those remains may belong to people the child knew well: their family members, neighbours or friends. Some of these fragments remain lodged in children's minds. They may come to regard life stained with blood and human remains as something ordinary in this particular part of the world.
A child in this genocide is not merely a witness to what is taking place but a direct victim, as confirmed by the terrifying statistical indicators documented in specialised UN reports.
A child who spends a prolonged period beneath the rubble does not emerge unscathed.
Suspended between life and death, watching the breath of those around them extinguished in utter darkness, the child nearly loses all hope of emerging alive - until a hand finally reaches down and, with immense difficulty, pulls them back to the surface of life.
In this new life, the child will find no home in which to live. They may be almost the only member of their family left alive.
Yet their compounded tragedy will offer no opportunity to contemplate all that has happened, because the moving machinery of genocide may crush them at any moment.
What have the horrors of genocide left of the conventions intended to protect childhood, in a world that has allowed all this visible brutality against Palestinian children to continue year after year, its atrocities broadcast live, without the world restraining them?

US missionary released following kidnap in Niger, Christian group says
- Published
An American missionary has been released after spending more than nine months in captivity, the international Christian organisation he worked for has said.
Kevin Rideout - who was kidnapped outside his home in Niger's capital Niamey last year - was "in good health in the care of US officials", SIM International said in a statement on Friday.
The New York Times, which first reported Rideout's release, cited unnamed US officials saying that he was now in FBI custody, though details of how he was released, as well as who he had been held by, remained unclear.
There had been concerns that Rideout had been taken by militants, who have increasingly used violence and abductions as tactics.
Rideout's kidnapping in October was carried out by three armed men who took him to the western Tillaberi region, a location known as a hotbed of militant activity, news agency Reuters reported, citing diplomatic sources.
It was feared he may have been taken there by militants belonging to groups like Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda affiliate which has been linked to several attacks in the region.
Islamist militant groups operating from neighbouring Nigeria, Mali and Burkina Faso have plagued Niger for years, targeting both civilians and the military.
The region has seen a wave of violence as jihadists have been fighting government security forces as well as Western and other allied troops.
Within days of Rideout's kidnapping, the US warned its citizens against travelling to Niger due to an "increased risk of terrorism, crime and civil unrest".
The New York Times reported that Rideout, who is also a pilot, may have been transferred to another group prior to his release.
SIM International said he would soon be reunited with his wife, their children and his extended family.
Rideout had been working in Niger as a Christian missionary for 19 years and was also a pilot for SIM International, which operates in more than 70 countries.
The organisation said Rideout's release was "incredibly good news" after months of uncertainty about his wellbeing.
"Krista and the rest of Kevin's family are profoundly grateful for the prayers offered on their behalf by people around the world throughout his captivity," it said.
It added that the family had requested privacy while they "reconnect after this time apart".
Rideout's release comes as several countries in West Africa and the Sahel have been struggling with terror attacks.
Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso and Nigeria have been dealing with violence that has been going on for more than a decade - resulting in the loss of thousands of lives and causing regional destabilisation.
The region has also experienced a wave of military takeovers, with a string of democratic governments overthrown.

‘Sent parents to heaven’: Kerala man arrested for stabbing parents; had history of drug, alcohol abuse
Ajeesh, was arrested after sending a video of the attack to a relative. Police said he had a history of drug abuse and claimed to have acted on a divine call.

Police arrested Ajeesh after he allegedly killed his father, Antony, 59, and mother, Valsamma, 55, at their residence in Ezhukumvayal around 9.30pm on Friday.

It’s the depths of summer. It’s still stultifyingly, dangerously hot. Going outside is a fool’s game unless you have 500 SPF sunblock and a personal AC unit. Be sensible: Stay inside and enjoy some of the best movies currently streaming instead.
August’s offerings include the return of Avatar: The Last Airbender on Paramount+, with a brand new adventure returning to the cast of the fan-favorite animated series as adults and struggling with newfound responsibilities. The same theme carries over to Heartstopper Forever on Netflix, where teen romance is dashed against the rocks of looming adulthood.
Elsewhere, there’s a double helping of liminal space creepiness from Japan, with the exceptional live action horror Exit 8 on Shudder, and the action epic Demon Slayer The Movie: Infinity Castle—one of the most successful animated movies in Japanese history—on Crunchyroll. And, if you’d rather not have to think in this heat, enjoy an action-packed pairing of Mortal Kombat 2 and Masters of the Universe, two films that aren’t so much “so bad they’re good”, as they are “turn brain off now for fun time.”
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender
Water. Earth. Fire. Air. Only the Avatar is master of all four elements—but Aang, the latest inheritor of the mantle, vanished when he was most needed. Frozen in suspended animation for decades, Aang was awakened by waterbender Katara and her warrior brother Sokka. Joined by earthbender Toph, and firebending enemy-turned-ally Zuko, Team Avatar went on to save the world. Now, as adults, they face an even more daunting task: rebuilding it. Yet with Aang the last living airbender, the world remains out of balance—until he discovers Tagah, an ancient airbender suspended as he once was. No longer alone, the group set out to find an ancient artifact belonging to a forgotten Avatar, in the hope it can restore airbending to the world. But why was Tagah frozen centuries ago, and can he be trusted now?
A direct sequel to the brilliant and beloved 2005 Nickelodeon animated series, this feature length adventure is a more mature outing, growing up with its original audience, and delivering some of the most breathtaking animation you’ll see all year. Sadly robbed of a wide theatrical release—and victim of a notorious leak of the full film—Avatar Aang still shines on the small screen.
Heartstopper Forever
One of the most successful comic book adaptations in years, Alice Oseman’s Heartstopper reaches its long-awaited conclusion with a final movie. Fans have followed the love story of Nick (Kit Connor) and Charlie (Joe Locke) through high school, battling early doubts, coming-out confusion, and mental health struggles along the way. Yet as Nick embarks for university, the pair are forced to ask whether their relationship can survive—especially when friends Elle (Yasmin Finney) and Tao (William Gao) are choosing to break up after graduation. A beautiful ode to young love and queer joy, Heartstopper Forever fizzes with emotion. Grab tissues.
Mortal Kombat II
It’s not big (only $129 million at the box office) and it’s not clever (superpowered martial artists stave off an interdimensional invasion via the fine diplomatic art of punching) but Mortal Kombat II is a hell of a lot of fun. Picking up from the stinger of 2021’s cinematic reboot of the long-running fighting game series, the focus switches to washed-up action movie star Johnny Cage (Karl Urban), who must prove he has what it takes to stand as one of Earthrealm’s defenders. Diving into some of the weirder fantasy elements of the source material, director Simon McQuoid delivers some incredible action set pieces, with fight scenes that deliver all the brutality fans expect, and a surprisingly sharp comedic edge throughout.
Masters of the Universe
When his home of Eternia was invaded, Prince Adam (Nicholas Galatzine) was sent to Earth for his own protection. Now, he’s a weirdo stuck in a dead-end corporate job who won’t stop talking about the fantasy world he came from—until his old friend Teela (Camila Mendes) tracks him down to take him home and fight off the forces of Skeletor.
As yet another go at bringing the 40-plus-year-old toyline-slash-cartoon advert for the toy line to the big screen, Masters of the Universe was probably doomed from the start. Yet director Travis Knight (Bumblebee, aka the only good live action Transformers movie) completely understood the assignment, delivering a wildly imaginative, colorful, and just-the-right-level-of-stupid adventure that embraces and pokes fun at its source material in equal measure. It’s charming, funny—shout out to Idris Elba as drunken, derelict mentor Man-at-Arms and Kristen Wiig as the voice of sardonic robot Roboto—and undeniably camp, and should tickle older fans’ nostalgia centers as much as it entertains their own little warriors.
Exit 8
A lost man (Kazunari Ninomiya) wanders through the stark white corridors of Tokyo’s subway system, searching for Exit 8. He’s trapped, not because of the labyrinthine layout of one of the world’s busiest transit systems, but because any wrong move sends him back to Exit 0. The only way out is to avoid “anomalies,” which may be as subtle as a changed poster in the looping tunnels, or blood flooding down from the ceiling—and each loop, the anomalies change, making escape feel maddeningly impossible.
Director Genki Kawamura brings the cult indie video game to life in this masterful slice of Japanese horror cinema, expanding on its claustrophobic sense of dread with a much-needed exploration of who the Lost Man is and why he’s caught in the unsettling liminal underworld. If you’re a fan of Backrooms, you owe it to yourself to watch Exit 8.
Spider-Man MCU Trilogy
With Spider-Man: Brand New Day riding high in theaters, it’s the perfect time to dive back into Tom Holland’s first quasi-trilogy as the webbed wonder. After debuting in Civil War (also on Disney+), Holland’s Peter Parker establishes his heroic bona fides facing the Vulture (Michael Keaton) in Homecoming, goes on a world tour and fights Mysterio (Jake Gyllenhaal) in Far From Home, and battles a multiverse of menaces in No Way Home—luckily with some assistance from previous cinematic Spider-Men Peter Parker (Tobey Maguire) and Peter Parker (Andrew Garfield). The real success of Holland’s films isn’t in the superpowered theatricality, but the way they bring Peter’s messy personal life straight from the comics to the screen, focusing as much on his supporting cast—chiefly love interest MJ (Zendaya), best friend Ned (Jacob Batalon), and Aunt May (Marisa Tomei)—as on his superheroic adventures.
The Blackening
When a group of Black college friends hold a reunion for Juneteenth, the vibe seems off. They’re meeting at a cabin in the woods for a start, which is a little too close to horror movie territory for anyone’s liking. Such genre-savviness begins to pay off when they discover a suspicious board game in the basement and find themselves playing by a serial killer’s twisted rules—starting with determining the “Blackest” member of the group to sacrifice.
With a cast of comedy greats including X Mayo, Jermaine Fowler, and Jay Pharoah, The Blackening is a self-aware and smartly satirical twist on horror movie conventions that brilliantly plays on its tongue-in-cheek tagline, “We can’t all die first.”
Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba—Infinity Castle
Based on the manga by Koyoharu Gotouge, Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba is set in an alternate Taishō era Japan where a corps of specially trained warriors hunt down ferocious demons. Infinity Castle follows on directly from the fourth season of the television anime series, which is also on Crunchyroll for anyone who cares to do the homework, but this full-length movie is a thrill ride even if you’re jumping in blind.
After narrowly surviving an attack by the Demon Slayers, Muzan—progenitor demon and all-around big bad—traps the heroes in his stronghold, the ever-shifting dimensional prison of the Infinity Castle. Cue one epic battle royale as the Demon Slayer Corps fights their way to freedom, navigating the unpredictable landscape and seeing off scores of powerful foes—including a rematch between series lead Tanjiro Kamado (Natsuki Hanae in Japanese, Zach Aguilar in English) and powerful demon rival Akaza. The first in a planned trilogy set to cap the entire Demon Slayer saga, Infinity Castle is a visually stunning supernatural adventure.
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
Set decades after 2017’s War for the Planet of the Apes (but still a long way out from Charlton Heston screaming at the Statue of Liberty in the 1968 original), Kingdom opens with society’s tables having fully turned. Evolved apes rule, while most humans have been reduced to feral, nonverbal states. When Noa (Owen Teague), a young falconer from a chimpanzee clan, encounters an unusually intelligent human, Mae (Freya Allen), the unlikely pair are drawn into the orbit of Proximus Caesar (Kevin Durand), a power-hungry ape-king aiming to open a lost vault of human technology.
While it all leads to an unusually explosive conflict for a world that’s reverted to blood and bone barbarism, the film packs in a surprisingly deep examination of humanity’s relationship with the world around us. It’s also the best the series has ever looked, with incredible effects work and striking location shoots in Australia creating a fully believable post-apocalyptic world. Newly arrived on Prime Video, Kingdom may be the fourth installment in the Planet of the Apes reboot-prequel series, but as a standalone entry, it makes for a strong entry point.

Amazon has acquired a massive off-grid power plant being built in Texas for one of its data centers that could be one of the biggest sources of greenhouse gas emissions in the US.
But size isn’t the only reason its climate toll will be so high. The plant will rely on a much less efficient set of gas turbines than regular power plants use; these kinds of turbines are also increasingly being put to use at other data center projects around the US. That could have big implications for the environmental impact of artificial intelligence—and the future of the US grid.
Amazon’s Texas power plant is permitted to emit up to 33 million tons of greenhouse gases a year. The project will rely solely on simple cycle turbines, which mix fuel and air in a combustion chamber to create energy, letting off a significant amount of waste heat in the process. Combined cycle units, which are generally used at on-grid power plants, add an additional steam turbine component to capture the waste heat and turn it into more energy. That means they release fewer emissions for the same amount of energy.
Permitted emissions on natural gas plants are usually much higher than their actual emissions. But even if Amazon’s facility emits half of what’s on the permit each year, it would still create more greenhouse gas pollution than 78 average-sized natural gas plants, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.
The Texas plant provides “on-site generation that won't raise electricity costs for Texas families,” Amazon spokesperson Heather Callahan writes in an email to WIRED, adding that the site would also have solar and battery storage and that the company is still committed to reaching net-zero emissions by 2040.
Using simple-cycle turbines is becoming an increasingly common practice for data center power developers looking for flexible power that’s quick to install. At least three power plants being developed in Ohio by oil and gas company Williams for Meta will also rely on simple cycle units, according to permit applications. In Abilene, Texas, Crusoe is building a power plant on its Stargate campus to power a Microsoft data center with 39 simple-cycle turbines. The permit application for Google’s Goodnight data center at another Texas site being developed by Crusoe describes relying on 20 simple-cycle turbines. And both xAI’s Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 data centers in Memphis are being powered by dozens of simple cycle turbines. All of them are permitted to release millions of tons of greenhouse gases. (Both Williams and Crusoe tell WIRED in an email that their gas plants comply with local and national regulations and are outfitted with emissions control technology.)
Britt Burt, a senior vice president at Industrial Info Resources, an energy market intelligence firm, says that he didn’t expect data center developers to lean so heavily on simple cycle turbines for power.
“It’s not the most efficient way to use a gas turbine,” he says.
For companies racing to get data centers online, though, it’s a lot quicker—and cheaper—to install a handful of simple-cycle turbines than wait for the additional equipment needed for combined-cycle units, especially given a yearslong backlog for turbine orders and associated parts.
“Right now, because of the way the supply chain is for turbines, they’re having to go with what they can get their hands on,” says Burt.
Then there’s the energy needs of data centers, especially those training AI models. Thanks to their fewer moving parts, simple cycle turbines can start up and shut down more rapidly than combined cycle units. That suits AI training, which requires big spikes of energy on demand. (In fact, those spikes are so big that many data center operators have reported turbines breaking thanks to the extreme stress of turning on and off.)
“If you have a highly fluctuating load, it's better to have 30 things that can individually turn on and off than to have one giant thing that doesn't like to be turned on and off,” says Stephen Lynch, a professor of mechanical engineering at Penn State and director of the school’s Center for Gas Turbine Research, Education, and Outreach.
Simple cycle turbines also generally don’t require water, which itself is an increasingly hot-button issue for communities near data centers. Burt estimates that a 250-megawatt combined-cycle plant could use about 75,000 gallons per hour. The permit application for the new Amazon plant specifically lists simple cycle technology’s lack of water use as an “environmental benefit.”
The federal government and a growing number of state governors across the political spectrum are encouraging data center power providers to bring or build their own energy to avoid raising consumer electric bills.
Some companies have promised to integrate their power plants with the grid eventually. Callahan, the Amazon spokesperson, said that the Texas plant is “designed to transition to grid-connected service as interconnection timelines allow.” Williams told WIRED earlier this month that it may consider the Ohio plants for interconnection in the future.
There are power plants designed with simple-cycle turbines, known as peaker plants, which are used to rapidly provide power to the grid when demand is high. But for now, the rapid construction of new islanded power plants with inefficient turbines—many of which are designed to last for decades—threatens to create a parallel fossil fuel grid that generates millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions.
If the AI bubble bursts or tech companies’ energy needs dip, though, it’s possible that the massive, inefficient gas plants could no longer have a purpose.
“We call that a stranded asset,” Burt says, chuckling.

Mumbai, Aug 16: The Maharashtra FDA has issued a show-cause notice to actors Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff over their advertisement for Vimal Elaichi, claiming it prima facie amounts to "indirect or surrogate" promotion of prohibited pan masala and tobacco-related products.
The use of the expression "VIMAL Elaichi" in the advertisement appeared to create an association with the Vimal Pan Masala brand and could mislead consumers while indirectly promoting the prohibited product, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said.
The issue was particularly serious because the advertisement used the same brand identity associated with Vimal Pan Masala, the FDA's Greater Mumbai division said in the notice issued on August 11, which described the three actors as brand endorsers and sought their response within 15 days.
Terming the notice a "final warning", it said the advertisement appeared prima facie to be a misleading advertisement relating to food and contrary to provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the regulations framed under it.
It also flagged possible violations concerning surrogate or indirect advertising under other laws and guidelines.
The FDA has directed the actors to immediately discontinue their participation in and endorsement of the Vimal Pan Masala/Elaichi advertisement and remove the promotional content from their official social media handles, websites and other digital platforms under their control.
It also directed them not to provide any further cooperation or assistance in the broadcasting, publication, dissemination or promotion of the advertisement in any form. The notice further asks the actors to furnish details of the due diligence undertaken by them or their agencies before participating in the campaign.
The action follows the FDA's examination of an advertisement for Vimal Elaichi, which it said was being disseminated through television channels, digital, social media platforms and other promotional media. According to the notice, the Vimal brand is prominently associated with pan masala in Maharashtra, where pan masala containing prohibited substances is banned.
The notice asked the actors to provide documentary evidence to show whether Vimal Elaichi is an independent product actually available for sale in the market or whether it constitutes a surrogate or brand-extension communication intended to promote Vimal pan masala or tobacco-related products.
They have also been asked to furnish copies and details of their endorsement agreements, campaign briefs, product information, payment or endorsement arrangements, as well as details of the advertising agency and brand owner involved in the campaign, said the order.
The FDA has sought details of all TV channels, digital and social media platforms and other media on which the advertisement was broadcast or published with the actors' participation, along with the period of such dissemination. The notice also seeks disclosure of any material connection between the endorsers and the advertiser or brand owner.
The actors have been given 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice to submit written explanations and supporting documents. They can also seek a personal hearing, either in person or through an authorised representative.
The FDA warned that if no explanation is received within the stipulated period, or if the explanation is found unsatisfactory, further action may be initiated without any further notice.
The notice comes against the backdrop of a prohibition order dated July 13, issued by the Maharashtra Food Safety Commissioner under Section 30(2)(a) of the Food Safety and Standards Act. The order remains in force for one year and covers specified tobacco, nicotine and areca-nut-based prohibited food products.
The FDA said the Vimal brand was prominently associated with pan masala in the market and that enforcement action was being taken against the manufacture, storage, transportation, distribution and sale of prohibited pan masala products in the state.
The department has also submitted copies of the notice to the Chief Executive Officer of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and the Central Consumer Protection Authority for information and appropriate action.
It also refers to the Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018, including provisions requiring claims to be truthful, unambiguous and not misleading, and Regulation 15 concerning discontinuation and corrective advertisements.
Under Section 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, the Central Consumer Protection Authority can direct discontinuation or modification of a misleading advertisement, impose penalties on endorsers and, in specified circumstances, prohibit an endorser from endorsing products or services for a prescribed period.
The Maharashtra FDA, under Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, has been conducting widespread inspections of food outlets and products to check safety, hygiene, and related issues.

Australian state to launch gun buyback after Bondi Beach attack
- Published
Australia's most populous state will launch a gun buyback scheme later this year, becoming the first to offer cash in exchange for firearms in the wake of the Bondi Beach terror attack.
Gun owners in New South Wales (NSW) will be offered up to AUS$1,000 (£523) to hand over eligible handguns, shotguns and rifles from 2 November.
Australian authorities had pledged sweeping firearm law reforms after 15 people were shot dead at a Jewish festival on Sydney's Bondi Beach, which is located in NSW, last December.
The state's premier Chris Minns said on Saturday: "We want those guns handed in, compensated for and safely destroyed."
He said the move could see hundreds of thousands of guns surrendered.
Gun ownership reforms already introduced by the state mean individuals can only own four firearms - although some people, such as farmers and sports shooters, can own a maximum of 10.
The scheme will be offered to those who have more weapons than permitted by the new rules, or who are no longer covered by a licence - with terms having been reduced from five years to two.
The scheme will be implemented in two phases. The first - from the start of November - covers types of handguns, shotguns and rifles.
Those handing over a revolver, for example, will be paid AUS$1,000, while an air rifle will fetch AUS$450.
The second phase will begin early next year and cover "higher-value firearms" valued above AUS$3,000, capped at AUS$10,000.
The National Gun BuyBack Scheme is being jointly funded by New South Wales and the federal government.
Businesses will be able to receive up to AUS$25,000 in support to help them adjust to the reforms, with help also offered to gun-dealers.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: "We must do everything we can to make sure the antisemitic terrorist attack in Bondi doesn't happen again.
"That includes meaningful nationwide gun reform."
On 14 December last year, 15 people including a 10-year-old girl and a Holocaust survivor were killed as Hanukkah celebrations took place near Australia's most famous beach.
Australian authorities had initially planned a nationwide gun buyback, though plans have been delayed over funding and how it would be implemented.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

When the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks.
The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students.
For families who say they lost their children to education system mismanagement and examination scandals, watching the protest scenes unfold on television came with mixed feelings. Some were happy that future students may be spared the same fate; others questioned why it had taken so long.
The Guardian spoke to four families about what happened to their children and how they feel today.
Anshika Pandey, 20, Delhi
Anshika Pandey, the eldest of twin sisters and four siblings, was, her father says, the calmest, quietest and most responsible member of the family. Revision books still lie neatly stacked, bags and accreditation cards hang from the nails where they were last placed. Her ambition was to be a doctor in the community where she lived, to be able to help the “poor people in need of medical care” some day.
Pandey studied for more than 12 hours every day, worked part-time at a store for nearly six hours and slept no more than five hours each night.
This year’s national eligibility cum entrance test (Neet) to gain entrance to medical training was her third attempt at becoming a doctor. After sitting the exam on 3 May, she was hopeful. But on 12 May she learned that the exam had been leaked for the second year in a row and there would be a resit.
“Anshika was deeply hurt. She had been hoping to enter college this year and was happy with the exam she had taken. Still, after cancellation, when I tried to console her, all she lamented was how could she hope to give another good exam,” says her father, Indradhar Pandey, a cab driver in Delhi.
Anshika remained calm and performed her household duties and engaged with everyone normally. But two days later, on 14 May, when everyone had left for work and her twin sister and younger brother were napping, she hanged herself.
Anshika’s dream had been to move her family, especially her siblings, from the slum where they lived. Her younger sister, Pragati, hopes to fulfil that dream and reminisces about how the two sisters had talked about it several times.
Anshika’s sketches and positive messages and mantra chants on the walls of their home, which she wrote to motivate herself, are now the memories her family is refusing to let go of.
Sufi Shaheen, 19, Delhi
Before leaving the house on the morning of 25 October 2024, Sufi Shaheen straightened her hair and put on her favourite jeans. As she left, she asked her mother for 10 rupees (8p), unlike other days when she would ask for 100. Then she headed for her joint entrance examination (Jee) lesson.
Her mother, Sultana Khatoon, asked her why she was leaving the house on an empty stomach. Shaheen replied she would be back soon. Twenty minutes later, she jumped from the seventh floor of a tutoring centre, about a mile away from her home.
It has been almost two years since she died, but Khatoon has not recovered from that day. She is being treated for severe depression and bouts of headaches.
“She was my only daughter of the four children and more like a friend. Every time I stepped out of the house, she would help me get ready. Even though she was deeply passionate about studying and becoming an engineer, she also loved dressing up and made everyone in the house do it too,” says Khatoon, as she looks through her daughter’s school photos.
Living with her parents and three brothers on her father’s modest income as a technical engineer, Shaheen had dreamed of becoming a software engineer and “excelling even more than the boys in her community”, says her mother.
A quick learner and highly motivated, Shaheen taught herself to draw and paint, and even learned to speak Japanese and Korean. But she had been stressed for several months and feared not being able to clear her second attempt at the national engineering entrance exam in January 2025.
When India’s National Testing Agency made changes to the Jee exam syllabus, Shaheen couldn’t sleep for days. She remained stressed, cried when talking to her brother and her best friend on the phone, and wrote a note to her parents in which she apologised and asked her younger brother, Masoom, to make their dreams come true.
“Almost two years later, Masoom was ranked 188th in the whole of India in his CUET [common university entrance test]. But we do not have Shaheen to celebrate this with,” says Khatoon.
Pradeep Kumar Mahich, 22, Rajasthan
“Even God will not be able to stop me from becoming a doctor this year,” were 22-year-old Pradeep Mahich’s words to his father right after his Neet exam on 3 May. This was his fourth attempt and, most importantly, he felt confident. But the announcement of the exam paper leak and resit broke his heart.
No one in the family had ever “dreamt so big”, says Pradeep’s father, Rajesh Kumar, a farmer in Rajasthan’s Sikar district. Kumar sold a large part of his farmland and took a loan of 11 lakhs (£8,600) under the farmer’s crop loan schemes.
“Sikar, the main coaching hub for Neet, is only an hour and a half from our village. My eldest daughter, Babita, who was preparing to join the police, and my son were both studying in Sikar, renting an apartment. This was his fourth year of tutoring, and the money from selling the land and the loan was slowly being consumed. I would send monthly expenses of £250 and Pradeep’s annual tutoring fees of £4,000, asking them not to worry about money and focus on his studies,” says Kumar.
“Pradeep had told me, ‘Papa, we will do a big celebration before I go to college. And one day I’ll return to serve the people of the village,’” says Kumar.
On 15 May, as he did every day, Kumar sent milk and curd to his two children on a bus that goes to Sikar; Pradeep came to pick it up at 9.30am then went home and told his sister he would help prepare lunch. But when his sister was showering, he hanged himself. She has taken a break from her studies and returned home.
Seeing students protesting on his television screen, Kumar says he is relieved that the eduction minister has gone but says there should be a proper investigation so that “no family suffers the same fate that we did”.
S Anitha, 17, Tamil Nadu
S Anitha belonged to an underprivileged lower caste, or Dalit, community from Tamil Nadu’s Ariyalur district. Born to a daily wage labourer, her mother died when she was seven, leaving her grandparents to raise her.
As a teenager, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. “At such a tender age, she was so focused that we used to feel proud of her,” says her brother, Manirathinam. “She knew what she wanted and never distracted herself with anything else. She never asked for any clothes, jewellery or food – her focus was clear and she knew the circumstances.”
She scored a perfect 100 in physics and chemistry at school and was offered a place to study aeronautical engineering at the state’s technological institute. But when she could not even meet the cut-off marks in the Neet exam, she realised that she had been studying a different syllabus.
Tamil Nadu had already criticised the national government for imposing an all-India examination – “disrupting the federal structure” – because it had a different education system. As a result, the state was exempted from Neet in 2016, but not in 2017, the year Anitha sat the exam.
When the supreme court ruled on 22 August 2017 that admissions to medical school would be based only on the Neet exam, she lost hope. On 1 September, Anitha hanged herself in her grandparents’ home. Her suicide became the subject of a public debate and led to widespread protests across the state and even in Delhi.
Her brother took part in last month’s protests in the capital and, while happy about the Indian education minister’s resignation in July, argues that all exams should become state-run, rather than by central government, as not everyone can afford the hefty tutoring fees needed to sit the Neet exam.
He now runs a free library and education centre in Anitha’s name.

Negotiators fear U.S. tariffs will be imposed, as provinces and Washington dig in on demands
Provinces control booze bans, demand sectoral relief, but U.S. offers not enough: sources
Some Canadian negotiators fear there may be no way to avert new U.S. tariffs from taking effect Wednesday, as Ottawa struggles to win relief from Washington on existing sectoral tariffs while also trying to persuade provinces to lift restrictions on American alcohol, sources tell CBC News.
Multiple sources — in both Canada and the U.S. — have been briefed directly on the negotiations and were granted confidentiality to speak frankly about the talks.
Negotiations continue to intensify, with Radio-Canada reporting that Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is expected to meet again Sunday with his counterpart, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. It would be their third meeting in a week.
For Ottawa, the goal in recent weeks has been to negotiate a "comprehensive agreement" with Washington.
Ottawa would like to see the Trump administration drop the new 50 per cent tariffs, set to kick in on Wednesday, on nearly $28-billion worth of Canadian goods, or about five per cent of Canada's exports to the U.S.
At the heart of that deal would also be an agreement for the Trump administration to lower existing sectoral tariffs that have been punishing the steel, aluminum, auto and lumber industries. Steel and aluminum currently face 50 per cent tariffs, while autos face tariffs of 25 per cent.
Sources say pursuing such a comprehensive, two-pronged deal is key to getting provinces on board with any agreement, including a commitment to put American alcohol back on the shelves. The Trump administration has made the resumption of U.S. alcohol sales in Canada a red line in the negotiations, sources say.
But the U.S. has so far not agreed to meaningfully reduce sectoral tariffs already in place, and the two countries remain far apart on some issues that need to be resolved, as CBC News reported on Friday.
Some provinces are refusing to lift their bans on American alcohol unless Washington offers relief on tariffs affecting their own industries. And that is putting Ottawa in a bind — with sources telling CBC News some negotiators now fear a deal may not be finalized if provincial opposition remains firmly entrenched.
Canada prepared to make concessions
Sources say provinces and territories have been told Canada would have to make concessions on the three issues the Trump administration has raised: provincial bans on U.S. alcohol, dairy import quotas and Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos.
Greer reiterated that resolving those disputes is a condition of any deal to avert Wednesday's tariffs.
"Those things have to be resolved, because that's the legal basis for those other tariffs," Greer told reporters Friday in Des Moines, Iowa. "The Canadians have come in and they want to have a conversation about it, and we're having those conversations."
The federal government has told the provinces that American alcohol must be put back on the shelves once a comprehensive deal is reached, as CBC News previously reported.
Ottawa needs provinces to move on booze bans
At issue for Ottawa: it needs provincial co-operation to make that happen, since it's powerless to force an end to the alcohol boycotts. The bans were put in place by each province, not the federal government, and restocking American alcohol ultimately rests with the provinces.
Complicating matters for negotiators, sources say, multiple provinces have said in recent days that they won't lift their alcohol bans until their own grievances are addressed in the trade deal.
Only Alberta and Saskatchewan, which have privatized alcohol retail systems, resumed the sale of U.S. booze. Other provinces have maintained their bans, although there has been division among them for months over whether to relent.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he will end the province's boycott only if negotiators secure what he describes as a "fair deal" that addresses tariffs on key sectors.
"If we get a fair deal that will protect our steel sector, our auto sector, our forestry sector, agriculture sector, manufacturing sector, then we'd be more than happy to bring booze back on the shelves," Ford said during a news conference in Guelph, Ont., on Thursday.
Dairy another potential flashpoint
Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette, meanwhile, maintained Friday that no concessions should be made regarding the supply management system that protects Canadian dairy, a key U.S. trade irritant.
Trump has repeatedly complained about the level of U.S. dairy farmers' access to Canada's market.
"For us, it is essential to preserve supply management; we have made this a red line that must not be crossed," Fréchette said.
Sources tell CBC News that any deal with the U.S. will have to involve Canadian concessions on dairy, though it's not known publicly what specifics are being discussed at the negotiation table.
Earlier this month, Fréchette also stressed: "The sale of alcohol falls exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Quebec government. Quebec, and Quebec alone, will make that decision."
No movement on lumber relief: sources
British Columbia Premier David Eby has long maintained that lowering tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber also needs to be part of any trade deal.
The premier previously said "there is not a chance in hell that U.S. alcohol is going back on the shelf in British Columbia," and he reiterated Friday that his position "remains unchanged."
"Our softwood lumber industry is under direct attack," Eby said, when asked whether his government would be willing to lift its ban on U.S. alcohol in exchange for a new trade deal. "That issue needs to be addressed.... The federal government is well aware this is British Columbia's issue at the table."
Sources, however, tell CBC News the current U.S. proposal does not include any meaningful reduction in softwood lumber tariffs. The Trump administration wants lumber negotiated separately, sources say, while B.C. wants it included in the broader deal.
"The softwood lumber sector is bigger than auto parts and steel combined in terms of the Canadian economy, and it needs to be front and centre at the table," Eby told reporters on Friday.
The stakes are particularly high for B.C. and Quebec: about 13 per cent of B.C.'s exports and 10 per cent of Quebec's could be exposed to the new levies if they take effect Wednesday.
Ottawa urges 'unified, Team Canada approach'
One source said it is "critical" for provinces to come on side "quickly," as all indications are that the U.S. is unwilling to extend Wednesday's deadline.
A separate provincial source characterized the Trump administration as doing a "perfect job driving a wedge" between Ottawa and the provinces, and among the provinces themselves. "This was calculated. It'll be hard for 14 governments to come to a consensus," the provincial source said, referring to the federal, provincial and territorial governments.
In a statement, LeBlanc and Janice Charette, Canada's chief trade negotiator to the U.S., said they "reiterated the importance of a unified, Team Canada approach" during a virtual meeting with provincial and territorial ministers responsible for trade on Friday.
Quebec's Economy Minister Bernard Drainville told reporters following that briefing that a big gap remains between Canada and the U.S. and "at the moment, there is no indication that Mr. Trump might postpone the application of the 50 per cent tariffs."
That possibility of talks ending without a deal has been contemplated for weeks. When Trump announced the new slate of tariffs in July, Prime Minister Mark Carney told premiers that the best deal may be no deal at all. Sources with knowledge of the discussion told CBC News at the time that provinces were asked to develop a list of possible retaliatory actions if the U.S. proceeds with the Aug. 19 tariffs.
CBC News reported earlier this month that the Canadian side has aggressively argued to the Americans that there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the tariffs come into force.

When was the last time you played? Took part in an enjoyable activity for the sake of it, with no particular outcome? A moment where you laughed, felt awe, curiosity, creativity? Where time flew by? If you’re over the age of, say, 7, your answer is probably not recently.
How to bring more playfulness to your everyday life
Go on, live a little.
According to Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, an organization that studies play and champions research-backed playful policies, American society is in a bit of a play drought. Attention spans are shrinking, the country is more polarized than ever, and some people might be more comfortable communicating with AI than other humans. “Our world is really overwhelming, and what we’re starting to see is these almost spontaneous bursts of playfulness infiltrate back into our society almost as a rebellion against the things that feel really hard and scary right now,” Sundstrom told Vox.
That desire for levity might explain the proliferation of “whimsical” online content and unconventional workout classes and events, Sundstrom said. In other words, play, which she defined as both a state (marked by experimentation and risk-taking) and a disposition (a curious, creative, and optimistic way of moving throughout the world).
Playfulness benefits us all, not just kids. Playful people perceive less stress and have higher well-being, and life satisfaction. It also just feels good to partake in an activity that takes you out of the difficulties of life, if just for a little while. To help push back against the forces of seriousness, Sundstrom outlines three easy ways to imbue your life with more play.
1. Figure out your “play style”
Play is highly subjective: What one person considers enjoyable might be another’s personal hell. And just because an activity brings you a moderate amount of enjoyment doesn’t mean it’s necessarily good for you. (Take mindlessly scrolling on your phone, for instance.) To be a more playful person, you need to consider — or remember — what makes you feel a little silly. The National Institute for Play developed six “play styles” to help people determine what activities light them up. For example, “creators” play through art, music, design, and performance while “competitors” like playing games or sports.
If you struggle to even pinpoint your play style, Sundstrom suggests recalling past memories of play. When was the last time you truly lost track of time or laughed so hard you cried with people you loved? What were you doing?
“Try and recall that vividly, because play is who we are before the world tells us who we have to be,” she said. “Whatever you loved to do early on, there’s a good chance somewhere inside of you that is still in there and is a great little spark for you to re-access play.” It’s likely you gradually stopped these playful hobbies, perhaps due to the demands of adult life, and picking them back up with no expectation can put you in touch with your younger self.
2. Make your environment more conducive to play
Based on your play style, you might consider low- or no-cost upgrades to your physical space to make play easier. “In physical spaces, the fastest and easiest things you can do are how can you add bright colors or something that feels inspiring to you, whether that’s a picture of your favorite place or a memory that jogs back play, something that is a visual cue to you that brings you back to a play state,” Sundstrom said. You might keep some scrap paper handy to doodle while you’re on the phone, use brightly colored files to organize your important documents, or use a colorful keyboard instead of a standard one.
Kids can make any space more playful. If you have children in your life, try to adopt their mindset: the curiosity, the wonder. And if you don’t have little ones, take inspiration from a childlike version of yourself and make decisions from their point of view, Sundstrom said.
Many adults, especially moms, feel pressure to curate a high-octane play experience for kids, Sundstrom said. But a more playful environment can simply incorporate an inside joke, a wink whenever you leave the room, or a silly way of greeting each other.
3. Find some bite-sized versions of play that you can add to your daily routine
Once you’ve figured out, say, adventuring and new experiences are what make you feel alive (also known as the “explorer” play style), what tiny measures can you take to regularly engage in play?
“Even 30 seconds of a dance break or belting your favorite song or creating a handshake with somebody as you enter or exit a room, that is enough to create that play spark and to start those brain activations that do foster the deeper creativity and adaptability and resilience that build the play mindset,” Sundstrom said.
The best places to infuse play are during moments of boredom, Sundstrom said. To allow yourself space to be bored, put your phone in another room during any downtime and when you would ordinarily feel the urge to pick up your device, do something playful instead. Anything from practicing an accent or turning on a random radio station and imagining what the musical artist looks like.
The world may be serious, but individuals can take ownership over how much whimsy and levity they bring to it. Who knows? You might make someone else’s day more playful, too.

AI has already changed how companies hire, right from resume shortlisting and initial assessments to interview screening. Thankfully, the same technology can also work in your favor. AI tools for job interview preparation can help you understand a role, research the company, prepare likely questions, practice mock interviews, and even point out where your answers fall short.
While mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are more than capable of helping with the basics, dedicated AI interview tools take things a step further. We tested eight such tools that offer everything from resume-based interview questions and technical interview practice to video analysis, peer interviews, and detailed feedback. Here is how they work, which one you should choose, and how to get the most out of them.

How to Use AI to Prepare for a Job Interview
Before we get to the applications, which indeed make job interview preparation an easy affair, you must understand the importance of a solid foundation to begin with. Fortunately, this groundwork only requires leveraging existing AI tools you may already be using. After getting to know the details of the job interview, mainstream AI models, such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, and more, can be directed to put you at an advantage from the very initial phase of your preparation. Below is what you must do first.
→ Understand the Role and Generate Role-Specific Interview Questions
Most, if not all, job descriptions are little more than a pile of technical and corporate jargon, often failing to clearly state the requirements. Misaligned interview expectations may already put you in a bad spot during the interview, so you must ensure that you are well-versed with the job description. AI models can help you do so with a few prompts, but you must include a few crucial elements to get the best results. With all this, don’t forget to upload your updated resume for a tailored response.
For starters, you cannot miss out on knowing the core competencies required for the job you’re applying for. AI can help you identify the top non-negotiable technical and soft skills that the recruiter expects of you. Such attributes are often not understood by many applicants, which prevents them from brushing up on existing skills or learning the required ones. Next, your prompt must include identifying the success metrics, or the key performance indicators of the role.
Because every hiring takes place to solve a specific problem of the organization, it’s crucial to have an idea about the performance expectations the recruiter may have from you. For tech roles, it usually revolves around solving existing issues, improving existing processes, and related tasks. In contrast, non-tech roles focus on increasing client retention, establishing business relationships, and related tasks.
Lastly, you must also ask AI to groom you based on your resume. It will help you determine whether your resume aligns well with the role and whether any specific skills need to be spotlighted. AI can not only identify potential loopholes but also help you present your projects to the interviewer in the most convincing way possible. With this initial study of the role’s requirements, you can certainly answer questions and defend yourself with confidence.
→ Study About the Company
While most candidates think they know the company they’re applying to well, the truth is, not many perform a proper deep dive. It is an important part of interview preparation, as knowing the company helps you give more relevant answers instead of generic ones.
AI makes company research much easier, but don’t simply ask it to “tell me about the company.” Start with its current market position, products, competitors, recent announcements, and anything else directly relevant to the role.
Foremost, your prompt should include information about the company’s current market position. You can assist the AI model by attaching the company’s press releases, financial reports, product launch notes, public announcements, and more. Financial reports can also be used to project the company’s future trends, map future goals, and more, which are worth knowing about.
It’s also essential to understand the company’s competitors, as it can help you frame your answers to interview questions in the company’s favor. While you are unlikely to find many, you can ask the AI model to identify and propose viable solutions to the company’s publicly available problems. It can be a significant advantage when handled appropriately and also serves as a good background for obvious questions, such as “What will you bring to the table?” and “Why should we hire you?”
→ Analyze the Interviewer
If you know who will be interviewing you, publicly available professional information can help you prepare better. Their LinkedIn profile, current role, past experience, or area of expertise may give you a fair idea of which parts of your background they are more likely to focus on.
You can provide this information to an AI model and ask it to suggest questions that someone in a similar role may ask. Don’t treat those questions as predictions, though. Use them simply to broaden your preparation and identify areas you may otherwise overlook.
This information is also useful when preparing questions to ask towards the end of the interview. Relevant questions about their team, role, or experience with the company will usually come across better than generic ones.
→ Generate Behavioral, Situational, and Technical Interview Questions
A recommended way to ensure success in an interview is to prepare for the likely questions. The question set should not only include the basic ones, but also challenging ones to put you on the spot. That way, your real-world performance will be sufficient for selection. To begin with, the basics: you can ask AI models to generate common behavioral interview questions, such as “Introduce yourself” and “Why should we hire you?” “What if we don’t select you?” “What makes you fit for this role?” and the like.
The answers to the above questions will be based on your resume and cognitive ability, which is what AI models can help you with. Next, to tackle the technical questions, your prompt must instruct the AI model to fire deep-dive technical, situational, and project-based questions at you. During all this, you can rate your technical skills and promptly improve any weak areas.
Despite the discomfort, ask the AI model to generate questions from the perspective of an interviewer who is not interested in hiring you. Understand the questions, as they can prove to be great at identifying gaps in your resume, incompetencies, and more. You can also ask the AI model to question the relevance of your past experiences, push back aggressively on your answers, and more. This will only improve your chances of getting selected.
→ Practice Mock Interviews With AI Voice Mode
In case you are unaware, most mainstream AI models offer voice modes that are perfect for back-and-forth questioning, making them ideal for interview practice. It’s not surprising that merely reading the questions and thinking you can answer them won’t cut it, which is why you need a simulation of the interview. It may cause you to memorize answers instead of coming up with your own, which may result in you sounding like a teleprompter, or worse, freezing on the spot if you forget the exact answer, leaving a bad impression.
Voice mode is best used on the mobile versions of AI agents. First, you must tell the AI its persona by verbally describing it, uploading the job description, interview details, or any other supporting documents. We also recommend uploading your resume to ensure a curated interaction. Next, you must instruct it to ask all types of questions, including behavioral, technical, and situation-based.
Remember, the purpose of this mock interview is to prepare you for the worst, so take away critical lessons and improve yourself. For this, you can ask the AI model to rate your answers and provide you with detailed assessments to help you identify your weak points. Not only will it cure the interview phobia that you may have, but it will also improve your speaking skills, conversational awareness, and your ability to answer curveballs.

Useful AI Prompts for Job Interview Preparation
Mainstream AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can be surprisingly effective for interview preparation if you give them enough context. A common approach among job seekers is to provide the actual job description and resume, then have the AI conduct the interview one question at a time instead of generating a generic list of questions. Here are a few prompts worth trying.
1. Analyze the Job Description and My Resume
I am preparing for an interview for the job below. Act as an experienced hiring manager and analyze both the job description and my resume.
Identify:
The five most important skills or requirements for this role
The parts of my resume that match them best
Important requirements where my experience looks weak or unclear
Questions an interviewer is likely to ask about those gaps
Technical or industry topics I should revise
Five achievements from my resume that I should make sure to highlight
Don’t invent experience or skills that aren’t present in my resume.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
2. Conduct a Realistic Mock Interview
Act as the hiring manager interviewing me for the role below. Use my resume and the job description as your primary context.
Conduct this like a real interview. Ask only one question at a time and wait for my complete answer before asking the next one. Ask natural follow-up questions based on what I actually say instead of following a fixed list.
Include a mix of behavioral, situational, resume-based, role-specific, and technical questions where relevant.
Do not give me hints or feedback while the interview is taking place. Once the interview is finished, score my performance on answer quality, relevance, clarity, confidence, and completeness. Then identify my five biggest weaknesses and tell me how to improve each one.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
3. Give Me a Difficult Mock Interview
Act as a skeptical interviewer who isn’t yet convinced that I am the right person for this role.
Use my resume and the job description to identify weak points, career gaps, vague achievements, missing skills, questionable claims, or areas where another candidate may be stronger.
Ask me one difficult question at a time. If my answer is vague, generic, evasive, or unsupported, push back and ask a follow-up question. Don’t compliment every answer or make the interview artificially easy.
At the end, tell me which answers could hurt my chances in the real interview and show me how I could make them stronger without exaggerating my experience.
4. Build My STAR Interview Stories
Help me prepare 5 reusable stories from my career for behavioral interview questions.
Use my resume and the experiences I provide to identify strong examples involving leadership, conflict, failure, problem-solving, teamwork, initiative, and working under pressure.
For each story, organize the answer using STAR:
Situation: What was happening?
Task: What was I responsible for?
Action: What specifically did I do?
Result: What changed because of my actions?
Keep Situation and Task brief and spend more time on Action and Result. Ask me for missing details rather than inventing them. Where possible, help me quantify the result.
Finally, tell me which common behavioral interview questions each story could answer.
Excel in Interviews With These AI Tools
AI has made preparing for job interviews a lot less daunting than it used to be. For most people, mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are already good enough for understanding a job description, researching a company, preparing likely questions, and improving answers.
Dedicated AI interview tools become useful when you want something closer to the real thing. Exponent Practice and Interviewing.io make more sense for technical candidates, Yoodli is particularly good for communication and behavioral practice, while MyInterviewAI works well for resume-based preparation. Big Interview helps with overall delivery, Huru AI makes quick job-specific practice easy, and Ophy AI covers the widest range of interview-preparation needs.
Whichever tool you choose, don’t stop after one mock interview. Upload your latest resume and the actual job description, complete a practice session, review where you struggled, and repeat it after fixing those areas. Two or three focused mock interviews will be far more useful than memorizing dozens of AI-generated answers.
Critique My Interview Answer
I will give you an interview question followed by my answer.
Evaluate the answer as a demanding hiring manager. First, tell me:
Whether I actually answered the question
What was convincing
What sounded vague or generic
Whether I gave enough evidence
Whether I spent too much time on irrelevant context
What follow-up question an interviewer would probably ask
If it is a behavioral question, also evaluate it using the STAR method.
Only after giving me this critique, provide a stronger version that retains my real experience and sounds natural when spoken aloud. Don’t turn it into a polished corporate script that nobody would actually say in an interview.
FAQs about AI Interview Tools
Can ChatGPT help me prepare for a job interview?
Yes. You can give ChatGPT your resume and job description and ask it to identify likely interview questions, evaluate your answers, conduct mock interviews, research the role, and point out gaps in your preparation. Voice mode makes the mock interview experience significantly more natural.
Are AI mock interviews actually useful?
They can be, especially when the AI asks follow-up questions and gives detailed feedback instead of simply generating a list of questions. They are particularly useful for repeated practice, although they shouldn't completely replace practice with another person when that is available.
Which AI interview tools are free?
Exponent Practice offers a limited number of free peer mock interviews, while Yoodli has a free tier. Huru AI provides free access to try its mock interviews, and Ophy AI offers free starting credits. The exact limits can change, so check each service before signing up.
What is the best AI interview tool for software engineers?
Interviewing.io and Exponent Practice are the strongest options on this list for software engineers. They focus much more heavily on coding, system design, algorithms, and other technical interview formats than general-purpose interview coaching tools.
Can I use AI during an actual job interview?
That depends entirely on the employer and interview rules. Some companies prohibit outside assistance during interviews and assessments. Unless the interviewer explicitly allows it, the safer approach is to use AI extensively during preparation and answer the actual interview questions yourself.
How many AI mock interviews should I practice?
There is no fixed number. Instead of repeating mock interviews endlessly, complete one, review the feedback, fix the weak areas, and try again. A few focused sessions with clear improvement between them are more useful than doing many interviews without reviewing your mistakes.
