Manizha was publicly lashed 39 times over her friendship with a man, and then jailed.
"We wanted to get married, but unfortunately we were arrested. I do not know how the Taliban intelligence found out, or whether someone reported us.
"In prison, I experienced things that I have never even told my mother. I had no desire to continue living. I used to say that the first thing I would do after getting out of prison would be to take my own life.
"I had become a source of shame for my family and friends... I could no longer think about marriage."
If you, or someone you know, has been affected by issues mentioned in this article, BBC Action Line has put together a list of organisations which can help.
Afghanistan has one of the world's highest maternal mortality rates - rules restricting treatment by male doctors mean many women and girls are unable to access healthcare.
Midwife Marzia recounted watching a 45-year-old mother of six die in front of her after she travelled to the clinic from a remote district.
"We managed to save the baby, but now I keep thinking about the baby's future and the future of her six other children. What will happen to them without their mother? What will happen to the whole family?
"We were all heartbroken. For us, losing a patient is always the hardest part of our job. We become exhausted, both physically and emotionally."
Maryam is expecting a baby girl and said she worries about her daughter's future.
"If things continue like this, what will happen to her? She will not even have the chance to finish school like I did, let alone go to university.
"If one day she gets married, becomes pregnant and needs a female doctor during childbirth, what if there isn't one? This is a matter of life and death."
'Speak up for us'
Some of the Afghan women we spoke to said they still have hope for the future.
Noori, 24, said she had chosen to study law and political science because she wanted to give women a voice and defend their rights.
She never finished her degree because of the Taliban take over, but she's still been able to find a way to help women.
"I did not lose hope. I decided to start working and become financially independent. I found a job at a jam-making company and started working there. I have now been working for three years.
"Now, I have decided to establish my own company so that I can provide employment opportunities for other women. I want them to become independent, strong, and successful women like me and have a better future.
"Currently, 10 brave women are working there."
Asma, who is 13, wants to become a doctor and is sure someday she will be.
"One day, everything will change... but we must continue with patience, and we will not lose hope," she told the BBC.
Ela, who is a dental assistant, urged the international community not to forget Afghani women and girls.
"Speak up for Afghan women, support their right to education and work," she said.
"Keep the world's attention on their situation. We need solidarity, not silence."

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Private equity firm Tiger Global Management has reportedly exited The Viral Fever (TVF), the digital entertainment company behind shows such as Panchayat, Kota Factory, Aspirants and Gullak, in a transaction that values the company at $22 Mn. The PE firm is said to have sold up to a 40% stake in the company to investors like Lighthouse India Fund-I, Frontier Globecap Ventures and LC Nueva Advisors LLP. The transaction marks a 73% decline from TVF’s $82 Mn valuation in 2019, according to a Mint report, citing sources. Inc42 has reached out to Tiger Global and TVF for comments on the development. This story will be updated if and when a response is received. Tiger Global first backed TVF in 2016 with an investment of around $10 Mn for 25% stake. The PE firm subsequently shored up more stake in the company by participated in additional funding rounds. The deal comes amid a leadership rejig at the OTT platform, seeing the appointment of three senior appointments across its creative and corporate team. Meanwhile, Shreyansh Pandey, who headed TVF Originals, is leaving after 11 years to start his own venture. Pandey has worked on shows including Kota Factory, Aspirants, Gullak and Cubicles. Founded by Arunabh Kumar, TVF started in 2010 as a YouTube-led experiment focused on comedy sketches, parodies and youth-oriented content. It gained wider recognition in 2012 with viral videos such as Rowdies and later moved into scripted digital series. Its early shows, including Permanent Roommates and TVF Pitchers, helped establish TVF as an early player in India’s web-series market, while formats such as Qtiyapa and Barely Speaking with Arnub helped build its YouTube audience. TVF crossed 1 Mn YouTube subscribers in 2015 and now has more than 6 Mn. It subsequently expanded into long-form content, producing popular shows such as Kota Factory, Panchayat, Gullak and Aspirants, turning it from a YouTube comedy channel into one of India’s better-known digital content studios. Tiger Global’s exit adds on to its ongoing exits within the Indian startup ecosystem. Last year, Tiger Global had offloaded its entire stake in listed EV major Ather Energy via a bulk deal for ₹1,204 Cr. The firm has also been cutting its stakeholding in Ather’s competitor, Ola Electric, since last year. Meanwhile, the deal comes at a time when India’s OTT ecosystem is undergoing a broader reset. The number of streaming originals released across major platforms fell 18% in 2024 and a further 13% in 2025 to 274, the lowest level since 2020, according to Ormax Media report. Industry estimates also suggest that OTT content budgets have been cut by 20%-50%, with the average cost of a web-series episode falling to ₹30 Lakh-₹1 Cr from ₹1-2 Cr earlier. India’s OTT market was estimated at $3.9 Bn in 2024 and is projected to reach $19.25 Bn by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 15.6% between 2025 and 2035.

How a former flight attendant posing as a pilot got free flights for years — and finally got caught
Dallas Pokornik worked for unspecified Toronto-based airline from 2017 to 2019
A former flight attendant from Toronto has pleaded guilty in U.S. federal court in connection with a fraud scheme reminiscent of the 2002 Steven Spielberg film, Catch Me If You Can.
Dallas Pokornik used fake identification to pose as a pilot and get hundreds of free flights on multiple airlines from January 2020 to October 2024, the U.S. Attorney's Office for Hawaii said in a statement released Friday.
Pokornik, 34, boasted online for years about his global travels, according to a social media account reviewed by CBC News. Until 2024, the account regularly shared photos and videos from destinations such as London, England; Los Angeles; Mexico City and Phuket, Thailand.
"Many of my friends are married. Many of my friends are having kids," a caption reads for a selfie video that appears to show Pokornik rolling a carry-on suitcase through London's Heathrow Airport in December 2023.
"I'm over here trying to avoid checking my bag and hoping for a window seat."
He was arrested in Panama and extradited to the U.S. in January.
Pokornik faces up to 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 US after pleading guilty last week in U.S. district court in Honolulu to one count of wire fraud. Pokornik also agreed to pay restitution to three unnamed U.S.-based "victim airlines," including one in Hawaii.
"This individual took advantage of travel security protocols for his own benefit and he will now face the consequences of his actions," said CJ Ammons, the acting special agent in charge of the U.S. Homeland Security investigations office in Honolulu.
U.S. prosecutors said Pokornik had worked as a flight attendant for an unspecified Toronto-based airline from July 2017 until October 2019.
A plea agreement seen by CBC News says Pokornik later showed a "false and fictitious" identification badge — claiming he was still employed by the Canadian airline — to obtain "travel benefits, including airline tickets that are reserved for pilots," from the companies identified only as airlines 1, 2 and 3.
Prosecutors said Pokornik even requested a cockpit seat reserved for pilots, known as a jump seat.
His fraudulent scheme came to a halt after an employee of one of the U.S.-based airlines took a picture of the forged identification. The photo was passed on to Pokornik's former employer, who confirmed the badge was fraudulent "because, among other things, it listed an expiration date in the year 2027," the plea agreement states.
Dan Bubb, a former pilot who flew for a regional airline in Las Vegas for about five years, starting in the late 1990s, said the case is surprising and "very unfortunate."
"But given a world of artificial intelligence and advanced technology, I think it's kind of a wake-up call to all of us that people can manufacture authentic-looking IDs, which seems to be the case here," Bubb, now a professor in residence at the University of Nevada, told CBC News.

He noted that anyone strapping in to a jump seat needs to show the captain their pilot's licence and company ID. "I think, moving forward, pilots are going to be a lot more vigilant about this, so I don't see this happening again," Bubb said.
John Gradek, a faculty lecturer in aviation management at McGill University's School of Continuing Studies, said Pokornik's experience in the industry also likely made it more difficult for authorities to uncover what was happening.
"This is not somebody off the street who doesn't understand the business. This is somebody within the business," Gradek said. "But even with all of that knowledge, at the end of the day, he still got caught."
The case has drawn comparisons to the hit 2002 movie Catch Me If You Can, in which Leonardo DiCaprio plays Frank Abagnale Jr., a cheque-forging con artist. Abagnale Jr. claimed in a book that he had posed as a Pan American World Airways pilot, among other roles, in a multimillion-dollar fraud.
Likewise, Pokornik never worked as a pilot for a Toronto-based airline, according to a Hawaii federal grand jury indictment.
Among major Canadian carriers, only Porter Airlines is headquartered in Toronto.
A Porter spokesperson told CBC News on Monday the company is "unable to verify any details related to this story."
The Montreal-based Air Canada and WestJet, which has its headquarters in Calgary, both said they have no record of Pokornik ever having been an employee.
Pokornik's sentencing hearing is scheduled for Dec. 8.
Court records show he remains out of jail — with conditions — as he awaits his sentencing. U.S. authorities seized his Canadian passport in January.
Pokornik's case is separate from Project Icarus, led by Ontario's Peel Regional Police. In June, the investigation prompted the high-profile arrest of a former Air Canada pilot accused of operating hundreds of flights over nearly 17 years without a necessary licence.
Geoffrey Wall, 59, was charged with several offences, including fraud, public mischief and uttering forged documents.

Topline
The northern lights could be visible in some parts of the northern U.S. on Sunday night, according to a forecast from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, although forecasters did not predict any space weather events that could cause more vivid lightshows.
Key Facts
NOAA is predicting a Kp index of four out of nine for Sunday night, meaning the aurora could appear brighter in certain places and more active with “motion and formations.”
However, forecasters are not predicting any major space weather in the next few days, which can enhance northern lights visibility.
Where Could the Northern Lights Be Visible?
NOAA predicts states along the U.S.-Canadian border could have a chance of seeing the aurora on Sunday night, including North Dakota, along with northern portions of Washington, Idaho, Montana, Minnesota, Wisconsin, South Dakota and Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. The lights could also be visible from most of Alaska, with much of the state’s interior shown with a high chance in NOAA’s forecast. However, the sun sets incredibly late in Alaska during the summer months, meaning the sky might not get dark enough for viewers to see a vivid aurora.
What’s the Best Way to View the Northern Lights?
Experts at NOAA recommend viewers generally travel as far north as possible, and position themselves on a vantage point like a hill with a clear view of the sky. Viewers should also make sure this site gets dark enough, and is away from sources of light like cities. The lights are typically most active in the hours just before and after midnight, according to NOAA, so viewers should aim to watch the sky between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.
What’s the Best Way to Photograph the Northern Lights?
A photographer who spoke to National Geographic said smartphones are capable of taking high quality images of the northern lights, provided users are using the correct settings and equipment. Prospective photographers should remember to bring a tripod and a remote timer for their devices. They should also ensure they turn off flash, switch their devices to night mode and shoot in RAW image format.

Hawaii braces for potential first direct hit by a hurricane in 34 years
- Published
Hawaii is bracing for what could be its first direct hit from a hurricane since 1992, as category one storm Lala churns off its coast.
Packing 75mph (120km/h) winds, Lala gained hurricane strength on Saturday. In a worst-case scenario, it could dump up to 25in (63cm) of rain on Big Island and produce a 3ft storm surge.
A hurricane warning is in effect for Big Island, while Maui County, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau are under a tropical storm warnings. Officials have told residents to prepare for "life-threatening" conditions, including floods and mudslides.
The storm is expected to either make landfall or pass close to the southern tip of Big Island on Saturday, before continuing west.
The last time a hurricane made landfall on Hawaii's Big Island was 155 years ago, according to the Associated Press news agency.
Over the weekend, Lala will continue moving westwards, and may weaken into a tropical storm, with the centre passing just below Hawaii's other islands.
Hawaii Governor Josh Green warned residents to brace for "an incredible amount of water".
He said on X: "Damaging winds, heavy rain, flash flooding and dangerous surf are possible across the state through the weekend."
Dozens of flights have been cancelled.
At Ellison Onizuka Kona International - Big Island's largest airport - 40% of flights were grounded, according to flightaware.com. Some 80% of flights were called off at its other main airport, Hilo International.
The more dire forecasts from the National Weather Service (NWS) have been issued for areas within Big Island's south-east.
"Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues," the NWS said, adding that rivers and tributaries "may rapidly overflow their banks in multiple places".
Residents were repeatedly urged by officials to prepare for the storm early.

It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

Death knell? Hong Kong’s five-year plan is a starting gun
The suggestions put forward during the plan’s consultation period offer grounds for optimism for a revitalised future
3-MIN READ3-MIN
David Dodwell is a journalist focused on Hong Kong and China since the 1970s. 
I’m a little perplexed and bemused by the brouhaha surrounding Hong Kong’s decision to draft its first five-year plan, as if the sky is falling in around the city’s famed laissez-faire economy.
Predictably, Yale University’s Stephen Roach (he of “Hong Kong is over” fame) warned in a commentary last month that “Chinese-style central planning” could “over-promise and under-deliver”. In a 2024 commentary, he said Hong Kong had been “shackled by the deadweight of autocracy”.
But from my vantage point, Hong Kong is decades overdue for a long-term planning framework that can provide strategic coherence to how we optimise our future as a conduit between a radically changing China and a turbulent global economy.
Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, way back in 1992 during his famous Southern Tour, was astutely aware that capitalism and communism were agnostic on the need to balance practical day-to-day administration with a clear long-term vision. Already, brittle Soviet concepts of “state planning” were old hat. He said: “A planned economy is not equivalent to socialism, because there is planning under capitalism too; a market economy is not capitalism, because there are markets under socialism too.”
Anyone familiar with the clever work of Yuen Yuen Ang at Johns Hopkins University will be aware that China’s five-year planning process has for many years been much more nuanced. She calls it “directed improvisation”: Beijing sets the big-picture objectives and local administrations are tasked with improvising to suit local circumstances.
Recall too Hong Kong’s old colonial days. Up to 1997, the British colonial government maintained the Central Policy Unit (CPU) to answer exclusively to the governor of the day on long-term strategic planning that aligned where necessary with the United Kingdom.

As the CJP protests gathered momentum, a parallel campaign began online against some of the women who participated in them. Accounts targeting the protesters circulated their videos, hurled abuse at them and published screenshots containing sensitive personal information, turning online trolling into outright doxxing.
Many of those targeted had either spoken to the media during the protests or posted reels and other content on social media with abusive language against Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Several Right-wing handles subjected them to sustained trolling and abuse while putting their private information in the public domain.
The most alarming instance involved a young woman from Noida. A clip of her using expletives against Modi during the Delhi protests went viral, following which Delhi-based Supreme Court lawyer Smriti Singh Chandel filed a zero FIR against her, invoking charges of defamation and “intentional insult to provoke breach of peace”.
Chandel also posted a photo of the FIR complaint on her Instagram handle, which revealed the home address of the accused individual. She also posted a video of men outside Gautam Budh Nagar police station holding the complaint copy and claiming they had access to the personal details of the female. Police had “assured” them, they said, that she would be arrested within days.
Young Female Protester Bears The Brunt
Confusion over the female’s age — whether or not she is a minor — and her name further problematised the case. After Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted a video saying that he “forgave” everyone who had abused him during the protest, the female protester posted an apology video, admitting her mistake, apologising to him and to the country. She claimed she was “influenced” by others using abusive language against the PM.
As reports began to suggest that the protester was in fact a minor, responding to allegations of doxxing a minor, trolls claimed that the girl in the apology video was not the same as the girl in the viral video. Several Right-wing influencers took to X to claim that a minor girl was being used to cover up for the actual 25-year-old protester, so that POCSO cases could be registered. Some even claimed she was using her younger sister for sympathy while some users went to the length of comparing facial features to prove their point.
The case significantly blew up when mainstream media aired her alleged name and face on national television. Times Now amplified the claim that the protester was a 25-year-old woman named Ruchika Singh. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor made the same claim, showing her face and revealing her identity.
CNN-News18 also made the same claim, while exposing her face; the channel on July 31 reported how they have “tracked down” the girl to her society complex in Noida, from where she had reportedly absconded. Citing repeated visits from the police as well as from strangers, the single mother-daughter duo reportedly had to leave their rented accommodation and shift elsewhere.
To make matters worse, on July 31, CNN-News 18 also claimed to have gained access to “exclusive voices” from the female protesters life that “nobody else has”. In an outright case of breach of privacy, a reporter from the organisation reached the “beauty salon” where the girl had allegedly learnt nail art till the month of June.
The reporter speaks at length with the owner of the nail salon, probing over the girl’s association with the salon. The owner mentions that the her name was not Ruchika Singh, as was being claimed by the media. He also claimed that on repeated failures to furnish her identity details, specifically her Aadhaar Card, the girl was reportedly asked by the management to not come back.
In an interview with ABP News, the victim of this doxxing episode clarified that her name is not Ruchika Singh and neither is she 25 years old.
The girl, who stated her age to be 15, reportedly faced constant harassment and threats from people in the neighbourhood, including threats of “murder and rape“. The mother, who also appears in the ABP interview, urges the public to stop the relentless abuse against her daughter.
The mother stated that despite the “PM forgiving her (daughter)”, an army of anti-social elements and police were repeatedly visiting their residence, which they were eventually forced to vacate given the increasing threat to their privacy and survival. “What will you get from harassing a child?” the mother asked, while extending gradtitude to Modi for granting her daughter “jeevandaan”. She repeatedly implores Modi and the masses to “let them live in peace and return to their home”.
Notably, Chandel, by her own admission, had “learnt” about the young girl’s name and details from social media users. The police complaint as well as the FIR went on to mention her as 25-year-old while the girl and her mother maintained that she is 15. “There are people claiming that it is her younger sister who has made the apology; they are saying I have hidden my daughter. This is bizarre; why would any mother throw her child into this vicious cycle of threats?” the mother said to The Print.
‘Arrest These Women’: Online Mob Justice
This was not an isolated incident. Several Right-wing accounts on X were determined to identify and locate female protesters. Retired IAS officer Sanjay Dixit, who runs the Hindutva propaganda page Jaipur Dialogues, specifically targeted women protesters who had allegedly abused Modi. In one of his posts, he shared a collage of twelve such women, urging the Delhi Police to “arrest them”.

NEW YORK — Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty on Friday to federal stalking charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, admitting matter-of-factly that he trailed the executive to an investor conference in 2024 and gunned him down on a New York City street.
Mangione, 28, said he even used a ruse to glean information about the event, contacting the health insurance company ahead of time under the guise of being an investor at a multibillion-dollar firm.
“On the morning of Dec. 4, 2024, I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan, and he died,” Mangione told the court as Thompson’s wife, Paulette, took several deep breaths and repeatedly wiped tears from her eyes. A supporter put an arm around the wife and held her tight.
Mangione is set for sentencing Dec. 18. When U.S. District Judge Margaret M. Garnett asked whether he understood that he could spend the rest of his life in prison, Mangione answered neutrally: “Yes.”
Mangione entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court, resolving one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s death. Mangione’s lawyers could now seek to have his separate New York state murder case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.
Surveillance video of the ambush showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson, 50, from behind. Police say “delay,” “deny” and “depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims. That detail — and revelations that Mangione’s private writings lambasted health insurers as greedy, according to authorities — made the case a fulcrum for debate about the industry and made Mangione a cause célèbre for some of its critics.
Mangione told the court Friday that he pursued Thompson “after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system.”
Mangione never was a UnitedHealthcare customer, according to police and the company. A University of Pennsylvania graduate from a wealthy Maryland family, he was arrested five days after the shooting, when he was spotted at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pa. It’s about 230 miles west of Manhattan.
Thompson led one of the United States’ largest health insurers, but he wasn’t well known outside the industry. Trained as an accountant, he had worked at parent company UnitedHealth Group Inc. for 20 years and became CEO of its insurance arm, UnitedHealthcare, in 2021. He and his wife have two sons, who were in high school when their father was killed.
Both the federal and state cases could lead to a life prison sentence for Mangione. A federal judge earlier this year tossed out additional charges that could have exposed him to a potential death penalty.
Mangione had complained about the prospect of two trials, telling a judge in February: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any commonsense definition.”
Under New York law, a state prosecution could potentially be barred if the federal case is resolved first.
The state’s double jeopardy protections kick in if a jury has been sworn in a prior prosecution, such as a federal case, or if that prosecution ends in a guilty plea. Mangione’s cases involve different charges arising from the same course of conduct.
In a letter last month, state prosecutors objected to the possibility of a guilty plea in the federal case wiping out the state case.
Garnett has delivered some setbacks to the defense, including ruling in January that prosecutors could use items collected from Mangione’s backpack during his arrest as evidence against him.
They included a 3D-printed pistol that investigators said matched the one used to kill Thompson and a notebook in which authorities say Mangione described his intent to kill an insurance executive.
In June, Mangione’s lawyers said they would pursue a psychiatric defense in the state case but reversed course a day later. The defense, involving claims that he was suffering from extreme emotional disturbance at the time of the killing, isn’t allowed in federal court.
—Michael R. Sisak, Larry Neumeister, and Alanna Durkin Richer

Israeli troops have forced two Palestinian families to leave their besieged West Bank homes, the day after a top Israeli commander personally promised he would end a violent settler campaign to drive them out.
Israeli soldiers also took over eight other homes in Qusra early on Thursday, telling the village’s mayor, Abdul Azim Wadi, that the buildings were needed for a days-long operation to remove the settlers. They later relinquished six. Settlers still roam the village.
The Palestinians’ ordeal began on Sunday when Israeli settlers and soldiers set up a tent blocking the entrance to three homes on the edge of the village. They severed water and electricity supplies and prevented an ambulance from reaching a sick toddler.
Amid mounting international pressure over the siege, Maj Gen Avi Bluth, who commands all Israeli troops in the occupied West Bank, visited Qusra on Wednesday to meet the trapped Palestinians and committed to “evacuate” the settlers from the village.
Bluth’s troops later removed the tent but left the militants, their bedding and other equipment. Soldiers retreated after a failed attempt to drive out the Israeli settler group with riot control techniques. The siege continued into a fifth day on Thursday, with the impact on the village only expanding after Bluth’s visit.
“The army arrived at around 10am and asked us to evacuate the houses because of a military operation in the area that would last for three days. We refused to leave,” said Qusai Ridi, one of the besieged Palestinians. “The army then moved us all into one house.”
He was allowed to return home in the afternoon, where he found Israeli soldiers had damaged a security camera system and stolen some equipment. They are still occupying the home of his neighbour Yousef Hassan, who is staying with Ridi.
Settlers are still patrolling outside in the area where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh was killed by a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault.
“I am afraid and do not trust that the army will actually evacuate the settlers. But I sincerely hope they do,” Ridi said.
His brother is an American citizen, and the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who is generally supportive of Israel’s settlement project, described the siege as a “horrific act of terror” carried out by Israeli terrorists.
On Thursday afternoon, Israeli soldiers left six homes they had taken over in the morning. The returning Palestinian families reported damage including a Qur’an with pages torn out and destroyed decorations.
Israel’s former prime minister Ehud Olmert said the siege was a “concerted and meticulous attempt at ethnic cleansing”, which left him disgusted and ashamed.
“These are crimes against humanity which are actively supported by the Israeli government and are assisted by the indifference and total lack of action by the IDF and the Israeli police. It’s unforgettable and unforgivable.”
The same terror tactics were used to force another Palestinian family out of their home in the neighbouring village of Jalud in July. Soldiers and settlers were filmed playing with a football together on the terrace of that house on Thursday.
An Israeli military spokesperson said soldiers had been ordered not to displace Palestinian residents of Qusra and would not operate inside the besieged homes.
“The soldiers were instructed that the Qusra residents will remain in their homes,” the military said in a statement. The spokesperson declined to comment on why those orders were being violated.
The chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), Eyal Zamir, has ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank. Domestic critics said the army’s failures in Qusra were more the result of a lack of will than shortage of forces.
“Yesterday’s events in Qusra illustrate the impotence of the IDF, the police, the GSS [Shin Bet] and other security organizations in the face of a group of bullies,” the commentator Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Israeli newspaper Ma’ariv.
“Instead of bringing a police van [and] arresting the criminals … [security forces] have been trying to negotiate with them. They are thugs. They believe themselves to be the lords of the land.”
Israeli militants target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only one indictment over those deaths.
Violence is deployed as part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, the rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes.

A Bleak, Violent Novel’s Unexpected Delights
For the characters in The Disappearers, seeing and being seen are matters of life and death.
This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here.
Before his latest book, Marlon James hadn’t written a novel set in Jamaica in more than a decade. In the years following his Booker Prize–winning A Brief History of Seven Killings, the author focused on his Dark Star Trilogy, set in a fantasy universe. But after that long literary detour, he returned to the land of his birth in his new novel, The Disappearers—which is set primarily in Kingston and follows a group of characters, all queer Jamaican men, who meet while rehearsing a play that will never be seen.
First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section:
For this group, which gathers in secret in 1988, seeing and being seen are matters of life and death. The Kingston they inhabit is murderously homophobic, and accordingly, the novel can be quite bleak. But The Disappearers offers some delights too. Recently, in her article about the book for The Atlantic, Stephanie Burt noted that “the novel opens up many pleasures for literary readers,” who may recognize the numerous titles and references sprinkled throughout. I was deeply affected by how, almost universally, the characters seek out anything that proves that gay life exists on a larger scale. Lowbrow works, such as porn films and magazines, are most accessible; Playgirl and Hustler are name-checked. The songs of Boy George, Sylvester, and Prince are lifelines—the homoerotic cover of Prince’s 1988 album, Lovesexy, is an especially powerful beacon. Many of the characters are well read, and they name-drop gay novels such as Andrew Holleran’s Dancer From the Dance and E. M. Forster’s Maurice. For one of the men in particular, the type of hustling, defiant gay life that John Rechy describes in his nonfiction book The Sexual Outlaw is pivotal.
The play they put on, a 1967 drama called Fortune and Men’s Eyes, explores homosexuality among a group of prisoners. Some of its characters see sex as a means for gaining or establishing power; others, as a convenient way to access pleasure. Some are what a modern audience might recognize as gay, whereas others choose partners largely because of their proximity. The cast share the characters’ disparate attitudes toward queerness. But in the Jamaica they live in, there is no room for nuance; any man seen as homosexual is a target for violence. Brutality will soon come to the rehearsal room.
In a way, James has written a gay novel about the uses of a gay novel. When his characters invoke Oscar Wilde and Edmund White, Hadrian and Michelangelo, they’re proving, to themselves and to the reader, that queer life existed long before they came around. But James is not an unskeptical cheerleader for the healing power of visibility and representation. The Disappearers’ major theme, after all, is that being recognized can be a bad thing: Owning these books is a hazard. Buying Lovesexy as a man in 1988 Kingston invites vigilantism. Staging Fortune and Men’s Eyes puts its cast and crew in danger.
So why try to do it? The director and ringleader, Havelock Titus, asks himself this question more than a decade after those hopeful rehearsals. He knew, even at the time, that the effort was a risk. He still doesn’t know “what success would have meant,” because the unstaged play “never had the chance to become a failure.” But Havelock knows on some level that he did it because, just like those who came before him, he wanted to create some kind of evidence that gay men communed and survived in his time and place. In short, he was tired of being erased.
Marlon James Returns to Realism, and to Jamaica
By Stephanie Burt
In his new novel, gay men struggle to escape violence in Kingston.
What to Read
The Age of Reform, by Richard Hofstadter
History can’t fully explain the present or predict the future, but it can help us understand the patterns of contemporary politics and the likely paths ahead. In 1955, Hofstadter, one of the great American historians of the 20th century, published The Age of Reform—a political and social history of the years 1890 to 1940, the period of populism, progressivism, and the New Deal. Rapid technological change, monopoly power, deep inequality, endemic corruption, mass immigration, nativist demagogues, the transformation of both political parties, repeated efforts at reform, recurring spasms of reaction: Perhaps no other age so resembles our own. Hofstadter is brilliant at analyzing types that feel quite familiar to us today—the crusading urban progressive, the small-town conspiracy theorist. He was a liberal who sympathized with the passion for progress while unsentimentally diagnosing its illiberal ideas and motives. The fevered moralism of that age seems a long way from the paralyzing cynicism of ours. But reading Hofstadter will remind you that reform and reaction not only follow each other, but also often coexist in the same moment; neither ever has the last word. Americans are always dreaming of a better country, and some have actually made it so. — George Packer

Durham 254-7 (50 overs): Rhodes 80, Ackermann 71*; Hollman 3-53
Middlesex beat Durham by two wickets
Luke Hollman scored a sensational unbeaten 83 to help Middlesex stun Durham with a two-wicket win in their One-Day Cup semi-final at Radlett to reach their first List A decider since 1990.
Middlesex will face Leicestershire in the final at Trent Bridge on Sunday, 20 September, after the Foxes beat Notts Outlaws by 23 runs in their last-four meeting.
Hollman put on a List A best showing with the bat as Middlesex's tailend turned the match around when struggling at 145-7 after 30 overs as they chased 255 for victory.
It was at that point that Hollman was joined at the crease by Tom Helm, who contributed 40 to their 79-run partnership that changed the complexion of the showdown.
Before that, it had seemed that Colin Ackermann, who had already starred with the bat for Durham with an unbeaten 71, had put his team in control when he snagged three quick wickets - including the scalp of opener Nathan Fernandes for 44.
While former England captain Ben Stokes re-joined Durham's bowling attack late on, he failed to add to the solitary early wicket of Josh de Caires as Middlesex saw out a milestone victory in which Hollman also delivered with the ball.
The spin bowler took 3-53, which included two caught and bowled and the scalp of Durham's top scorer Will Rhodes for 80, while Naavya Sharma and Zafar Gohar took two wickets apiece to limit Durham to 254-7.

Hello, and welcome back to This Is India.
For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?
Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”.
The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty, which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began.
Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added.
By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including:
 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons
  564,970 parts of explosive ordnance
  298 components of military vehicles
Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.)
An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes.
Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam.
Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay, writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”.
The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war.
Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel, and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back: “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.”
The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations.
The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party. The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court, demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive.
“In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern.
Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers, in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023.
India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests.

Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president?
- Published
For now, beleaguered Fifa president Gianni Infantino still has some allies in world football, particularly in parts of the world where less well-off football associations have benefited from his presidency.
Infantino's position has been under scrutiny since his controversial plan to sell stakes in Fifa's global competitions to private investors was scrapped having been opposed by some regional governing bodies.
Late on Thursday, the executive committee of the African confederation (Caf) unanimously confirmed its support for Infantino, after leading African football administrators sent messages backing him.
Five of the seven African countries on the Fifa Council - Egypt, Morocco, Niger, Mauritania and Comoros - have already supported him publicly.
Support from the continent largely stems from Fifa's Forward programme, a funding scheme Infantino introduced in 2016 that many African federations have become increasingly reliant on to fund football projects in areas where commercial and government investment in the sport is limited.
Our reporters and correspondents have explained below where some of Africa's key footballing nations stand.
Morocco
Morocco's rise as one of Africa's football success stories has largely been driven by government funding, but the country has also become a key partner for Fifa.
Morocco's capital, Rabat, is home to Fifa's Africa regional office, they have hosted Fifa Club World Cups, a women's U17 World Cup and will co-host the men's 2030 World Cup alongside Spain and Portugal.
Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) president Fouzi Lekjaa reaffirmed his support for Infantino after he withdrew the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal last week.
In a statement, Lekjaa described Infantino's decision to withdraw it as "wise", adding it put the unity of Fifa's 211 member associations first.
Infantino also received the backing of senior football executives at a meeting in Morocco on Wednesday, following a turbulent period after the proposal's collapse.
Reporting by Celestine Karoney
Egypt
Egypt is home to the Confederation of African Football headquarters and remains one of Infantino's strongest institutional allies in Africa.
The relationship is reinforced by the influence of Hany Abo Rida, a Fifa Council member and one of the continent's most prominent football administrators, who has maintained close ties with Infantino since his election in 2016.
During Infantino's presidency, Egypt has benefited from Fifa's Forward programme, which has funded infrastructure projects, youth development, coach education and women's football.
Like other African member associations, the Egyptian Football Association has also received increased development funding under Fifa's expanded investment strategy, while new and expanded football competitions have created additional commercial and sporting opportunities.
But support for Infantino in Egypt is accompanied by growing expectations. Officials and observers increasingly argue that Fifa's engagement with Africa should extend beyond financial assistance. Greater emphasis is being placed on good governance, transparency, sustainable football development and giving Cafmore room to shape the continent's own priorities.
Reporting by Mohamed Alkaaoud in Cairo
DR Congo
The Congolese Football Federation (Fecofa) has welcomed Infantino's decision to withdraw the controversial Forward Enterprise proposal, calling it "wise" in a statement earlier this month.
Pointing to a decade of work promoting football worldwide - and in particular his support of African nations - the federation stressed that the episode should not overshadow Infantino's wider record.
Fecofa stressed that the episode, born of good intentions, should not overshadow Infantino's wider record. It pointed to his decade of work promoting football worldwide, and particularly his support for African federations and those with fewer resources.
The federation said it had "greatly benefited" from Fifa's programmes, citing investment in development and infrastructure.
The declaration was signed by Véron Mosengo‑Omba, elected president of Fecofa in May 2026. His election ended a period of uncertainty following the resignation of Constant Omari Selemani in 2021 and the subsequent Fifa‑appointed Normalisation Committee established in April 2023.
Mosengo‑Omba assured Infantino of Fecofa's "full support" would continue beyond 2027, recalling mandates renewed in Paris in 2019 and Kigali in 2023. The statement underlines the Democratic Republic of Congo's alignment with Fifa leadership at a time when divisions remain sharp elsewhere in world football.
Reporting by Emery Makumeno
Nigeria
The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has largely aligned itself towards a supportive stance for Infantino's leadership, despite the wider backlash globally.
For a football federation facing chronic funding constraints and enormous infrastructure needs, Infantino's proposed plans would have been difficult to dismiss.
Former president of the NFF and deputy chairman of Fifa's Men's National Teams Competitions Committee, Amaju Pinnick, argued that Infantino's plan would deliver a much-needed financial boost to every member association without over-relying on local governments.
Nigeria is eligible for up to $8m (£5.95m), for the current Fifa Forward funding, despite failing to qualify for the last two men's World Cup tournaments.
The most prominent Forward project currently under way in Nigeria is the redevelopment of the NFF Technical Centre in the capital, Abuja. The project, funded with approximately $4.88m, includes the reconstruction of training pitches, and the construction of a modern accommodation complex for Nigeria's national teams.
Reporting by Emmanuel Akindubuwa
What others in Africa have said
The Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture of South Africa, Gayton McKenzie, posted on X saying that Infantino had been "very good to African football".
"Africa should be cautious in joining the public lynching of Infantino. He has been very good to African football.
"We can debate his ideas but let's not forget who has been a friend to us. Many of those calling for his head want the old status quo back too."
Speaking to the BBC after Infantino's proposal emerged, football officials from Malawi and Uganda said Fifa investment had transformed the game both on and off the pitch, arguing such funding is vital given the financial realities facing many African nations.
"Malawi needs money. Malawi needs stadiums, our government cannot manage to give us even $1m every year for football," Malawi FA president Fleetwood Haiya told BBC's Newsday programme.
"Our government is not able to make sure that they have medical supplies in hospitals [and] at the same time to look at football," he said.
President of the Gambia Football Federation, Lamin Kaba Bajo, told BBC Sport: "As far as I'm concerned, most of my colleagues are concerned, we'll encourage him [Infantino] to stay, and we'll do everything within our means to ensure that he is re-elected come next year, 2027.
"That's my personal opinion as president of the federation, and a good number of African memberships also stand on that line. He is here to stay."
But support for the project on the continent was not universal. Teen jailed for exam cheating in Guinea dies after sickle cell complications, father says
- Published
The father of a teenager from Guinea with sickle cell disease who died days after he was arrested for cheating in an exam has told the BBC he blames the authorities for his death.
Mamadou Djouma Bah, 17, was transferred to hospital after his health deteriorated while in prison and later died "under the care of his treating physician", according to the prosecutor.
His father, Mamadou Saliou Bah, has called for an investigation, telling the BBC that his son did not "receive good medical care" in detention.
People with sickle cell are often at an increased risk of contracting serious infections or they can become anaemic, which is when red blood cells cannot carry enough oxygen around the body.
- What is sickle cell disease? 
  - Published19 June 2023
Sickle cell disease is a lifelong illness, common in people of African descent, and caused by a faulty gene that produces unusually shaped red blood cells that can become stuck in blood vessels.
This can lead to severely painful episodes, which experts say can sometimes be prevented by wrapping up warm and drinking plenty of fluid, and daily antibiotics can reduce risk of infections. Other treatments can include blood transfusions.
The sudden pain in the chest, limbs, back and joints - from a lack of blood circulation - may cause organ damage.
'Dad, I'm dying'
Djouma Bah - who was a social sciences student - had allegedly been caught using his phone during Guinea's national school-leaving baccalaureate on 15 July, when he was arrested with other students, also suspected of exam fraud.
Two days later, he was convicted for cheating and sentenced to six months in prison, five of which were suspended.
He was serving his one month in a prison in the city of Kindia, about 137km (85 miles) north-east of the capital, Conakry, when his health deteriorated.
The teenager was subsequently transferred to the regional hospital for treatment.
Saliou Bah told the BBC that when he visited his son in hospital, the boy said he could not breathe properly and asked to lean against him.
"Then he looked at me and said: 'Dad, I'm dying,'" Saliou Bah said.
"Those were his last words."
The teenager spent around two days in hospital before being discharged to go home, where he died, according to officials.
Education Minister Alpha Bacar Barry said he was "deeply saddened by the news" and extended his "sincere condolences" to the family.
Human rights organisations are also calling for an independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death and the prosecution of other students.
On Wednesday, students demonstrated over the detentions of their fellow classmates, calling for their release.
"A student should not be sent to prison. These young people are the future of our country," Saliou Bah said.
"I also ask the authorities to release the other students who are still detained before they too lose their lives.
"We lost our son; we lost our future."

The first flight of the largest battery-electric aircraft to take to the skies lasted nearly half an hour while costing just $5 of electricity. That aviation feat comes at a time when jet fuel prices have skyrocketed because of the US war with Iran.
The test flight of Heart Aerospace’s X1 demonstrator aircraft took place at Plattsburgh International Airport in upstate New York on August 12. The X1 aircraft is comparable in size to a small regional airliner and can achieve a maximum takeoff weight exceeding 25,000 pounds with the help of four wing-mounted electric motors. The battery-electric propulsion system delivered more than one megawatt of power during the maiden flight.
All-electric aircraft can offer quieter and cleaner flight without the emissions that come from burning jet fuel. They may also prove more reliably cost-effective than conventional aircraft that come with jet fuel costs subject to geopolitical disruptions.
But the initial success of the X1 demonstrator does not mean Heart Aerospace is planning to commercialize an all-electric aircraft. Current battery-electric systems can only typically sustain short flights of about 100 to 200 miles, which is why they have been limited to air taxi operations by companies such as Joby and Archer.
Instead, testing of the X1 and a planned follow-on X2 aircraft will shape development of Heart Aerospace’s main offering to the airline industry—a 30-seat hybrid-electric regional airliner known as the ES-30.
That planned production aircraft for commercial flights would combine two inboard electric motors with commercial turboprop engines that run on jet fuel, enabling 125 miles of all-electric flight and 500 miles of flight range when operating in hybrid mode.
Looking to innovation as jet fuel prices rise
Having the extended 500-mile range would enable the ES-30 hybrid-electric airliner to operate in popular short-haul corridors that connect major US and European cities. United Airlines has committed to eventually purchasing 100 aircraft from Heart Aerospace, with other major airline customers also having signed letters of intent, according to Flying magazine.

'Fury' at Tarling death as cycling union calls for better helmets

The cyclists' union has expressed "fury" over the death of British rider Fin Tarling during Friday's stage of the Volta a Portugal.

And the union's president Adam Hansen told BBC Sport there needs to be better helmet safety as cyclists hit record-breaking speeds during races.
"We are speechless and filled with anger," said the Cyclistes Professionnels Associes (CPA) on social media.
"It is not right that a young athlete's life should end this way, and we are furious that even today it is still not possible to prevent such serious accidents.
"We share in the grief of his family, friends, team, and everyone who knew Finlay. Rest in peace, young rider; we pray for you, and we will carry you in our hearts."
Tarling was the younger brother of Josh, a time trial specialist for British super team Netcompany Ineos, who has won a stage of the Giro d'Italia and a European Time Trial title.
Fin Tarling himself had finished strongly in the time trial a few days earlier in the race he would never finish.
He was part of a new generation of male and female British riders on the World Tour who grew up on the success of highly decorated road cyclists, such as Mark Cavendish, Chris Froome and Lizzie Deignan, during a golden decade for British participation in the sport from 2012.
Just like all young professionals, Fin spent hours every day trying to extract as much performance as possible. But he was known to love every element of cycling and was always in the saddle.
His parents, Michael and Dawn, frequently attended races and even set up their own team in their home in Ceredigion, west Wales.
BBC Sport understands organisers are considering a tribute to Tarling at the men's Tour of Britain, which starts on 2 September.
