  - Published10 hours ago
- Britain's Finlay Tarling dies in Volta a Portugal accident 
  - Published1 day ago
Concerns as cycling gets faster and faster
As tributes to Tarling flowed in on Saturday the investigation into a "collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle" had begun, according to the National Republican Guard in Portugal.
Portuguese media are reporting the driver is unlikely to face charges., external
Cycling might not seem as dangerous as motorsport or boxing, but on descents out on public roads lycra-clad competitors can reach up to 60mph protected by nothing other than a helmet.
Although reporting on incidents has grown, the feeling in the sport is that there are more fatalities now as speeds increase.
In a sport where the peloton used to pick its moments to exert energy, today's racing is "full gas from the word go" as riders try to find pace advantages in all areas of stages.
At the Tour de France last month the record average speed was broken on stage 11 as riders reached 50.91km/h (31.6mph)., external
Six riders have died during road races in the past three years.
These include high-profile fatalities such as Switzerland's Muriel Furrer, who was not spotted leaving the road during the 2024 Road World Championships' junior road race, leaving a head injury untreated for more than an hour.
Furrer's compatriot Gino Mader was killed a year earlier during the Tour de Suisse following a high-speed crash on a descent.
Tarling's death is the first in a road race in 2026 and the full circumstances are yet to be disclosed.
"One thing we have to look at is helmets," Hansen told BBC Sport.
"They need a major upgrade. Bike helmets only need to meet standard testing like all helmets, EU standard CE EN 1078 is only rated for 19.5km/h and I do not believe this is enough for road racing."
BBC Sport has contacted the sport's world governing body the UCI for comment on helmet standards.
1 of 3
'To close every single road and driveway is difficult'
There are hazards everywhere along a road course in cycling and it is impossible to control exactly what lies around any corner across a stage which could be in excess of 100 miles.
In the biggest races in the sport, such as three-week Grand Tour the Tour de France, some stages take place on fully closed roads, but many World Tour events use a 'rolling roadblock'.
This is where police and organisers use motorbikes and cars to ensure the road is clear at certain junctions and temporarily enforce a closure in theory until all competitors have passed through.
It is a costly procedure which often involves more than 30 vehicles.
It is understood Friday's stage was using a rolling roadblock and that Tarling was adrift of the peloton, which is common for a rider who does not need to keep pace with the main bunch after a certain distance, or who may need to fall back for a team service car.
"The organisation is [generally] very good, but what happened [on Friday] is a bit of a hole in the system," added Hansen.
"When the breakaway or the main group goes past, sometimes the drivers [from the general public] think that's the whole race. But in fact there are riders behind and on some mountain stages the difference can be 45 minutes.
"If people do not know racing, then they just naturally think the race has past and go onto the course, where in fact there can be many groups."
There have been many examples where riders have had collisions or close calls with cars entering a live stage route regardless of the type of closure.
German Max Schachmann was hit by a car during Il Lombardia in 2020, and the 2023 Tour Feminin des Pyrenees was cancelled before the final stage after riders refused to compete following several close calls with vehicles on the route., external
Hansen added: "To close every single road and driveway is difficult and it gets to the point how little risk the organisers want to take and if it's even possible for them to have people at all those points."

Liechtenstein changes its rules to allow women to inherit the Alpine principality's throne
Liechtenstein’s royal house says the tiny country’s rules of succession will be changed so that a woman could in the future inherit the principality’s throne
BERLIN -- BERLIN (AP) — Liechtenstein 's royal house said on Saturday that the tiny country's rules of succession will be changed so that a woman could in the future inherit the principality's throne.
Hereditary Prince Alois announced the change in his speech marking the country's national day. He said it was approved on Wednesday by the necessary two-thirds majority of family members who can vote on such matters.
“The ability to combine continuity and renewal is also a principle that we foster inside the princely house,” Alois said, according to a text of his remarks posted on the house’s website. “In our centuries-old history, it has served us well to make decisions in a long-term and very well thought-out way.”
“The line of succession will be adjusted from male primogeniture to absolute primogeniture,” Alois said. “That means that in the future, the first-born child will, regardless of sex, become the heir to the throne and later the princess or prince of Liechtenstein.”
A statement from the princely house specified that the change will only apply to descendants of the children of Alois and his wife, Hereditary Princess Sophie, who are born in the future — so it won't affect the line of succession for now.
Prince Hans-Adam II remains the head of state, but in 2004 handed over most of his powers to Alois, his eldest son, who is now 58. That was in line with a tradition of Liechtenstein monarchs giving up the reins to their heirs.
The eldest of Alois' four children is 31-year-old Prince Joseph Wenzel. The second-oldest is Princess Marie Caroline, 29.
Liechtenstein, a wealthy nation of 40,000 people that borders Switzerland and Austria, has an unusually powerful monarchy by European standards. The ruling prince has the power to veto referendum results, appoint judges and fire the government.
The principality is traditionally conservative and in 1984 became the last European country to grant women the right to vote in national elections. Male voters narrowly approved the change, which Hans-Adam had backed, in a referendum.
Last year, Brigitte Haas became its first female prime minister.

As an only child, I really lucked out. My parents have always been there for me, not just as role models, but as friends, too.
Growing up, our family trips were always just the three of us, so I always saw my mom and dad as a unit. But in my early 30s, I started traveling with each of them separately, and realized how different those experiences could be.
When you strip someone away from their roles, they have the chance to just relax and be who they want to be. No responsibilities, no work, no need to take care of anyone or anything. I'm so glad I've had the chance to learn more about them as people and their interests beyond our comfort zones.
I got to see a different side of my father
This year, I surprised my dad with his dream trip to Islay, Scotland. He'd been talking about visiting for years, so we booked a tour for his 60th birthday. We spent our days touring whisky distilleries and traversing lesser-known coastal towns with our Glaswegian guide and the several other strangers we were with.
Usually, at home, my dad finds solace on his weekends away from the office. Instead of exploring Boston, he enjoys spending time just being up on his favorite shows. On our trip, this wasn't the case. Each morning was filled with new adventures, from skipping along the beach and distillery tastings on Islay, to scouring Edinburgh for his favorite spots he wanted to take me. Instead of having to listen to my ideas and passions, I got to explore his.
In Scotland, the travel version of my dad was unlocked. He was calm, spontaneous, lived in the moment, and just made the most of each day. My dad's sometimes a man of few words, but since it was just us, we chatted about all sorts and just laughed about our Scottish escapades.
My mom and I got to act like friends
A few months before, I had taken my mother on a much-needed retreat to Curaçao for Mother's Day weekend. We enjoyed a weekend of private lagoons, beaches, day trips, and relaxing time to do absolutely nothing — something we both needed.
Maybe it's a mom thing, but in our regular day-to-day life, mine seems to have it all figured out. She's the voice of reason, the one suggesting plans, and overall just someone you can always go to. She's usually pretty relaxed in general, no matter the situation, but I saw a version of her just so content and happy with really taking it slow. No time of day to wake up, nowhere to be, no priorities. We both found laughter and happiness in the simple things- a spontaneous trip to a brewery, people watching, and silly jokes with our tour guide driving around the island.
In Curaçao, my mom and I were just friends on a girly holiday. Most of our days were spent by the beach with drinks or floating around on pool noodles, but my favorite times were when we'd just hang out in our villa, chatting in our towels over a glass of wine.
I will continue to travel solo with my parents
From seeing the northern lights in Iceland to mingling with the locals in the Bahamas, some of my most memorable trips over the years have been with my parents, but getting the chance to travel with them separately was so special.
More on traveling with parents
My mom and dad will always be my parents, but on these trips, I had the chance to see them as individuals. Away from the daily hustle of life, away from responsibilities, and just as friends. I can't wait to plan our next one-on-one trips!

Warnings of possible measles outbreak as study finds 1.7 million Australians are vulnerable
In short:
A new study has found an estimated 1.7 million people are susceptible to catching measles, according to 2019 data.
The paper, to be published today, says susceptibility was high for key groups of Australians born from the late 1970s onwards.
What's next?
Travellers at a higher risk of bringing the disease into Australia are being urged to get another jab, as well as adults in at-risk age groups.
An estimated 1.7 million Australians are not protected against measles, putting the country at risk of more outbreaks, according to new analysis from the peak immunisation research organisation.
The National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance (NCIRS) study found almost seven per cent of the population was susceptible to measles in 2019.
The paper will be published today in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health, and lead author Zoë Croker said susceptibility was high for key age groups of Australians born from the late 1970s onwards.
The number of people susceptible included Australian babies who were not yet eligible for measles immunisations.
"The concern is that there will be more measles outbreaks that will be harder to contain," Ms Crocker said.
"We'll start to see more cases and a higher chance of there being a death associated."
'A warning sign'
Ms Crocker said the world-first study combined blood samples testing measles immunity, with vaccination data and represents the most comprehensive national estimate currently possible.
The analysis found overall measles immunity was 93.3 per cent, which epidemiologist Adrian Esterman said Australians must take as a "warning sign".
"[That] is not good enough. That means that we are at risk of getting major measles outbreaks,"
"We don't really want it to get any worse."
The World Health Organization has a target of achieving 93-95 per cent vaccine coverage, to establish herd immunity and prevent the spread of measles.
Australia achieved measles elimination status in 2014 but continues to have imported cases in overseas visitors and returning residents.
There were very few measles cases in Australia during the pandemic, but numbers have increased in the past two years.
Who is at risk and why should we be worried?
Anyone who is not fully vaccinated is at risk. Babies and young children are particularly at risk because they are not routinely vaccinated until 12 months old. So are those with reduced immunity and unvaccinated pregnant women because they can not be immunised while pregnant.
The paper identified the key age groups with higher levels of susceptibility to measles, which included infants and young children and people aged 42-49 years, 31-33 years and 25 and 26 years.
Ms Crocker said those groups were highly susceptible because of generational gaps in immunisation programs.
"The biggest gaps are in people born around the year 2000, as well as those born in 1993, 1994 and 1995, which was when that second dose of measles-containing vaccine was introduced," she said.
"Close behind are people in the early vaccine era, so born in 1977 to 1983… they're more likely to only have a single dose of measles-containing vaccine."
Ms Croker said people born during or since 1966 may also be more susceptible because they may have missed vaccination altogether or only be partially vaccinated.
However, she said some of these people may have life-long immunity from childhood measles infections.
Professor Esterman, from Adelaide University, said the numbers were daunting.
"We are at that stage where we need to be worried, we do not want our coverage rates to drop any more than they are now,"
"If a single infectious person goes into a room with a group of people who haven't got immunity, they will infect, very quickly, 12 to 15 of them. It's the most infectious disease we know about."
Overseas travellers urged to get another jab
Travellers are a higher risk of bringing measles into Australia, according to NCIRS associate director Frank Beard.
"We'd strongly encourage people in the current climate of increasing global outbreaks of measles to check … records of measles vaccination," Dr Beard said.
"If they haven't had good evidence that they previously received two doses at any time, then we strongly encourage them to get vaccinated again."
Professor Esterman said those aged between 20 and 40 years old were catching measles during overseas travel.
"Almost all of those cases are coming from people who've gone to Asia, so it could be the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, where they have quite large measles outbreaks … they come back and bring it with them," he said.
"There's a huge role here for GPs. If a patient is going overseas and talks to a GP about what they need in terms of protection, the GP should immediately ask them, what's your measles status like?"
Dr Beard said he would "strongly encourage" all adults in the at-risk age groups to consider getting another measles vaccine.
'We'll see more outbreaks'
Ms Crocker said measles would circulate more throughout Australia if herd immunity dipped below 93 per cent.
"It means that our public health system is less likely to be able to chase down every case and we are at a greater risk of measles then becoming more prominent in Australia."
Professor Esterman fears Australia will fall below the threshold for herd immunity, which will lead to "more and more outbreaks".
"It does mean that there will be some pockets of the Australian population which have got much lower coverage than that and that's where you start seeing these small outbreaks occurring," he said.
"It's in those pockets of the population, which have got lower coverage rates.
"This is telling us that there's something wrong, which we need to do something about."
The latest immunisation data shows childhood vaccination coverage declined for a fifth year in 2025.
Ms Crocker said her paper may "underestimate" susceptibility to measles, given childhood immunisation rates have dropped in recent years.

(Bloomberg) -- At least five people died in Indiana amid severe storms and floods, with President Donald Trump approving an emergency declaration for the inundated Midwestern state.
Power outages peaked at more than 300,000 homes and businesses, said Governor Mike Braun, after powerful storms brought record flooding forcing residents to flee their homes, closing roads and snarling rail traffic.
Flooding poses a risk not just for Indiana residents but also for its massive railroad network that helps connect the US throughout the Midwest and East. Rail disruptions as well as rain and strong winds could also upend Indiana’s agricultural industry, particularly corn and soybeans that dominate the state’s crop economy.
Additional storms Sunday could worsen the deluge with major flooding expected along the White River near Indianapolis, while moderate flooding is forecast for portions of the Wabash and White Rivers, the National Weather Service said in a statement at 4:51 a.m. local time on Sunday.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency authorized assistance on Saturday for more than half of Indiana’s counties in order to aid response efforts for “conditions resulting from severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes and flooding” that began on Aug. 11.
Rains continuing over the weekend were set to sweep not only the Hoosier State, where as much as 11 inches (28 centimeters) had fallen through early Saturday, but across the Midwest. Flood watches and warnings stretched from Iowa to West Virginia.
Braun declared a statewide emergency on Thursday and asked for a federal declaration, which Trump granted late on Saturday after a telephone conversation. “This ongoing emergency has resulted in deaths and injuries, destruction of homes, business and infrastructure, the displacement of families, and the disruption of emergency services and communications,” the governor said.
The White River, which runs across central and southern Indiana, has reached record heights in some places. One woman died when she was swept away after driving into floodwaters, the Associated Press reported. Hundreds of homes near the river in Indianapolis, the state’s largest city, were evacuated on Saturday.
“Indianapolis is experiencing its most severe flooding in 30-plus years. Conditions are shifting rapidly,” Joe Hogsett, mayor of the city of about 900,000 people, said Saturday on X.
In Noblesville, a suburban community north of Indianapolis, the river rose more than 20 feet (6 meters) since Tuesday, setting a record crest of 24.6 feet.

Seven killed in Israeli strike on southern Lebanon, country's PM says
- Published
An Israeli air strike has killed seven people in southern Lebanon, the nation's prime minister has said, in one of the deadliest attacks since an agreement aimed at reducing hostilities was announced in June.
The strike hit a house on the outskirts of Ansar at about 04:30 (01:30 GMT), in the Nabatieh district, where authorities say displaced families were living. Those killed included three children and two women, Lebanon's state-run news agency reported.
Israel's military said it had struck "Hezbollah terror infrastructure" in response to what it described as an earlier action against its soldiers.
The attack came as Israeli strikes intensified across parts of southern Lebanon overnight.
Later on Saturday morning, another round of strikes hit the town of Deir al Zahrani, killing two and injured nine others, according to the Lebanese ministry of health.
Social media footage shows large plumes of grey smoke permeating through the streets of the village as sirens ring in the background.
Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam condemned the attacks, saying the civilians killed were not "military infrastructure".
"Israel must halt this escalation," he said. "For the security of our people and their right to life on their land are not subject to negotiation or bargaining."
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the incident that had prompted its strike on Ansar took place in the Ali al-Taher Ridge, a strategic high ground overlooking much of south-eastern Lebanon and of the war's most fiercely contested positions.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) also reported a series of strikes around the ridge.
Near the border, several homes were reportedly destroyed in Bint Jbeil, while Israeli forces opened heavy machine gun fire towards houses, according to NNA.
Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah - the armed group affiliated with Iran - launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.
Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.
The June ceasefire framework calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.
Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun condemned the Israeli strikes that had killed an entire family in Ansar and its "repeated violations" of the framework, which he said sent a "clear message" to the US-led negotiations.
Hezbollah was not involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.
The IDF says it will continue to remove threats to Israeli citizens and soldiers operating in the security zone - the 10km-deep military buffer in southern Lebanon occupied by Israel.
Despite a reduction in fighting following the June agreements, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.
On Friday, Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem criticised the Lebanese authorities over the implementation of the framework, accusing them of putting pressure on the Lebanese army while Israeli attacks continued.
"How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" he said.
Lebanese and Israeli negotiators are set to meet for an eighth round of negotiations in September, but a final date has not been set.

A new survey in Arunachal Pradesh has documented recurring experiences of widespread harassment of members of the LGBTQIA+ community in the State.
Also read | On India’s rainbow trail | Queer-focused walks are finding an audience in the country
According to the Itanagar-based HimKai Research Institute (HRI), the pestering or provocation has led to identity concealment, discrimination-related distress, and low confidence in institutional protection among the LGBTQIA+ respondents in the State.
LGBTQIA+ expands to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer or Questioning, Intersex, and Asexual.
The HRI conducted the anonymous online survey between June 2 and August 2. It received 62 submissions, one of which was excluded during geographic eligibility and data-quality screening because the self-reported home district could not be mapped in Arunachal Pradesh.
“Among the 61 respondents included in the analysis, 49.2% said they hid their gender identity or sexual orientation most of the time or always because of fear of discrimination or violence. Half of valid respondents said they felt accepted within their family rarely or never, while 44.3% said they felt safe in their local community rarely or never,” the HRI report said.
“Experiences of harassment and discrimination were reported across several settings. Some 91.8% of respondents reported verbal harassment at least rarely, while 52.5% reported physical threats or violence at least rarely. Among valid responses, 85.0% reported discrimination in school or college at least rarely, and 63.2% reported workplace discrimination,” it said.
The survey also found that 72.9% of valid respondents felt compelled to change their behaviour or appearance sometimes or more often to retain work or education. A further 57.9% said their identity affected access to employment or income opportunities at least rarely.
Religious, cultural exclusion
“Mental wellbeing emerged as a significant concern. Among valid responses, 76.7% reported experiencing stress, anxiety or emotional distress related to discrimination sometimes or more often, including 48.3% who experienced it most of the time or always. Access to mental-health or peer support was uneven: 41.0% said such support was available most of the time or always, while 36.1% said it was available rarely or never,” the report said.
The findings also point to a gap between awareness of rights and confidence in institutions. While 56.7% of valid respondents agreed that they were aware of their legal rights, 63.3% disagreed that laws and policies adequately protect LGBTQIA+ persons, and 66.7% disagreed that police and authorities respond sensitively to LGBTQIA+ issues.
Religion, culture and social belonging received particularly cautious assessments. Some 72.1% did not agree that religion or faith practices are accepting of LGBTQIA+ persons. More than half disagreed that their identity is compatible with their cultural or tribal background or that local traditions allow space for diverse identities, with 51.7% of valid respondents disagreeing that they feel a sense of belonging in society.
Healthcare emerged as a comparatively more positive area. Among valid respondents, 56.7% said that they felt comfortable accessing healthcare most of the time or always, and 75.0% said healthcare providers treated them with respect most of the time or always.
“Friends were the most frequently reported source of support, mentioned by 37 respondents, followed by LGBTQIA+ networks, mentioned by 12.
Six respondents mentioned. Awareness and sensitisation were the most common single priority identified for improving LGBTQIA+ lives in Arunachal Pradesh, followed by legal protection,” the report said.
HRI director Ranju Dodum said the study was intended to begin building locally grounded evidence on experiences that are often discussed without adequate data.
“LGBTQIA+ experiences in Arunachal Pradesh cannot simply be assumed from national conversations. Family, community, tribal identity, religion, education and employment all shape how people experience acceptance and safety here. This is a baseline study and its numbers must be read with methodological caution, but they point to questions that deserve deeper research and serious public discussion,” he said.
The report recommends sustained sensitisation programmes in schools, colleges, workplaces, healthcare institutions, police and public administration; confidential mechanisms for reporting discrimination; stronger mental-health and peer-support systems; safe community spaces; more inclusive education and workplace practices; and locally grounded engagement with families, community institutions and faith leaders.
The survey sample was predominantly young, with 90.2% of respondents between 18 and 35 years.

Jason Arday, Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism, is found dead
LONDON — A British sociologist who resigned last week from the University of Cambridge following weeks of public accusations of plagiarism and media scrutiny was found dead Friday.
Jason Arday, who was 37 when he became Cambridge's youngest Black professor in 2023, resigned after he came under intense media pressure, with weeks of allegations about plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.
The Times and Telegraph newspapers, along with the BBC and Sky News, reported that Arday, 41, was found "unresponsive" inside a home in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.
News of his death comes the same week as the release of his memoir, "Great and Unfortunate Things," a highly anticipated work that Simon & Schuster had decided to release despite the doubts about his credibility. In a statement issued through his publisher, Arday's family said that they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."
"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," the family said, adding that for three years Arday was "subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse ... by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him."
The Metropolitan Police said only that a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead in Battersea, without naming the man, in accordance with its policy.
"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," the police statement said.
Cambridge Vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice, who earlier announced that the university will investigate the circumstances around Arday's employment, said she was "desperately saddened" by the news.
"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she said.
In resigning as professor of sociology of education, Arday wrote in a statement that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."
He said his stepping down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me." He has denied plagiarism, but admitted to some mistakes when working on his doctorate.
Supporters, including more than two dozen academics and politicians, had described the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to undermine Arday and other Black people who hold "positions of influence."
Arday's appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens.
Cambridge has opened investigation into plagiarism accusations
In his memoir, Arday wrote of himself as born to achieve and born to struggle. He remembered a family "legend" that the 1980s hit "Everybody Wants to Rule the World" was on the radio at the time of his birth. He described how a midwife noted his long fingers and told his mother that it was a sign he was meant for greatness. In his early 20s, he recalled, he was on a relief mission in Brazil when an aid worker placed a hand on his arm and also predicted an extraordinary life.
"But I also believe you're destined for very sad and difficult things as well," she warned him.
Questions about Arday's qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a one-time Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his critique of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests.
On July 24, the Times of London published an analysis of Arday's 2015 Ph.D. thesis highlighting what it said were multiple examples of passages that were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.
British media also raised questions about Arday's claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($7.4 million) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.
Dozens of Cambridge academics had signed a letter calling for an independent inquiry into how Arday was appointed. Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.
The university then changed its stance and said it opened an investigation "following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."
Prentice, the university's vice-chancellor, said this week that Cambridge will run a review of its hiring processes. She stressed that "our staff of color are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community."
"This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge," she said Thursday.

Why Trump is tearing up a beloved national park
Big Bend National Park is the latest casualty of Trump’s border wall obsession.
Welcome to The Logoff: Remember President Donald Trump’s first-term border wall? It’s still being built — through a pristine Texas national park.
What’s happening? The Trump administration is preparing to build hundreds of miles of roads through Big Bend National Park in southwest Texas as part of its latest border security project, despite a bipartisan outcry over damage to the beloved park.
Starting last week, bulldozers and heavy machinery began to clear land for the construction of about 200 miles of patrol road, new border barriers, and electronic surveillance measures to cover the park’s 118 miles of shared border with Mexico. The construction is proceeding after the administration overrode environmental laws intended to protect places like Big Bend earlier this year.
What does a border wall look like in 2026? In this case, “wall” is a bit of a misnomer. Despite Trump’s fixation with an actual, physical wall circa 2016, the Trump administration’s current project isn’t always 30 feet high and topped with concertina wire.
Instead, the Big Bend project is part of what the administration has described as a “smart wall,” which will combine stretches of traditional wall elsewhere along the US-Mexico border with patrol roads and vehicle barriers like those planned for the park, all blanketed with surveillance.
It’s a small retreat from the administration’s original plan for a border wall through Big Bend, which sparked outrage earlier this year. Still, the administration intends to build about 700 additional miles of “primary” wall, spanning all four border states. The whole project is slated to cost around $47 billion.
Why Big Bend? It’s hard to say. As the New York Times reported earlier this year, the park has long been considered low-priority given its remote location and inhospitable weather. Only about 1 percent of those apprehended for crossing the US-Mexico border have been detained in Big Bend.

As rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief stepped outside his home in Murrah, a remote mountain village in Indian-administered Kashmir. His daughter had asked him to move the family’s car to a safer place as the rain got heavier.
“I had only just parked it,” Latief recalled. “When I turned around, I saw the water coming.” Minutes later, a cloudburst sent mud, boulders and water crashing down the hillside.
Latief, 48, had spent years building the house, where five generations of his Gujjar family lived together. Within minutes, the torrent swallowed it, trapping eight family members inside. He survived only because he had stepped outside. By dawn, everything he had built lay in rubble.
When the Guardian reached Murrah four days later, electricity, roads and mobile networks were cut off. Floodwaters had washed away roads and footbridges, leaving the only way into the village a 90-minute walk through rain and landslide debris. Residents carried sacks of flour, cooking gas cylinders and medicines across the broken crossing.
Murrah is perched high in the Pir Panjal range above the town of Bafliaz, in Poonch district, about 125 miles (200km) south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir’s main city. The village is home to mostly Gujjars, one of the largest pastoralist communities in the Himalayas, whose livelihoods have long depended on livestock, farming and seasonal migration through the mountains.
The hillside remained too unstable for excavators to reach. Soldiers, disaster response teams and local volunteers searched the debris by hand while others combed the swollen Suran River for the missing.
Latief now lives in the house of his brother, Mohd Bashir, just above the landslide. Inside, women gathered to mourn while men quietly received visitors offering condolences. Verses from the Qur’an echoed through the house.
“I built that house for my family,” Latief said, holding up pictures of his 16-year-old son Sajjad Ahmed, an aspiring cricketer, whose body was still missing. Days before the disaster, the family recorded videos together.
As mourners gathered, news spread that another body had been found several miles down the river; the room fell silent as another funeral procession passed through the village.
Among those searching was Mohammad Razak, 45, who had spent four days combing the river with a team of volunteers. “We’ve been searching every bend of the river,” he said. “We’re still hoping we’ll find them.”
Murrah was among the worst-hit places after a series of cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides swept Jammu and Kashmir this month, killing at least 28 people. Scientists say rising temperatures are increasing the likelihood of short, intense rainfall events across the western Himalayas. In steep mountainous terrain, these rains can trigger rapid flooding and landslides, putting remote communities at increased risk. For mountain communities, the climate crisis is also exacerbating longstanding geographical and social vulnerabilities.
The destruction stretched far beyond Murrah. About 30 miles away in Rajouri, the Manawar Tawi River burst its banks, washing away roads, dozens of vehicles and the town’s main Bela bus station.
Low-lying settlements along the riverbank were submerged in mud and debris. Several houses collapsed across the Pir Panjal mountains, livestock were swept away and hundreds of families were displaced.
About 180 miles north, in Gurez Valley near the line of control with Pakistan-administered Kashmir, residents say they are seeing the same pattern. A cloudburst in Achoora village on 20 July damaged the crops of 11 families and blocked the valley’s only road.
Residents say increasingly erratic rainfall is disrupting farming and making traditional livelihoods more precarious. It followed a series of cloudbursts that hit Gurez and neighbouring Tulail over the past month, damaging homes, farmland, bridges, and roads.
“People knew when the snow would come and when to plant crops,” said Aamir Asghar Khan, 26, a resident of Achoora. “Nothing seems predictable any more. The rain is getting more intense every year, and the frequent cloudbursts are threatening our livelihoods.”
Heavy rainfall also triggered devastating floods and landslides in Ladakh and across the border in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, reinforcing concerns that increasingly erratic weather is affecting communities across the western Himalayas.
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (Icimod) said the western Himalayas were experiencing frequent bursts of intense rainfall capable of triggering floods, landslides and cloudbursts. Accelerating glacier melt is likely to increase flood risks in the short term before reducing water availability in coming decades.
“The challenge our mountain communities face is twofold – too much water at times and too little at others,” an expert from Icimod said. “Adaptation requires work on both fronts, managing flood risk and water scarcity together.”
ICIMOD said priorities included expanding community-based early warning systems, installing more weather stations in high-altitude areas, restoring damaged watersheds and designing roads and other infrastructure for future weather conditions rather than historical weather patterns.
Dr Suheel Rasool Mir, a Kashmir-based sociologist who studies Indigenous communities in Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, said pastoral communities were among the first to bear the consequences of erratic weather as their livelihoods relied directly on forests, rivers, grazing lands and seasonal migration.
“For Gujjar, Bakarwal and Dard-Shin communities, these disasters are not simply natural hazards,” he said. “As climate extremes become more frequent, they lose not only homes and livestock but also the ecological knowledge and ancestral livelihoods that have sustained them for generations.”
For Latief back in Murrah, only one hope remained. “I just want to find them,” he said. “Then we can bury our family together.”

17 arrested, HK$3.67m seized in crackdown on scam group using Malaysian ‘runners’
Police say arrests connected to phone scams that targeted 22 people and resulted in losses of HK$2.5 million between June and August
Hong Kong police have arrested 17 people and seized HK$3.67 million in a crackdown on a fraud syndicate that recruited foreign “runners” from Malaysia to collect crime proceeds from victims.
The force’s Kowloon West crime squad said on Sunday that the arrests were made in connection with “guess who I am” phone scams that duped 22 victims out of about HK$2.5 million between June and August. The single largest loss was HK$700,000.
Such cons typically involve scammers calling victims and impersonating relatives or friends to request quick cash to settle bogus claims of arrests or other emergencies.
Police said the crime syndicate had recruited runners from Malaysia to collect the cash directly from victims and take it to three transit points. They were offered HK$500 to HK$1,000 a day, with their flights and accommodation also covered, the force added.
“When officers successfully located the address of a victim and arrived at their door to investigate, the victim was still unaware that he had been scammed and firmly believed the money he had handed over earlier was paid to police [for bail],” Senior Inspector Ng Yin-pak said.
“Police successfully recovered the entire HK$200,000 in defrauded funds for the victim in the operation.”
Following an investigation, officers have arrested 12 Malaysian men, aged 20 to 48, on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud over the past two months.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Gregory Brooks, a 57-year-old based in Rochester, New York. It's been edited for length and clarity.
After reluctantly resigning from my technology services job at a community college in May, I was terrified to be out of work.
I'm not a young guy anymore. Starting over at 57 feels like a mix of humiliation and frustration — and it feels harder than when I was younger. I think for the most part, young professionals are more willing to work late, sacrifice work-life balance, and hustle to climb the corporate ladder. I'm not looking to build my career the way I did as a 20-something hustling to finish my Ph.D.
I want to do my job well, but I'm not that young adult running around all excited trying to impress everybody.
I worked with a lot of older students at the community college who expressed feeling inadequate, being surrounded by younger students who were academically ahead of them. I'm fighting those same feelings, but I've been through unemployment before, and I know how to get through.
I've been mass applying out of a sense of panic
I was panicked to be out of work because the jobs I've had in the past have been local, and I haven't found many opportunities in Rochester. I figured I might need to apply to jobs that require travel, which isn't ideal. I'm getting to a point where I really like getting home every night to my wife and dog.
I thankfully earned a Project Management Professional (PMP) certification while in my last role, which is kind of an ace in my pocket. It's something I've been leaning into heavily while searching for IT and project management roles.
I've been applying to jobs on LinkedIn and Indeed, reaching out to friends for leads, and contacting local IT recruiters. To some extent, I've been mass-applying out of panic and desperation, but I've been trying to refine my search a bit more.
I've made it a goal to do some sort of job searching and connection-making each day, and taking each step as the little win that it is.
The rejections have taken a toll on my self-esteem, and my age could be working for or against me
Rejections are all part of the process, but it's taken a big toll on my self-esteem and contributed to situational depression. My job was a big part of my identity, and leaving it was a big blow.
I have a lot of worry about what my next role will be, what it will look like, and whether I will even find a role where my skills are a good fit.
An employer could see me on a video call and question if I'm going to leave the company soon to retire, but they could also see my age and think it means I probably won't leave after a couple of years for something better.
They might think I bring wisdom and experience, but they also might see my age as a hindrance. We all look at people and make assumptions, so I absolutely think age is a consideration in the job market.
It's exhausting to think some jobs may have that expectation of having that "rah-rah" energy.
I'm staying engaged in hobbies and focusing on positive self-talk
Thank God I have reading as a way to escape from reality. I'm a voracious reader, and I like legal thrillers and the occasional financial thriller. My wife and I also have an eight-month-old Labrador retriever puppy who's been keeping us outside and on our feet.
Read more stories about job hunting, unemployment, and starting over after 50.
It's also been important for me to have conversations with myself each day, reminding myself that I've made it through this before and that I'll make it through again. It's always hardest when you're in the tunnel.
I know what unemployment was like last time. I have no problem admitting that it's been a tremendous stress, so it's important to have a positive way of dealing with it. Because of that, I've decided to see a counselor, just like I did 11 years ago when I was out of work
Counseling helped me navigate unemployment 11 years ago — and it's helping me now
The first time I saw a counselor, I shared successes and frustrations with the job search, the severe toll the depression and anxiety were having on my interest in doing much of anything, and the agonizing guilt that I was somehow letting down my wife by not finding a job quickly enough.
My counselor engaged me in mindfulness, through which I recognized and owned my present emotions, whatever they were. If I were feeling sad, I'd accept it. I also had to own what I could do in the present to address the sadness, like going for a walk or reading my book.
The anxiety and depression returned almost immediately this time around. I had my second Zoom session with a new counselor recently, and I still need time to build trust with her. It takes time to not only build a relationship, but give her time to find her footing as a helper and me to find my footing as a person in need of help.
It's been difficult separating my worth from a job.
Acknowledge how you're feeling and lean on support
If you're job-seeking, lean on your support network, not only for job hunting, but for your mental health. My wife is very supportive, and after 25 years of marriage, we've learned how to support each other and understand each other's idiosyncrasies.
The biggest thing I'd recommend for older job seekers is to acknowledge what you're feeling. There's this taboo, especially for older men, around expressing your feelings.
Be honest, and if you're feeling down, acknowledge it. "I'm feeling down today. What can I do to at least find some light?"
Are you navigating a career change in your 50s? Contact this reporter at tmartinelli@businessinsider.com to share your story.

Taliban leaders mark 5 years in power in Afghanistan as UN official warns of crisis
Taliban rulers have celebrated the fifth anniversary of their return to power in Afghanistan
KABUL, Afghanistan -- Taliban rulers and other officials gathered at Afghanistan’s traditional Loya Jirga assembly hall on Saturday to celebrate the fifth anniversary of their return to power, touting having brought stability and an end to conflict after decades of upheaval.
A top United Nations official, however, warned of a grave human rights crisis in the country where girls above the age of 12 are denied an education.
The Taliban seized power on Aug. 15, 2021, as the U.S. and other NATO troops withdrew following a costly two-decade war. The U.S. withdrawal led to chaos at Kabul airport as crowds of people tried to flee the country in desperation.
Soon after taking power, the Taliban administration imposed a ban on girls’ education beyond the sixth grade and later also banned higher education for women, despite having pledged before the takeover that women would be allowed access to education, employment and public participation.
Women have also been banned from public spaces such as gyms and parks, from taking part in sports and traveling to distant locations without a male guardian.
At the Loya Jirga, high-ranking officials were joined by some foreign representatives and thousands of ordinary citizens for speeches marking what they said was Afghanistan's liberation from American forces.
The Taliban government remains isolated internationally, with Russia being the only country to have recognized it formally.
“We pray to Almighty God to forever protect our homeland from occupation, aggression, wars, and insecurity, and to enable our people to enjoy peace, tranquility, and prosperity under the auspices of the Sharia-based government,” the Taliban government’s deputy spokesman, Hamdullah Fitrat, said during the ceremony.
There were no women present.
Celebrations were also held in provinces across Afghanistan, where Taliban flags and posters emblazoned with slogans in praise of the Taliban’s return to power were displayed along major roads and marketplaces.
In a video message, Richard Bennett, the U.N. special rapporteur on the human rights situation in Afghanistan, said the country was undergoing a deep human rights crisis.
“While the era of war has ended, it’s questionable whether there’s real peace, and the human rights situation has steadily deteriorated, most dramatically for women and girls,” Bennett said. “My mandate has concluded that this system amounts to the crime against humanity of gender persecution.”
“The crisis extends well beyond gender discrimination, even beyond gender apartheid,” he continued. “Across Afghanistan we continue to document arbitrary arrests, torture and ill treatment, extrajudicial killings, corporal punishment, enforced disappearances, restrictions on freedom of expression, attacks on journalists and human rights defenders, persecution of ethnic and religious minorities, discrimination against LGBT plus persons, and the reduction of civic space.”
Bennett warned the international community against “normalizing” the Taliban’s policies, saying it would legitimize the discrimination and tell “victims their suffering is negotiable.”
In an interview with The Associated Press this week, Molvi Hayatullah Mahajar Farahi, deputy minister in the Taliban government for broadcasting at the Ministry of Information and Culture, said despite “challenges and difficulties” the administration has in the past five years delivered security, infrastructure and created jobs.
Farahi, when asked, did not address the issue of the education of girls and women but said “the level of investment made in universities surpasses anything seen in the past."
The U.N. agency on education and culture, UNESCO, estimates that some 2.4 million girls have been excluded from secondary education.
The world body’s agency on women’s rights, U.N. Women, said this week that women and girls are facing the harshest restriction in the world and that the bans are damaging Afghanistan’s future, with the lack of teachers, doctors, nurses and midwives threatening the country’s social and economic foundations.

India’s AI story has grown beyond building an Indian equivalent of ChatGPT. The current phase is about building the infrastructure, data and applications that can make AI work for India and give Indian companies an edge in markets beyond the country. The government is already doing its bit. The IndiaAI Mission, with an outlay of roughly ₹10,300 Cr, is backing around 20 indigenous sovereign AI model proposals, spanning 12 large and eight small language models. It is also building a public dataset platform and offering subsidised access to GPUs for startups, tackling two of the biggest constraints facing India’s AI ambitions: data and compute. But the more interesting signs are emerging outside the government programme. A new generation of AI founders is moving beyond the race to build yet another general-purpose model and tackling problems that require deeper domain expertise. Some are building the data infrastructure needed to teach machines how the physical world works. Others are developing sovereign inference platforms, AI systems that can operate across India’s many languages, and tools tailored to the quirks of Indian enterprises and consumers. This shift matters because India’s AI advantage may not come from building the biggest model, but from building systems around AI that are difficult to replicate — proprietary datasets, local-language capabilities, domain-specific intelligence, and applications designed around problems that Western AI companies have historically overlooked. The opportunity is already drawing capital. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, H1 2026, Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn in the first six months of 2026, nearly four times the amount raised during the same period last year. The funding boom, however, is only one part of the story. The more telling signal is where founders are choosing to deploy that capital. As India marks its 80th Independence Day, we are back with yet another edition of Inc42’s AI Startups To Watch. This edition of the AI Startups To Watch offers a glimpse into what India’s next AI layer could look like — from the data needed to train machines on the physical world and AI-powered cinematic content to enterprise productivity, deeptech healthcare and education. These are not simply startups using AI as a feature. They are attempting to build businesses around some of the hardest problems that emerge when AI moves from the laboratory into the real world. With that thought, here are the five emerging ventures that made it to the eleventh edition of Inc42’s AI Startups To Watch. Editor's Note: This is not a ranking. The startups featured here are a curated selection by the Inc42 editorial team and are listed alphabetically. Clairva | Contextual Intelligence For World Models As AI moves from understanding language to operating in the physical world, the training data behind these systems is changing. A robot learning to navigate a kitchen or a world model trying to understand human movement cannot learn everything it needs from text and internet images. Clairva converts real-world video into structured behavioural signals that models can use for training, fine-tuning and evaluation. Founded in 2025 by Sunil Nair, Dushyant Verma and Sabari Raju, the startup sits at the intersection of AI training data, multimodal AI and embodied AI. Its pipeline structures elements such as movement, object interaction, task sequence, gesture, speech and cultural context, combined with consent, licensing, provenance and usage-right information. The output is a model-ready dataset whose origin, permissions and structure are known. Clairva is deliberately building deep supply in markets where AI training data remains thin: India, Southeast Asia and the wider Global South. It follows a B2B model, licensing datasets to AI labs, robotics companies and multimodal developers, and recently raised $500,000 in pre-seed funding led by Venture Catalysts. The startup is targeting a combination of markets. Among them, the AI training dataset market is projected to reach $16.3 Bn by 2033, while the embodied AI market is forecast to hit $23.06 Bn by 2030. Coreworks | Offering AI-Powered Business Intelligence Founders, marketers and analysts often spend days assembling presentations, only to have a number questioned in a meeting without being able to trace where it came from. Coreworks is building a platform that connects directly to a company's data and generates a finished report or presentation, with every figure traceable to its source. Founded in 2025 by Prashant Kumar and Pavan Sondur, the platform reads data semantically, surfaces the metrics and trends that matter, and produces an editable deck in minutes rather than days. Each metric links to the exact formula, cell, or row behind it, so updating the source automatically updates the output. Users can upload their own brand deck so the output matches their design language. The startup is targeting the report and presentation automation space, targeting India's augmented analytics market, which is estimated to reach $2.89 Bn by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 17.6%. It is positioning itself as an alternative to the manual process of assembling and verifying board-ready decks from raw spreadsheets. eNLife Research | AI-Powered Early Detection For Neurodegenerative Diseases Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's are often detected only after symptoms appear, when treatment options have narrowed. India-based eNLife Research is combining biomarker research with AI-powered analytics to build an end-to-end pipeline from detection to personalised intervention. Founded in 2025 by Deepak Kumaran Nair, Jojo Jacob and Anish Mathew, the research organisation works across biomarker discovery, early detection systems, nanoscale precision therapeutics and personalised treatment protocols based on individual genetic and biomarker profiles. Its technology platform combines multiple biomarker modalities with AI analytics for early detection and risk assessment, targeting 95% accuracy and a 24-hour turnaround for results. eNLife's diagnostics are built on blood-based and neuroimaging biomarkers alongside large population studies, going beyond conventional scans to enable early detection. It is working towards accessible, affordable diagnostics that can be deployed in routine healthcare years before symptoms appear. The platform says it has more than 28 publications, over 1,700 study participants, six active studies and 15-plus collaborations. eNLife Research is capitalising on the growing push for early diagnosis in neurology, focusing on India's Alzheimer's disease diagnostics market, which is projected to reach $600.2 Mn by 2033. Kalpnk | An AI-First Filmmaking Studio Filmmaking has long been a slow and expensive process, with commercials taking weeks to produce and costs that put premium content out of reach for many brands and storytellers. Kalpnk is a studio using AI workflows to create cinematic content, from brand visuals and commercials to short-form reels and AI films. Founded in 2025 by Sameer Talawdekar, Aayush Raj and Manav Soni, the studio is led by filmmakers and writers, with AI enhancing their vision across ideation, moodboards, images, animation, editing, sound and music. It produces high-impact 10- 15-second brand reels, premium commercials and pitch decks and storyboards for studios. Kalpnk says it delivers a finished commercial in about five days on average, cutting production time by around 85% and cost by roughly 70%. The studio operates on a cloud-based, global-commission model, targeting brands and storytellers seeking faster, more flexible production. It operates in the AI-generated video market that is becoming an increasingly attractive option for brands in India. The market is projected to grow from about $31.8 Mn in 2025 to $142 Mn by 2033. UpKraft | AI-Powered Extracurricular Learning Music, dance and other extracurricular skills are often taught inconsistently at home or in communities, with little structure or visible progress. UpKraft is building structured extracurricular learning at home, in housing societies and in schools, led by expert tutors and powered by AI. Founded in 2025 by Tejasvi Singh Kushwah, Varun Mangal and Kritika Varandani, the platform covers guitar, piano, drums, violin, vocals, dance and fitness, with certified and vetted instructors, level-based learning paths and clear progress tracking. Its AI Practice Studio provides real-time feedback to help learners fix practice gaps. For tutors, UpKraft offers an all-in-one toolkit covering student enrolment, a 2,000+ song library, payments, scheduling and automated parent updates. For schools and academies, it provides admin tools, an AI practice companion and global resources, supporting classroom, hybrid or remote teaching. The startup is targeting the structured extracurricular learning and edtech space, serving learners, tutors, academies and schools while expanding into certification-aligned music education. UpKraft is targeting the after-school and extracurricular program market, which was valued at about 34.46 Bn in 2026 and is projected to reach $62.38 Bn by 2033. If you’ve followed mental health topics on TikTok or Instagram lately, you have probably heard the term emotional regulation. But emotional regulation isn’t just a trendy buzzword. It’s a nuanced concept that psychologists like me have been studying for decades.
At its core, emotional regulation is how well someone can manage their emotions – whether positive ones like excitement and joy, or negative or more uncomfortable ones like jealousy and anger.
I study emotional regulation – which scientists refer to as simply “emotion regulation” – within the context of relationships, including understanding how children learn to regulate their own emotions. The goal of healthy emotional regulation is not to erase difficult feelings, but to be able to manage those feeling more effectively so they do not become overwhelming.
Emotional regulation versus temperament
People often confuse emotional regulation with temperament, which is your natural, inborn style for how you approach or react to the world. Psychologists describe three different types of temperament that a person can have: easy and flexible; active, outgoing and excitable; or cautious and quiet. Temperament is genetically and biologically driven – in other words, it is something you are born with.
Emotional regulation, on the other hand, isn’t something people either have or don’t have. It is a set of skills that develops over time, beginning in childhood as children learn from and interact with the people around them. And like other skills, emotional regulation can be strengthened with instruction and practice.
There are two types of emotional regulation: self-regulation, or managing your own emotions, and co-regulation, which involves helping others manage their emotions. Both are important in romantic relationships, at work and in parenting.
Co-regulation is especially important as a way to help kids respond to intense feelings.
Taming emotional cycles
Emotions don’t exist on their own. They are part of an ongoing conversation between your mind, your body and your behavior. The way you think affects how your body responds, your body’s reactions influence how you feel, and your feelings shape what you do.
For example, imagine someone cuts you off in traffic. Within moments, several things happen at once. You may feel a surge of rage as your heart starts racing, your palms begin to sweat, and thoughts like “What a #$% jerk!” flash through your mind. Those reactions may lead you to respond by rolling your eyes, swearing at the steering wheel or flipping off the driver.
Each of these reactions influences the others, creating an emotional cycle that can escalate or de-escalate, depending on how you respond. Understanding this cycle is important because changing just one part of it can shift the entire emotional experience.
Responding instead of reacting
Everyone engages in emotional regulation throughout the day – whether consciously or not. Healthy emotional regulation allows people to use their emotions as valuable sources of information rather than letting them take over their lives or ruin their day.
Emotions can signal that something feels threatening, unfair, exciting, disappointing or important, prompting you to pause and consider what might have triggered the reaction.
In the traffic example above, anger may be a clue that you perceived the other driver’s behavior as dangerous or disrespectful. Your emotion doesn’t mean your interpretation is wrong or right, but it does provide useful information about how you are experiencing the situation, which can help you decide how to respond.
Many people use emotional regulation strategies intentionally during the day to deal with uncomfortable or intense emotions. These include taking a walk, venting to a friend or shooting hoops. Or they might include less healthy options, such as doomscrolling, being irritable with loved ones or pouring that third glass of wine.
Multiple factors, such as life stressors – even sleep quality – can make it harder for people to regulate or contain tough emotions, increasing the risk of less-than-healthy coping strategies.
When emotional regulation falls short
We psychologists can’t talk about emotional regulation without talking about its opposite state – emotional dysregulation. That’s when you are not able to successfully use coping skills to deal with tough feelings, and those feelings then interfere with your ability to function.
Instead of using strategies that might serve as life rafts for when the seas of daily life become difficult, the waves wash over you – which can feel like you are drowning in the intensity of these feelings.
Yet it isn’t the emotion itself that’s the problem. Rather, it’s how you interpret the emotion, the story you tell yourself about it, and how you respond to it. When emotions become difficult to manage and begin interfering with how you think, act or function, that’s emotion dysregulation.
Prolonged emotion dysregulation has profound costs that extend far beyond how you feel in the moment.
Emotional dysregulation can affect a person’s physical health, including heart and immune system functioning, disrupt sleep, contribute to mental health problems and make it more difficult to be present and responsive in your relationships. It can also impair your memory, concentration and performance in everyday activities – not to mention your finances.
Research suggests that learning to address emotional dysregulation early on can reduce the risk of long-term consequences, including serious mental health conditions such as major mood disorders and borderline personality disorder.
Emotional regulation can be learned
Learning emotional regulation strategies begins with identifying your feelings and building a vocabulary to describe them. You can’t regulate what you can’t name.
Children learn emotional regulation skills by watching people around them. Parents and other caregivers can help their children by serving as an “emotional container,” naming emotions and modeling how to express them in a healthy way.
In the moment, emotional regulation strategies can include breathing or mindfulness techniques that help calm the body’s nervous system and turn down the intensity of emotions.
Longer term, skills from cognitive-behavioral therapy, one of the most effective forms of talk therapy for anxiety and depression, can help. These skills include learning to view difficult experiences as opportunities for growth, questioning unhelpful thoughts instead of automatically believing them, and accepting emotions without letting them take over.
Rather than trying to avoid or eliminate difficult feelings, the goal is to notice them and recognize that your emotions are not always accurate reflections of reality – in other words, that feelings are not facts. Then you can choose how to respond.
Talking through difficult emotions with someone you trust can help you feel understood, gain perspective and make it easier to respond thoughtfully rather than react impulsively.
Taking care of your body also supports emotional regulation. Getting enough sleep, eating a balanced diet and moving your body regularly helps your brain function at its best, making it easier to manage stress, think clearly and respond thoughtfully.
For healthy long-term emotional regulation skills, practicing matters. Just like working out your biceps in the gym, if you use these skills consistently, your capacity for responding can grow.
Jessica Griffin, Associate Professor of Psychiatry and Peditrics, UMass Chan Medical School

Shopian , Aug. 16: Former PDP MLA from Wachi, Aijaz Ahmad Mir, on Sunday said he was detained by police at his residence in Zainapora in south Kashmir’s Shopian district ahead of a proposed protest at Ghanta Ghar, Shopian, demanding the introduction of a comprehensive crop insurance scheme for apples and cherries.
Mir told Greater Kashmir that police had locked the gate of his residence and prevented him from leaving. “They have also sealed the roads,” he alleged.
Mir had called on farmers to gather at Gole Chowk, Shopian, to press for the introduction of a comprehensive crop insurance scheme amid growing concerns over weather-related losses.
Recent hailstorms and windstorms have damaged apple orchards across Kashmir, spelling losses for hundreds of growers across more than two dozen affected orchards. With growers lacking a comprehensive insurance safety net, farmers have been left exposed to mounting losses from extreme weather.
Despite his detention, Mir said the protest went ahead. Taking to X, he said, “Despite being placed under house detention today, the voice of our farmers could not be silenced. Hundreds of fruit growers gathered at Ghanta Ghar, Shopian, and peacefully protested in support of our genuine demands.”
The protesters also sought adequate compensation for affected growers and measures to safeguard the horticulture sector, a key pillar of Jammu and Kashmir’s rural economy.
Reacting to Mir’s detention, PDP leader Iltija Mufti criticised the move, alleging that it was aimed at preventing a peaceful sit-in by Mir and hundreds of Kashmiri apple farmers seeking a comprehensive crop insurance scheme.

In a post on X, Mufti described the detention as an act of “high-handedness and intolerance” and said horticulture, which she called the backbone of Jammu and Kashmir’s economy, was reeling from losses worth hundreds of crores because of the government’s “apathy” and refusal to address farmers’ concerns.
“Our farmers deserve a secure, dignified livelihood,” she said.

The debate over whether a social media ban for under 13- or 16-year-olds should be implemented or not, and amid the Union government’s standoff with Meta, an interesting intervention appeared in the Lok Sabha last week, with a private members’ Bill listed in that House by Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MP Baijayant Panda, throwing a little light on what such a move could look like in its legislative form.
The ‘Safeguarding Healthy Internet Environments for Little Digital-Natives (Shield) Bill, 2025’ was listed on Friday (August 7, 2026) but could not be tabled as both Houses of Parliament adjourned early.
It is “now well established by multiple studies that many social media algorithms are not only designed to foster addiction but also to embellish and reinforce narrow and extreme viewpoints, rather than shed light on all angles of any issue,” Mr. Panda told The Hindu.
It was “particularly harmful for young teenagers and children”, Mr. Panda said. Many social media platforms had acknowledged these conclusions, and consequently, several countries had started imposing restrictions on social media access to minors, especially those under the ages of 16 or 13, with the Centre also seized of the issue. “I had drafted a private member’s Bill for this purpose a year ago, after wide consultations with all stakeholders,” he said.
“Opposition parties need to reflect and rethink their blanket disruption of Parliament even on issues such as this, where there is no dispute with the Treasury Benches,” the BJP legislator said.
The Bill specifically states that no child under 13 years of age shall create an account on any social media or online gaming platform without verified parental consent, and that every intermediary shall provide parental control dashboards enabling guardians to monitor activity, manage privacy settings, and restrict screen time.
Any harmful content reported by an individual, guardian or parent shall, subject to verification by the intermediary, be removed or disabled within 36 hours of receipt, or 24 hours if it involves child sexual material. Every application shall have a reporting button titled ‘Report Child Harm’ accessible to all users.
Any intermediary who fails to comply with the Act shall be liable to a penalty of up to ₹10 crore, and wilful or repeated violations will lead to suspension of the intermediary's services or blocking under the provisions of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Officers designated by intermediaries who fail to observe due diligence in matters, specifically child safety or content removal obligations, either because of connivance or neglect, will be personally liable and could face imprisonment for up to 3 years, a fine of ₹10 lakh, or both.
An annual child safety and risk assessment process, identifying exposure risks related to content algorithms and interactions on a service, has to be carried out and submitted to the government. Information collected about users via the verification requirement cannot be used for behavioural profiling, the Bill says.
As more and more countries appear to be bringing legislation that restricts social media usage by children, the Bill listed by Mr. Panda appears to be a timely signal of similar efforts in India.

I’m already growing hoarse in Golden Gate Park as Charli XCX takes the stage at a San Francisco music festival. The crowd starts jumping as a guitar hook hits, and I reluctantly comply, bouncing around on these aging knees as my chunky Puff necklace almost flies off the chain.
During a lull in the set, someone next to me compliments the necklace, which has stainless steel swirls and a bulbous orange center. Their eyes grow wide as I flip the cap off and explain that it’s a hidden USB flash drive—I plugged the Puff into my phone to show off the animations.
When Harry Isaac and Sebastian Bidegain, working together under the Noware moniker, posted an early prototype of their retro-futuristic necklace on social media in 2025, it quickly racked up over a million views with thousands of waitlist sign-ups to buy one. The duo has spent the last year attempting to turn the online attention on their prototype into a mass-produced reality. Now, Noware is finally ready to ship units this October.
The pair arrived at the WIRED office wearing Puff necklaces, naturally, that match with their trendy gorpcore outfits. They seem nervous, albeit excited, to show off their creation. Neither has had a wide release for their products before, though both are well-versed in whimsical designs. Isaac previously went viral for making an electric scooter that shoots out bubbles. Bidegain was already sculpturally approaching electronics, with prototypes like a vape camera and lo-fi sampler built into a rock.
The design ethos of the Puff is just as much about aesthetics as it is about usefulness. Noware’s marketing materials show a cool girl with a Puff clipped onto her purse, where a Labubu might have sat last year, as well as styled on her neck with a pile of other silver chains. Bidegain says the “squishy, doughy” textures of food partially inspired Puff’s design, as well as cellular biology and tactile devices, like old phones and radios.
“On one end, I want anyone to be able to wear it, just if they think it's pretty,” he says. “Though, I also want people who actually find utility in flash drives as part of their workflow: photographers, DJs, IT people.”
The small screen in the middle of the necklace is my favorite aspect. When it’s plugged into my phone or laptop, Puff’s center lights up with a customizable design. The Noware duo showed me goopy animations that reacted to the direction I held the phone as well as an aquarium mode. They even put the WIRED logo on it through custom software anyone can use to craft their own designs. The Puff doesn’t have an internal battery, so the USB drive can live as a piece of jewelry far longer than the expiration date of most electronics.
The necklace’s biggest drawback is its price: a whopping $179 for only 128 GB of storage. A basic flash drive with similar storage costs around $30. The duo doesn’t want the Puff to remain that expensive and hopes to reach a more accessible price. “We want it to get cheaper over time, but we're just trying to make it exist first,” says Isaac. They blame it partially on the inflated cost of memory right now, thanks to the AI boom. Depending on how Puff’s initial release goes, future iterations may include more budget-friendly options, like a nonmetal version.
This experimental device from two New York City-based makers was the perfect accessory for a weekend-long festival, with its retro-futuristic vibe and sharp colors.
“We're very interested in making electronics that are more opinionated, playful, and personal,” Isaac says. It was a lighthearted conversation piece as I made small talk with vendors, and at least one friend assumed I was hiding drugs in it. (Nope, just a bunch of nudes.)
