There’s a lot of discussion about Jewish voters in politics this cycle.
What American Jews want from the midterms
Though a small electorate, Jewish voters are being pushed to the center of political debates this midterm cycle.
With Democrats embroiled in loud arguments over Israel and Gaza, Republicans have been hoping to capture more of the Jewish vote by linking criticism of Israel to antisemitism. “How a Jewish person can vote for a Democrat is beyond me,” President Donald Trump said last month. His administration has made cracking down on anti-Israel campus activists — a top early priority — and has called Democrats “Palestinian” or “jihadists.”
Meanwhile, Democrats have pointed to the rise of openly antisemitic influencers within the conservative movement, which has become a divisive topic on the right that also runs into debates over Israel, as a pressing threat to Jews.
But what do Jewish voters themselves actually want? That’s a nuanced question, and one that we have fresh polling and voting data on to help us dissect this cycle.
American Jews aren’t a large voting bloc — just over 2 percent of the population — but there are also significant communities in some key swing states and competitive districts. As a matter of partisan politics, Jews have historically voted Democratic by wide margins, but Republicans have long hoped to peel them off, often by emphasizing their support for Israel. Though it’s been a common refrain from pro-Israel and Republican activists for decades that a GOP realignment was just around the corner, it wasn’t until the 2024 presidential election that these voices got a firm boost. Nationally, and in local communities, Jewish support for the Democratic Party seemed to drop slightly.
Key takeaways
- Jewish voters remain strongly and consistently Democratic overall, despite a modest Republican shift in 2024.
- Domestic concerns — especially democracy, affordability, healthcare, and abortion rights — are key issues, while rising antisemitism and personal safety have become major unifying anxieties.
- Views on Israel are complex: Most Jewish Americans identify as pro-Israel while criticizing Netanyahu or Israeli policies, and many distinguish legitimate policy debate from antisemitism — even as they worry that anti-Israel rhetoric can cross that line.
Elections since then have been difficult to parse. In last year’s New York City mayoral election, for example, Zohran Mamdani won about 33 percent of Jewish voters, compared to the 63 percent that went for Andrew Cuomo in a race where divisions over Israel and antisemitism featured strongly. In the primary, many Cuomo voters also backed Mamdani ally Brad Lander, a Jewish progressive who was sharply critical of Israel — and who went on to easily defeat Rep. Dan Goldman in a congressional primary in a heavily Jewish district this year while running to his left on Israel issues. Meanwhile, in New Jersey, left-wing Democrat Analilia Mejia won a special election for a House seat while harshly criticizing Israel. But her candidacy led some Jewish strongholds to swing massively toward Republicans.
So, what happens to the Jewish vote in the 2026 midterms? This segment of voters is no monolith, experts say, and finding the “right” way to talk about Israel is no guarantor of electoral success. Polls show Jewish voters hold competing priorities in their minds: They’re increasingly concerned about antisemitism and their personal safety in America, and they hold complex and divergent views on Israel, which often is not a defining voting issue, even as it seems to be the dominant way strategists and pundits talk about this electorate.
Here’s what the latest data has to say about what Jewish voters want and how their politics are changing this cycle.
The remarkable consistency of the Jewish electorate
Aside from Black voters, there have traditionally been no more loyal Democratic voters than Jewish Americans. Since 2008, between 60 and 80 percent of these voters picked the Democratic candidate, while about 60 percent have consistently identified with the party over the last two decades.
That changed slightly after 2024, when exit polls suggested a six-point swing toward Donald Trump compared to 2020. Jewish communities in New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania, meanwhile, shifted more dramatically — which analysts for the election data site Split Ticket argued last year represented a 5 to 10 percentage-point swing against Democrats.
There are plenty of arguments over how and why this happened — pollsters and experts I spoke with told me that, despite the majority of Jewish American voters still siding with Democrats, the voting group mirrored other traditionally Democratic voting groups’ swing against the incumbent.
“Biden won the election, Harris lost the election,” Tali deGroot, the national political director of J Street, told Vox. “That means that every single community likely saw shifts with fewer people voting for the Democrat.”
Others argue it was a return to more of a baseline of voter behavior. 2020 was the aberration, with remarkably high support for Biden because of pandemic conditions.
But what still stands out beyond these trendlines is the steady support Democrats receive from these voters — whether because of the high level of college education among these constituents (a blue-coded trait in the Trump era), the geographic location of these voters (primarily in Democratic states like New York and California), or the socially liberal beliefs many of these voters hold (Jews historically support abortion rights, for example).
Even heading into 2026, Democrats still hold overwhelmingly strong support from these voters, Jim Gerstein, a founding partner of the polling firm GBAO, told me.
“What’s remarkable is actually how consistent Jewish voting behavior and political beliefs and values have been for years and still through today,” Gerstein said. “You have these massive developments in domestic, international, political events, actual things that happen in the real world, and the Jewish vote is just remarkably stable.”
Entering 2026, Gerstein argues, two dynamics remain at play that are preserving their Democratic lean. The long-held liberal ideological bent of Jewish Americans, along with the issues they prioritize, broadly align with the Democratic Party. And, on the other end, their antipathy to Trump and the Republican Party is “intense,” a force that pushes these voters away from the GOP, even if there were broader reasons to realign.
“Not only do they identify with the Democrats, they share positions on the major issues, shared values,” Gerstein said. “And they also have a strong opposition to the Republican Party and leading Republican figures.”
These dynamics also reveal themselves when looking at various denominations within the Jewish electorate. The largest segments — nondenominational, Reform, and Conservative Jews — lean heavily Democratic and have remained more or less steadily Democratic over the last few years. A smaller segment, Orthodox Jews — who make up about a tenth of the Jewish population but are growing — lean toward Republicans, are more strongly supportive of Trump and Israel, and have been shifting right over the last five years.
“The Orthodox population is in its own political world relative to the rest of the Jewish population,” Gerstein said. “To the extent there’s any shifting [broadly], there’s been some shifting among Orthodox to make them even more Republican. That is offset by the fact that the Reform population is much larger. They are extraordinarily Democratic, and if anything, are moving a little bit more Democratic.”
How Jewish American voters are feeling about 2026
Polls of Jewish voters this year suggests these dynamics are largely baked into the electorate at this point. A national AP-NORC survey of voters, with an oversampling of Jewish Americans, in June found that Jewish adults’ approval of how Trump is handling his job is nearly 10 points lower than among all American adults generally.
“We see that same pattern on most of the issues that we asked about, such as the economy, immigration, and Iran,” Emily Alvarez, a senior research scientist at NORC, told me. “But when it comes to his handling of Israel, they’re actually slightly more likely than the general public to approve. It’s a very small difference, but it is a difference, and it’s kind of a reversal of that trend that we saw with the other issues.”
NORC’s polling also suggests that domestic, kitchen table issues continue to be the dominant priorities of these voters generally. More than 80 percent of Jewish adults say the economy and healthcare are top priorities for them this year. About 56 and 66 percent say Israel or foreign policy are important concerns.
This June finding roughly matches the priorities that two other pollsters identified this year. The Mellman Group’s polling for the Jewish Electorate Institute from March found that Jewish voters largely say Democrats are better aligned with their views on abortion rights, healthcare, fair elections, and supporting the middle class.
And polling from GBAO on behalf of the Jewish Voters Resource Center in the spring found that the future of democracy (37 percent) and the cost of living/affordability (32 percent) are the top two issue priorities of Jewish voters, broadly speaking. Concerns over antisemitism round out the top three (25 percent).
Fear of discrimination and antisemitism is the biggest unifying concern for Jewish adults. When GBAO asked respondents about dealbreaker issues, 20 percent cited antisemitism as being their red line for supporting a candidate. And AP-NORC’s polling found that 62 percent of Jewish adults feel they are less safe than before October 7.
And while Jewish voters tend to be more aligned with Democrats on issues, the polling also found they remain wary of partisan politics — a common trait among many demographics in recent cycles.
“Jewish Americans really feel a sense of political dissatisfaction. They don’t feel particularly well supported by either political party. Very few say Democrats or Republicans support them well,” Alvarez said. “Republicans tend to feel a lot better supported by Republicans, and then they feel really supported by President Trump, but then far fewer Democrats feel the same way about their own party or about the president.”
The Israel factor
It’s hard to disentangle the effect of the Israel-Gaza war from the current political environment for Jewish voters.
Sam Markstein, the political director of the Republican Jewish Coalition, told me that October 7 was a defining moment for many Jewish voters who had preexisting misgivings about the Democratic Party. Changing political and public opinion on Israel and acts of violence against Jewish people and at places of worship, as well as shifts among Democrats and the left’s broader tension with AIPAC, suddenly made safety and antisemitism more pressing issues.
“After October 7, American Jews focused a lot more on their safety,” Markstein told me. “The main questions we heard, time and time, was who would best keep us safe, who would stand up for our students on the college campus quad, who would make us feel better about walking with our young kids to shul on Saturday morning, who would actually stand with the Jewish community and empower us to wear our Stars of David in public and not have to hide it.”
While concerns about antisemitism are widespread, views on Israel and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict itself are nuanced, particularly among Jewish Democrats, various pollsters told me.
AP-NORC’s polling, for example, found that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was broadly disliked by American Jews, with six-in-10 adults expressing unfavorable views. By contrast, Mamdani, the New York City mayor who recently explored arresting Netanyahu, was viewed favorably by 44 percent of Jews, with 39 percent expressing an unfavorable view. 30 percent of Jews said they believed Israel had committed genocide in its war in Gaza, while 49 percent said it had not.
One important wrinkle that’s often divided Israel critics is the context of that criticism. Many Jews are concerned about Israel’s security and direction and hope to see a new government with a stronger commitment to forging peace with Palestinians and neighboring states. Michael Bloomfield, a lead pollster and managing director for the Mellman Group, told me that “what often gets forgotten is that almost all American Jews, 86 percent, consider themselves pro-Israel,” including a similar share of Jewish Democrats.
But a rising segment of the left — including candidates like Abdul El-Sayed — often describe Israel’s founding vision of a homeland for Jews as inherently oppressive and sometimes calls for replacing the country with a secular and binational Arab-Jewish state. By contrast, New York’s Brad Lander, also on the left, describes himself as a “liberal Zionist” who wants a peaceful two-state solution that preserves Israel’s existence.
Polling this year, sponsored by the Jewish Electorate Institute, found that, while many Jewish Democrats are critical of Israeli government policies and the US partnership with Israel in the war in Iran, they are still strongly supportive of Israel as a state.
Overall, nearly nine in 10 American Jews describe themselves as pro-Israel, they found, but only about a quarter, 23 percent, consider themselves both pro-Israel and supportive of Israeli government policies. Six in 10 are pro-Israel and critical, half of whom are critical of “some” and another half who are critical of “many” policies. That broadly aligns with partisan identification. While 84 perfect of Jewish Democrats are “pro-Israel,” 73 percent of them are critical of Israeli policies. Republicans, a smaller share overall, are less likely to be critical.
There are also differences based on religious and cultural identity within the Jewish electorate, apparent in the NORC polling. Jews with a religious affiliation or strong attachment to Israel as part of their religious identity tend to be more supportive of Israel’s actions than secular Jews. About half of those with religious affiliation say the Gaza military campaign is justified, while a quarter believe Israel has committed genocide, compared to about two in 10 secular Jews who say the Gaza campaign is justified, and 4 in 10 who agree with the genocide charge. Three-quarters of that cohort say they are “not too” or “not at all” emotionally attached to Israel.
While concerns about antisemitism are rising, there’s room for nuance, Bloomfield told me.
“There is a policy debate about how much aid Israel should get, there’s a policy debate about where our relationship should be,” Bloomfield told me. “That is different than the worry when it gets to antisemitism and feeling uncomfortable in the Democratic Party.” The Mellman poll for JEI found that a majority of American Jews agree with the statement that “too many supporters of Israel claim any criticism of Israel is antisemitism as a way to avoid legitimate debate over Israeli policy.”
Nearly half of Jewish Republicans (47 percent) agree with that, along with 59 percent of Democrats. At the same time, 83 percent of Jewish Americans agree that “too many critics of Israel use tropes and generalizations about Jews to play into antisemitism, whether they mean to or not.”
Those nuanced views speak to the moment of uncertainty that many Jewish Democrats feel right now, he said. Israel, and the US relationship with it, does not dominate their vote choice or decision-making, but the way the party’s rising leaders, activist class, and press talk about it may become a bigger pressure point later this cycle. In the latest Mellman/JEI polling, few Jews say they’ve been following the discourse and debate over AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups’ spending in primary contests. Some 62 percent of all Jews say they have not heard much — including a majority of Jewish Democrats.
That number has likely gone up since then, given high-profile contests like Michigan’s Senate primary this month, which featured extensive arguments about pro-Israel spending and whether criticizing them shaded into antisemitism. And the salience of these debates may change in either direction depending on the news. Democrats could pursue a more aggressive policy to pressure Israel if they win the House, for example, or Israel might find room for a reset if Netanyahu loses his premiership later this year.
“There are cross currents and Jews can feel both ways at the same time,” Bloomfield said. “We ourselves can be concerned where people use antisemitism as cries as a way to get out of legitimate debate. On the other hand, there’s even more of us concerned that a lot of what is being debated by Israel often does veer too quickly into something that’s antisemitism. We can have both feelings at the same time.”

LONDON: The spotlight has now turned to the universities of Cambridge, Durham and Glasgow for allegedly overpromoting Jason Arday, and particularly to Cambridge, as the former professor’s death continues to dominate UK media coverage.
Arday, 41, was found dead at his London home on Friday, just over a week after resigning from his post as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge following intense media scrutiny of the integrity of his academic research, qualifications and achievements.
Upon resigning, Arday had said: “The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me.”
In his forthcoming memoir, Arday had claimed he was diagnosed with 
autism
 at the age of three, was unable to speak until he was 11, and was unable to read and write until he was 18. At the age of 37, he became the youngest Black full professor in Cambridge’s history.
Before his death, the UK media had carried interviews with Arday’s contemporaries who contested these claims.
“The most casual observer could see he was a vulnerable fantasist,” said James Cleverly, the Black shadow communities secretary. “The death of Jason Arday is tragic and makes me so angry. A number of people at a number of academic institutions have serious questions to answer. 
They put him into positions he was clearly not qualified for so they could have a Black wunderkind to show off. They pushed him into the spotlight for their own benefit.”
Dorothy Byrne, former president of Murray Edwards College, Cambridge, condemned Cambridge, Glasgow and Durham universities for not asking serious questions during his appointment process. While stressing that there is an “important question” over whether journalistic coverage was “excessive”, Byrne told Times Radio: “If those universities had asked the questions and taken action when criticisms were made and questions were raised over several years, I do not believe that we would be where we are today with this terrible event having happened.” She said journalists were in fact asking the questions “which those universities should have asked”.
Before his death, all three universities said they were investigating the circumstances surrounding Arday’s appointment.
“The system that overpromoted him should have been the target, not him,” wrote Matthew Syed in ‘The Times’.
A GoFundMe page set up by Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon OBE had by Sunday raised almost £100k for Arday’s family and his funeral costs. “There are serious questions for academia, institutions, journalism... about whether sufficient care is shown when somebody is known to be vulnerable,” he said.
Lord Woolley, the Black principal of Homerton College, Cambridge, has called for an investigation into the “vicious media onslaught”.
A spokesman for Cambridge said Arday was given “the provision of counselling, support and advice, and security measures, including the installation of panic alarms and the screening of racist emails and post. Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation.”
Stand Up to Racism co-convener Weyman Bennett said the witch-hunt targeting Arday had spread “the far-right lie that Black people are only appointed because of the colour of our skin, rather than our ability”.

A rumor spread online in August 2026 that Massachusetts Democrats had installed a demonic statue in front of the state Capitol building. According to the claim, the statue was of Molech (also spelled Moloch, which is how we'll refer to the figure from here on), an ancient god who, according to multiple passages in the Old Testament, was related to child sacrifice.
(X user @Howodd69)
The story spread after Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat, signed a bill into law that makes it possible for all women to receive an abortion after 24 weeks of pregnancy, based on a physician's "professional medical judgment." (Anti-abortion advocates online suggested the state had legalized "abortion until birth," a claim Snopes separately fact-checked.)
Readers wrote in looking for more information on the supposed statue.
To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. If the statue were real, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or The Boston Globe, would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We didn't find any credible reporting about the Moloch statue. The story originated with The Babylon Bee, a satirical news site that describes itself as a "Trusted Source for Christian News Satire." The Babylon Bee originally posted the story on Aug. 13, 2026.
Snopes has alerted readers to several instances of rumors originating from satirical articles published by The Babylon Bee, including a fictitious story suggesting that new government-run grocery stores in New York City would require shoppers to have a "special mark" on their hand or forehead — the number 666, often associated with Satan or the Antichrist.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Japanese summers are now so sweltering that the Meteorological Agency created a word to describe a whole new category of hot.
The term “kokushobi” (literally, “cruel hot day”) was coined to describe the brutal heat of temperatures 40 degrees Celsius and above. In previous years, mōshobi (“fiercely hot days”) of 35 C or higher had ranked as the hottest, but by July, cities across Japan had already experienced multiple consecutive kokushobi days.
With dangerously hot summer days now a fact of life, my kitchen repertoire during August focuses on sōmen — the chilled, thread-thin wheat noodles that have refreshed heat-weary Japanese since at least the eighth century.

Sunday at the Edinburgh Intl. Film Festival turned into Edinbranagh, with a morning screening of the four-hour epic “Hamlet” followed by a wide-ranging onstage conversation with Kenneth Branagh, which began with him receiving the inaugural EIFF Outstanding Contribution to Cinema award.
“Festivals are more important to our industry than ever before,” Branagh said, holding the award and arguing they offer a lifeline to films struggling to find a traditional theatrical path. He promptly turned the honor back on the packed audience: “You are the reason, certainly the reason why I stand here.”
Hosted by Guardian critic Peter Bradshaw, the talk jumped across Branagh’s sprawling career.
Popular on Variety
He recalled preparing his 1991 thriller “Dead Again” from Sydney Pollack’s office when he felt the room move. Then Pollack’s Academy Awards started sliding.
“I started to see the two Oscars do a sort of dance on the top shelf,” Branagh said. “It was an earthquake.”
“Dead Again,” his neo-noir follow up to “Henry V,” had its own shaky beginnings. Early previews were “disastrous,” with audiences heading for the exits. The fix? Restore screenwriter Scott Frank’s original idea of rendering the past in black and white. “Suddenly the preview score went through the roof,” Branagh said. “We were loved again by our studio family.”
Christopher Nolan offered a different kind of ordeal. On “Tenet,” Branagh asked whether his Russian oligarch should speak Russian backwards while moving backwards through time.
“I saw this terrible, dangerous light in his eye,” he recalled. Nolan’s answer: “Yes, I think you would.”
So Branagh spent lunch learning backwards Russian.
Then came Hogwarts.
Branagh had assumed Gilderoy Lockhart in “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets” might mean three or four weeks’ work. Instead, “I was on it for nine months.” The crew list, he said, was “the size of a telephone directory.”
On his first day, Branagh thought he saw Daniel Radcliffe and Rupert Grint, only to discover stunt doubles and stand-ins filling an entire classroom while the young stars were at school. When the real actors appeared, Hogwarts had become its own ecosystem: “Notes were being passed. Little darts were being thrown at people.”
For Branagh, the scale was staggering, children essentially living inside a fictional school while surrounded by “the entire British film industry.”
The conversation kept circling back to Shakespeare. Branagh said his early theater company had a “missionary zeal” to make the plays feel immediate rather than bogged down by reverence. He wanted his parents to be able to watch Shakespeare “and not feel they had to read the play beforehand.”
“When Shakespeare was real, there was nothing in the way,” he said. “You just had truth. If it was truthful, you felt it, you understood it.
That instinct fuelled his directorial debut “Henry V,” made despite producer David Puttnam’s late warning that the film could collapse and damage Branagh’s career, a sentiment Puttnam later retracted in a gracious note of apology. Branagh said one of the most useful lessons he learned as a director could be summed up in three words: “I don’t know.”
The afternoon’s most personal moment came with “Belfast.” Written during the pandemic, the semi-autobiographical film emerged, Branagh said, after the story had sat inside him for roughly 40 years.
His sister’s reaction to the script: “My God, for a very private man, you’ve really put it all out there now, haven’t you?”
Branagh grew emotional.
“It was cathartic,” he said. “It was necessary. Somehow it was necessary.”
After a career spanning Shakespeare, superheroes, Poirot, Hogwarts and Hollywood, his closing advice to an audience member was simple:
“Keep practising and enjoy.”

A good – and bad – week for Italy's art police and museum security
The good news came first.
In late March, a gang used a tractor to batter down a fence before two masked burglars broke into the Magnani Rocca Foundation, a private museum about 12 miles from the northern Italian city of Parma. They climbed in through a window door, and grabbed three paintings off the wall before disappearing – the whole operation caught on camera, yet completed in under three minutes.
The roughly $10 million haul included Cézanne's Still Life with Cherries (worth an estimated $7 million), Renoir's Les Poissons (with an approximate value of $3.5 million) and a Matisse aquatint, Odalisque on the Terrace ($23,000). It was the latest in a run of high-profile thefts that have hit museums and galleries across Europe.
This past Friday, officials said the paintings had been recovered during some searches that prosecutors had ordered. That investigative effort was led by the Italian police branch known as the carabinieri, working alongside a specialist team focused on cultural heritage protection.
Yet authorities gave few further details, and the investigation remains open.
A new theft
Then came the bad news.
The following night, a Saturday, was an Italian holiday known as Ferragosto, when much of the country was out celebrating. In the Sicilian city of Messina, a major religious festival held every August 15, called La Vara, had also drawn thousands to the streets.
While attention in the city may have been elsewhere, thieves got past the alarm system at Messina's Museo Interdisciplinare Regionale (MuMe), and broke open a security case. They soon left with four wooden panels by the city's famed Renaissance painter, Antonello da Messina.
Antonello, born around 1430 and trained in Naples, absorbed influences from Provençal and Flemish painting styles that remained visible in his own work.
In Saturday's heist, thieves made off with three of the five surviving panels from an altarpiece by Antonello known as the Polittico di San Gregorio. The work originally had six panels, but one was destroyed along with the monastery that housed it in the 1908 Messina earthquake. It was the only work by the artist that had never left his home town.
The thieves also purloined a small double-sided painting, with the Virgin and Child on one side and Christ on the other, that the Sicilian regional government had bought from the auction house Christie's back in 2003.
Antonello's work is highly prized in his home country. Just this February, the Italian government spent $14.9 million at a New York auction to bring another Antonello work, called Ecce Homo, back home. That portrait of the suffering Christ is believed to date to around 1460, and was purchased at Sotheby's. It will be housed in a museum in Abruzzo, on the mainland.
Giving further details on the March theft, authorities explained that nine people of Moldovan nationality have been placed under investigation. They had experience in stealing, police said in a statement, but knew too little about the art market to sell the works.
Two thefts, a growing trend
The two incidents highlight a recent spate of art thefts across Europe.
More than a dozen major art heists have been recorded since January 2025 alone – prompting the International Council of Museums to team up with Interpol in response.
Among them: an October 2025 raid in which thieves spent less than eight minutes stripping the Louvre's Apollo Gallery of jewels worth more than $100 million, an incident whose fallout eventually pushed out the museum's director.
And earlier, in January 2025, a gang had used explosives to blast apart a door at the Netherlands' Drents Museum, before stealing a loaned 2,500-year-old Romanian gold helmet. The national heirloom was only returned to the Romanian authorities 14 months later.
Late last year, Interpol's Stolen Works of Art database contained more than 57,000 listed items, and the agency itself has warned that plenty of stolen art never makes it into that count at all.

Qatar denies capturing three Iranian pilots after downing fighter jets
- Published
Iran has called for the release of three Iranian pilots it said were captured by Qatar after two fighter jets were hit by air defences during a military operation at the start of the US-Iran war.
In a letter to the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Iran's Brig Gen Mohammad Bagherzadeh said the pilots - Javad Salehi, Abdul Majid Dashtian, and Imran Behroshian - had been held captive for six months.
He said the body of a fourth pilot, Majid Kazemi, was returned after he was killed in the same operation on 2 March 2026 - the third day of the war.
Qatar "categorically denied" Iran's claims and said it was "surprised by these misleading statements".
Gen Bagherzadeh said the three pilots had been captured by Qatar after they ejected from their jets during the combat mission on a Qatari military base.
In the letter to ICRC chief Mirjana Spoljaric, published by Iranian media, he accused Qatar of violating "the inalienable rights of these prisoners, contrary to all international laws and regulations".
The letter also claimed the three pilots had not been allowed to meet or contact their families.
Qatar's foreign affairs spokesperson Majed Mohammed Al Ansari said contact had been made with the pilots "after they violated Qatari airspace", but it did not receive a response.
"The necessary measures were taken to defend our territory in accordance with international law," he added in a statement on X.
Al Ansari said Qatar's search and rescue teams "carried out their duties to the fullest extent in searching for the pilots' remains".
He said Qatar contacted Iran to "co-ordinate the handover of the remains of one of the pilots that were recovered", and that Tehran had yet to respond to an invitation to review details of the search and rescue operation.

Hunger Games, MAGA Style
A gym-class-style competition might be the oddest 250th celebration yet.
The semiquincentennial events that President Trump has personally directed have been a celebration of his very particular version of America. The bloody UFC fight on the White House lawn was followed by the sparsely attended Great American State Fair and a world-record-breaking July 4 fireworks show held alongside a dangerous lightning storm. Next weekend will bring a high-speed car race through the museum-lined streets of Washington. But of all of these festivities, the Patriot Games in Ohio this week might have been the oddest.
Organizers convened 120 teenagers from across the country—in their telling, the “next generation of leaders, competitors, and champions,” but also whoever happened to respond to an online request for personal essays and video entries—at a high school in Geneva, Ohio (population 5,924), roughly 45 miles northeast of downtown Cleveland. For three days, they competed in gym-class staples such as ball tosses, long jumps, tug-of-war, dodgeball, and an arcade-style basketball game called Victory Hoops. The field was narrowed to eight contestants who competed before the president on Tuesday night, clambering through a Ninja Warrior–style obstacle course while wearing red, white, and blue. One boy and one girl were crowned champions, and each was given a $125,000 scholarship.
Over the past several days, ESPN has streamed more than 26 hours of this contest, and I have consumed many of those hours—but I have yet to fully understand why this competition happened or what it has to do with American history, or even with American culture at this moment. I could barely follow how the various events were scored. It was like watching a nationally televised field day—with wholesome moments and cheerful contestants along the way—but it was unclear what the grand takeaway was supposed to be. (Perhaps that will be revealed when the event is condensed into a one-hour special airing tonight on ABC.) More than anything, it was a reality-television-style snapshot of the America that Trump most wants to see. The contestants were overwhelmingly white, in a country where roughly half of children are not, and many spoke openly of their Christian faith or their affection for this particular president.
When Trump showed up on Tuesday night, accompanied by the ESPN commentator Pat McAfee, the crowd erupted. “He’s got that Michael Jordan glow,” one spectator said. “We love you, Mr. President!” one man yelled. “2028!” another exclaimed. Outside the arena, a football-field scoreboard displayed a score of 45–47 in Trump’s honor. The crowd chanted “USA! USA! USA!” when he arrived and danced to his favorite song, “YMCA,” before he left.
“I didn’t know what to expect,” Trump told ESPN’s Laura Rutledge during an onstage interview, a few yards from dozens of teenagers. “I’m very proud of the group of people in this room. You see the spirit and the love of the country, our great country. And our country’s never done better.”
In that moment, it became clear that this gathering, like so many others this president has overseen, was actually all about Trump. This was his vision of the Hunger Games, MAGA style. He was front and center, watching the grand finale unfold and eyeing golden trophies he could present. But who were these contestants, and how were they chosen? Why these random events? And what does this all say about our country, and how does it mark our 250 years as one?
The Patriot Games, it must be said, seldom made for great television. I watched kids’ arms quiver as they tried to keep their chin up and over a bar—at least one lasted scarcely a second. Some struggled to cross the monkey bars in an obstacle course. Others tripped over the hurdles on the track, knocking over almost every one. (“A natural hurdler? Not really,” the announcer remarked.)
In one contest, the teenagers were asked to navigate an obstacle course of sorts: bear-crawl under a net, high-step through tires, weave between slalom poles, climb up and down a cargo net, walk across a beam, flip a tire (once for girls; twice for boys), traverse the monkey bars, carry two jerricans, leap onto hanging panels, and push a red button. In another contest, they went through a circuit of various sports. They attempted to kick a soccer ball into a bull’s-eye, catch three tennis balls, run through a maze of tackling dummies, throw a football into a target, serve a volleyball three times, hit a T-ball, and, finally, run around a few bases. In between challenges, some kids offered brief, out-of-breath analysis. “I did a lot better than I thought I would on the monkey bars,” concluded Gabriel Hayes, who was representing the Shawnee Tribe. “I just got kinda tired, to be honest,” said Remy Taylor, from Delaware.
The announcers revealed the kinds of small biographical details familiar to anyone who has watched the Olympics, attempting to humanize the athletes by highlighting their love of macaroni and cheese, Greek mythology, or Legos. Some were members of JROTC or the Future Farmers of America. Many came from military families, and aspired to carry on that tradition. There were at least three sets of siblings. Multiple boys wore a cross necklace, and several of the girls had a cross painted on their body. “I just want to say, it’s the glory for God. Thank you, Lord, for this opportunity,” said Max Biondolillo of Florida, after finishing the obstacle course. “Thank you, Jesus. That’s all I can say. Thank you, Jesus,” Seylah Brown, representing North Carolina, said after completing the circuit of sports.
The biographies suggested that the organizers might have struggled with recruitment in some deep-blue jurisdictions. The boy representing Puerto Rico has a southern accent and resides in Texas. Elsie Bruckart was the contestant for Vermont, but her hometown was listed as Bellbrook, Ohio. Her cousin Rebekah Roberts competed for Maine, but her hometown was Cornish, New Hampshire. Bobbi Vickers was representing Massachusetts, but she is from California. “I get a bunch of questions, like Why are you representing Massachusetts and not your home state?” Vickers told CNN. “But I think it’s really cool, because a lot of my family is from there and my favorite basketball team is actually the Boston Celtics.”
People familiar with the process told me that the athletes were selected through applications that required submissions of performance data and athletic statistics, along with a personal-essay and video submission. Freedom 250 did not respond to questions about why certain states were represented by competitors living in other states, or why there was such a lack of diversity among the contestants.
Danielle Alvarez, a spokesperson for Freedom 250, the Trump-aligned group that organized the games, said in a statement that the Patriot Games were one of the “unforgettable signature events” meant to “celebrate our country and inspire the next generation.” Organizers told me that they’d sought to create a range of challenges, aiming to show that the winner has mastered many different skills.
Often, during the events, the producers displayed the scores for only the top-10 contestants, shielding from embarrassment those who struggled. The announcers remarked several times that just because a contestant hadn’t performed well in one discipline didn’t mean they wouldn’t do better in another. Coaches shouted encouragement from the sidelines like summer-camp counselors: Give it your all! Finish the race! Be proud of the process! Some contestants had said beforehand that they had little clue before they arrived in Ohio what events would be included. “I’ve never really played soccer before,” said the girl representing Michigan. “I don’t know how to throw a football,” said the girl representing the Virgin Islands.
“It was hard. It was challenging. I mean, I’ve never played any of these sports. Like, I’m a cheerleader,” Laynie Arrowood, the 16-year-old representing the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma, told the sideline reporter good-naturedly. “I’m not good at throwing football—obviously not good at soccer! But it’s okay. I tried my best.” Most of the contestants did seem to be enjoying themselves, and several said they’d made close friendships over the days they’d spent together. Some said they understood how Trump’s involvement had politicized the competition but were baffled as to why they had come under scrutiny. “We can’t vote,” Jonah Beauregard, a 17-year-old from Massachusetts, told The Boston Globe. “We can’t do anything in our power to do anything to help it.”
Trump announced in May 2023 that, if elected to a second term, he wanted to host “major sporting contests for high-school athletes” as part of the country’s 250th celebrations. “These Patriot Games will allow young Americans from every state to show off the best of American skills, sportsmanship, and competitive spirit,” he said in a campaign video.
America has a rich athletic history, and the youth-sports industry in this country generates an estimated $40 billion in annual revenue. But to find a precedent for these games, you’d have to go further afield. The Roman emperor Nero, in 59 C.E., began hosting the Ludi Juvenales, a series of youth games in a festival to mark the transition from boyhood to manhood. In ancient Greece, athletic competitions began when boys turned 12. And the International Olympic Committee stages a Youth Olympic Games every four years for those ages 15 to 17.
Andy Hall, an ESPN communications director, told me that Freedom 250 approached the network last year about televising the event. He said that the network is not paying for the rights to carry it, but he would not say whether it was being paid and declined to provide any viewership data on how many people were streaming the content. (The link was buried inside the ESPN app and took me some time to find.) He said that the network had no role in organizing or planning the games, and that it was televising them as it would games organized by other entities. The content will all be repackaged into an hour-long ESPN special that will air tonight on ABC. Representatives for ABC did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and Hall declined to further comment. The Federal Communications Commission ordered a review earlier this year of the network’s licenses. Airing the president’s competition on its national platform may buy the network some goodwill.
On Tuesday night, Trump sat as the finalists worked through a course that involved swinging from ropes, carrying two kettlebells, and climbing up a wall. Kennadi Fuhrman, a soccer player from Kansas, won the girls’ competition, crediting “God, all the way.” Rockwell Myers, a tennis player and ballroom dancer from Utah, won the boys’. “It’s been amazing, and it’s taught me so much,” he said. “It really, really puts an emphasis on how important it is to put God first in your life and make him your No. 1 priority.”
Trump came onstage and helped present the trophies and oversize checks. “Incredible people. I like the audience also, I have to tell you. But what a great bunch of young athletes,” he said. Confetti went off, falling onto the contestants. One blue piece stuck in the president’s hair.
Michael Scherer contributed to this report.

New Delhi, Aug 16: India will host the BRICS Senior Officers' Meeting of the Environment Working Group (EWG) and the Contact Group on Climate Change and Sustainable Development on Monday, followed by the 12th BRICS Environment Ministers' Meeting the next day.
The event will be held at Bharat Mandapam here under the overarching theme of India's BRICS Chairship 2026: 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability', said a statement issued by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on Sunday.
The BRICS EWG was established in 2015 during the first BRICS Environment Ministers' Meeting in Moscow. It was envisioned as a platform for BRICS to address fundamental environmental priorities, exchange experiences, share best practices and strengthen collective action among member countries.
The Contact Group on Climate Change and Sustainable Development was established in 2024 as a mechanism for cooperation on climate change issues among BRICS member countries.
The BRICS Environment Ministers' Meeting will bring together ministers, senior officers, policymakers and experts from the member countries to engage in substantive discussions, foster consensus and strengthen environmental cooperation, the statement said.
It said the Senior Officers' Meeting will include an inaugural session and deliberations on the priorities of the BRICS EWG and the Contact Group on Climate Change and Sustainable Development.
The priorities include promoting sustainable lifestyles, afforestation, forest fire management and disaster resilience.
During the BRICS Environment Ministers' Meeting, there will be deliberations on the outcome document and thematic discussions that underscore the collective commitment of the member countries to environmental cooperation and sustainable development, the statement said.

Matcha is booming in the U.S. Consumers are increasingly willing to pay $5 to $8.50 for a Matcha drink. The trend is also showing up in Japan’s export data: the export value of Japanese tea reached a record 72.1 billion yen ($452 million) in 2025, up 98% from the previous year. The U.S. accounted for 35% of those exports, with Matcha making up 85% of the Japanese tea exported to the U.S.
The question is: Are Americans ready to taste Matcha as tea—not just as an ingredient?
In the U.S., Matcha is often consumed as a sweetened iced or hot latte made with dairy or plant-based milks such as oat and almond. Matcha also appears in smoothies and other beverages. These formats have helped make Matcha approachable to American consumers, while its vivid green color has made it particularly well suited to social media.
This format of making an unfamiliar product into a familiar one can be seen in the evolution of sushi in the U.S.
California rolls and other American-adapted sushi helped introduce Japanese cuisine to a much wider American audience. Today, sushi is firmly established in the American dining landscape, while traditional Edomae-style sushi has also developed a devoted following.
Could Matcha follow a similar path from an American-style introduction to a deeper appreciation of the original Japanese product?
From Matcha Lattes To Matcha As Tea
In a Matcha latte, Matcha is combined with milk and often sugar, making it part of a larger flavor profile. One traditional way to experience Matcha is to whisk the powder with hot water and drink it on its own.
Whisked with hot water, Matcha develops a velvety, foamy texture and can reveal layers of vegetal freshness, natural sweetness, savory umami and gentle bitterness. The flavor profile varies considerably depending on factors such as cultivar, growing region, production methods and preparation. Some of those nuances can be harder to perceive when Matcha is combined with milk and sugar.
Preparing Matcha is relatively simple, but the experience may be unfamiliar to consumers accustomed to sweetened Matcha beverages. That creates an opportunity for education—not only to introduce consumers to traditional preparation, but also to help them understand the differences in cultivars, origins and quality.
Across the U.S., a growing number of specialty tea businesses are offering consumers opportunities to experience Matcha beyond the latte. New York-based Sorate and Kettl, for example, have built businesses around Japanese tea and tea culture.
Matchaful offers another example of this emerging education-focused approach. It launched Ritual Bar in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, in August 2026. The eight-seat space is designed to introduce customers to Japanese tea culture through guided tastings, workshops and classes. Guests can participate in Matcha flights and hands-on whisking sessions, either through scheduled classes or walk-in experiences.
Matchaful founder Hannah Habes has worked closely with a tea farm in Japan since 2012 and visits the farm regularly to maintain a direct relationship with its growers and production.
“Great Matcha has a distinctive taste and flavor that reflects the craftsmanship of the tea farm. We want our guests to develop a deeper understanding of Matcha culture,” she says.
At one guided tasting, a flight of organic Matcha demonstrated how different cultivars can produce distinctly different experiences. Okumidori, a cultivar often associated with lower bitterness, offered mellow umami and a rich depth of flavor, along with a vibrant green color and an aroma reminiscent of fresh leafy greens. Tsuyuhikari showcased a different profile, with subtle sweetness and flavors reminiscent of snap pea and cashew.
The tasting was also designed as an educational experience, allowing guests to ask about cultivars, processing methods and regional differences in Japanese tea culture. For consumers accustomed to Matcha primarily as a latte flavor, such experiences can provide a way to understand the product on its own terms.
Matcha's growth, however, has been driven in part by aesthetics, social media and its positioning as a wellness-oriented lifestyle beverage. The bigger question is whether that consumer interest can extend beyond the latte and whether education can create demand for higher-quality Matcha consumed as tea.
Habes believes it will. “The pandemic seems to have triggered consumer interest in Matcha powder and our sales have been strong ever since. More people now drink it at home like a coffee ritual for its taste and health benefits. I think they are also becoming more curious about the tea itself.”
Major chains such as Starbucks and numerous independent coffee shops serve Matcha beverages, while dedicated Matcha bars have emerged in cities including New York and Los Angeles.
For Matcha businesses, education could become more than a way to teach consumers how to whisk tea. It could become a way to differentiate products, justify premium prices and deepen consumer interest in the farms, cultivars and craftsmanship behind the powder.
The Matcha latte may ultimately play the same role that the California roll played for sushi: an accessible introduction to something unfamiliar. Whether today's latte drinkers become tomorrow's Matcha enthusiasts will depend on whether the industry can turn curiosity into appreciation.
That is the next stage of the Matcha boom and potentially the bigger business opportunity.

A team led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine has found that several inherited traits in the mouse genome break the rules Gregor Mendel laid down in the 19th century about how genes work. This is not because the genes mutate but because of chemical modifications of the genome that can jump across generations, change depending on whether an animal is male or female, and even copy themselves from one copy of a gene to another.
Their findings were reported recently in Nature Genetics.

“But better to get hurt by the truth than comforted with a lie.” — Khaled Hosseini
At its core, LiveMint's quote of the day by Kite Runner's Khaled Hosseini means that honesty, no matter how painful, is always more valuable than a false sense of security built on deception. It highlighted a fundamental choice in human relationships: the choice between temporary comfort and enduring reality.
“Hurt by the truth”: The truth can be blunt, disappointing, or deeply painful. However, pain caused by the truth is rooted in reality. It allows you to process the actual situation, adapt, grow, and eventually heal. Knowing where you stand, even if it hurts, builds a foundation of trust.
“Comforted with a lie”: A lie might protect your feelings in the short term, making you feel safe, loved, or secure. However, this comfort is an illusion. When the lie is eventually uncovered (as it almost always is), the resulting pain is twofold: you suffer the reality of the truth and the betrayal of the deception.
The quote speaks to the courage required for genuine integrity. It takes bravery to tell someone a painful truth, and it takes strength to hear it. It is a reminder that a harsh reality is always a better foundation for life than a pleasant illusion.
The quote is incredibly relevant today, especially in the current digital and social landscape, where the tension between comforting illusions and harsh realities is a daily struggle across several areas of modern life:
Era of algorithmic echo chambers: Social media algorithms are literally designed to feed us comforting lies. They track our preferences, biases, and beliefs, and then serve us content that perfectly aligns with our worldview. This creates an "echo chamber" where we are constantly comforted by the illusion that everyone agrees with us. Stepping outside that bubble to face the truth—that the world is complex, divided, and often at odds with our beliefs—is uncomfortable and painful, but it is the only way to stay grounded in reality.
Rise of AI, deepfakes, and misinformation: We are navigating a digital landscape where seeing is no longer believing. Deepfakes, AI-generated images, and sophisticated misinformation campaigns make it incredibly easy to manufacture a "comforting lie" tailored to any political or social agenda. Choosing the truth today requires active effort, scepticism, and the willingness to accept that the reality of a situation might be far less convenient or satisfying than the viral fake narrative.
Toxic positivity vs. authentic mental health: Modern internet culture often pushes a narrative of “good vibes only”—a comforting lie that dictates we should always be happy, productive, and thriving. This toxic positivity forces people to suppress their actual struggles. The mental health movement is currently fighting this exact battle, emphasising that acknowledging your pain, trauma, or burnout (the hurtful truth) is a necessary prerequisite for genuine healing and resilience.
Modern dating and “ghosting”: In contemporary relationships and dating culture, avoiding the "hurtful truth" has become the default. Practices like ghosting, breadcrumbing, or giving vague, polite excuses to end a relationship are all attempts to avoid the immediate discomfort of a truthful rejection. However, as the quote suggests, being comforted with silence or a fake excuse leaves people confused and unable to move on. A blunt, honest rejection hurts initially, but it provides the closure needed to heal.
The modern world makes it easier than ever to wrap ourselves in a cocoon of digital, social, and political illusions.
Hosseini’s quote serves as a necessary warning: a society—or an individual—that prioritises temporary comfort over harsh reality ultimately loses the ability to navigate the real world.
The quote is from Khaled Hosseini’s acclaimed 2003 novel, The Kite Runner.
It appears in Chapter 6 of the novel. The line is spoken by the narrator and protagonist, Amir, regarding his childhood friend and servant, Hassan. Amir is reflecting on Hassan's unwavering loyalty and honesty.
Hassan is a character who never lies, and Amir notes that while the truth can sometimes be blunt or painful to hear, he would rather receive that honest pain from Hassan than be placated by a falsehood.
It is a core thematic quote of the book, contrasting Hassan's pure integrity with Amir's struggle with deceit and guilt as the story progresses.

There has been a steep rise in scammers luring victims into phony investment opportunities using deepfakes of celebrities and politicians, Australia’s corporate watchdog has warned.
And Anthony Albanese is the figure most commonly co-opted.
Real footage of the prime minister, overlaid with fake audio promising Australians can invest $4,000 to earn $40,000 a month, appears in one video online.
“This is not just another scam product,” the deepfake Albanese says, falsely describing it as an “official platform” with a government guarantee.
The Australian Securities and Investment Commission (Asic) dealt with more than 19,400 scams last financial year, almost triple the amount in the year before.
Artificial intelligence is making it increasingly easy to generate deepfakes, it warned.
Fake celebrities were just the beginning. Scammers have built networks of fake brands, websites, reviews, news articles and videos that work together to convince victims to ultimately give them money, which ends up going to overseas criminals, Asic said.
According to reports to the National Anti-Scam Centre’s Scamwatch, Australians lost $7.4m to the top 10 impersonated public figures, and Albanese was at the top of the list.
In one video, a deepfake of the prime minister promises people can earn $35 an hour, which is “about $850 per day” and “over $25,000 per month”, according to the Australian Financial Review. The disinformation and dodgy maths are presented with an American accent.
“Greetings. From the first day I became prime minister, I wanted to improve the tax system. We will not fully get rid of taxes, of course, but any resident will be able to receive dividends from them,” the fake says.
Economists Tom Piotrowski and Stephen Koukoulas; ABC financial journalist Alan Kohler; and politicians Jacqui Lambie and Angus Taylor (showing Lambie confronting Taylor on Insiders about patronising people) make up the top five.
They were followed by entrepreneur Dick Smith, billionaire Gina Rinehart, economist Alan Oster, Pauline Hanson and the late radio legend John Laws.
“It is important to note that scammers are receptive to broader changes in the news cycle and will opportunistically change which celebrities they impersonate to capitalise on topical issues,” Asic warned.
Last financial year, Asic took down 5,476 phishing scam hyperlinks, almost four times as many as the previous year; 7,051 fake investment platforms, 2.5 times higher; and 3,106 cryptocurrency scams, an increase of almost 30%.
“The presence of polished content, familiar branding or convincing testimonials does not mean an investment is legitimate,” the Asic chair, Sarah Court, said.
“AI is making investment scams more convincing and harder to detect. A simple online search is not enough to verify whether an opportunity is legitimate.
“Before investing, consumers should verify website addresses, check whether a person or company is legitimate and who they claim to be, and be wary of urgent calls to act.”
Scamwatch advises consumers to stop before sharing money or information; to check the details independently; and to protect yourself and others by reporting any scams to them, your bank, or cyber.gov.au.
Asic said consumers should check for a certified Australian financial services licence, but also be aware that scammers misuse those licences, so they should check against Asic’s professional registers.
Commonwealth Bank research published earlier this year found about nine in 10 Australians were confident they could spot an AI scam, but in reality they can do so less than half the time.
Deepfakes are also increasingly being used politically. Independent MP Zali Steggall has proposed a bill to crack down on deceptive political advertising, which would require AI-generated content that could mislead voters to be clearly identified.

For some artists, using AI during the creative process is like ripping the soul out of an intimate human experience.
Tyga, however, doesn't have those qualms.
During an August interview with Vibe, the rapper revealed he relied on at least one AI music program while crafting his ninth studio album, "$tarface." The 80s-inspired project, released last month, sees Tyga don a new "Miami Vice"-esque alter ego who has a penchant for Jheri curls, sleek retro Ferraris, and synthpop.
"I've never spoken on this with anybody because I always felt like it's similar to a magician explaining how he does his tricks," Tyga told the outlet.
AI has certainly cast a spell across Hollywood, where the technology is transforming how the entertainment industry functions, from studio executives to background actors.
While some creatives view AI as a powerful tool that can speed up production, cut labor costs, and streamline repetitive tasks, others aren't sold. Many artists are concerned that AI will displace human workers, cheapen the creative process, and steal their work without proper compensation. AI sat at the crux of the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild strikes, which both lasted over 100 days, crippling the industry.
Tyga, though, has embraced the adapt or die mentality. He said he used AI to add certain elements to "$tarface," like 80s-era synths, but did the vocals and lyrics himself.
"I know people are going to be mad about me saying this, but it's where technology is going," Tyga told Vibe. "It's no different than when Auto-Tune came out. Some people were opposed to it, but real artists took it and used it."
"There's nothing wrong with using technology as a tool," he added.
Unsurprisingly, the backlash was swift. Pitchfork rated "$tarface" 0.0 out of 10, the lowest score the music publication has awarded an album since the late 2000s, in part due to Tyga's use of AI.
"Given the amount of actual effort or even labor put into $TARFACE — which is to say, about zero — the margins on this thing must be amazing," Drew Millard wrote for Pitchfork. "Stream it out of morbid curiosity if you must, but know that even a single listen runs the risk of making it profitable and therefore encouraging the music industry to commit such atrocities again."
Doja Cat, who collaborated with Tyga on two songs, criticized his decision during a livestream last week.
"Nobody asked me anything about Tyga, but I felt like saying this," the rapper said. "Tyga is a penis for making an AI album."
Audiences on social media haven't been much kinder. Despite the backlash, Tyga joins a growing number of artists proudly using AI in their artistic endeavors.
Superstar producer Timbaland faced backlash in 2023 for using AI to recreate the voice of The Notorious B.I.G. on a song, but he hasn't caved to critics in the years since. In fact, he's gone all-in. Timbaland launched an AI entertainment company, Stage Zero, in 2025 and aims to pioneer a new genre called "A-Pop." His AI artist, TaTa, released her debut music video that October.
"TaTa is a living, learning, autonomous music artist built with AI. TaTa is the start of something bigger," Timbaland told Billboard last year.
Grimes, the dream-pop artist linked to billionaire Elon Musk, has worn AI as a badge of honor. In 2023, she launched Elf Tech, an AI software that allows users to create songs with her voice. Artists can commercially release the finished songs as long as they split 50% of the master-recording royalties.
Nick Carter of The Backstreet Boys has also used AI in new projects. In a 2025 interview with The Comics Beat, Carter said he used AI to create the official lyric video for his "Hey Kid," and a comic book-themed music video series.
In some cases, the artist isn't even human. Tilly Norwood is an AI pop star created by Particle6. Her debut music video, "Take the Lead," has amassed over 475,000 views since March.
Another example is Fenix Flexin, whose summer hit "Rubberz" was ravaged by AI allegations since its release in June. The rapper initially distanced himself from the AI accusations, but later admitted to using the technology during production, according to Rolling Stone. Even so, "Rubberz" resonated with audiences and charted on Billboard's Hot 100, the Stereogum reported.
Tyga, meanwhile, doubled down on his use of AI during an interview with TMZ last week.
"At the end of the day, I'm better than the AI and I've proven that for the last 15 years. So, it doesn't bother somebody like me, but I think maybe there's people that are scared that it's going to, you know, take their position and replace them," Tyga said. "It's just a part of technology."

Following his transformation for The Smashing Machine, Dwayne Johnson is back together with Benny Safdie for their next project.
While speaking to Deadline on Sunday at D23, the Golden Globe nominee revealed that he’s begun production on the Safdie-helmed Lizard Music, for which he undergoes “five hours of makeup every day” to play a man in his 70s.
“We’re in full production. It’s called Lizard Music, I’m with Benny Safdie again. That’s my guy,” he said. “Imagine Willy Wonka but from the mind of Benny Safdie.
Johnson continued, “And I play a septuagenarian man. Now, I didn’t know what the hell that meant. So, I had to Google it, it means you’re in your 70s. So, we transform, and it’s five hours of makeup every day. We’re with Kazu Hiro, who is a legend in Hollywood. He was also nominated for Smashing Machine, for our prosthetics, and he is helping me transform.
Watch on Deadline
“So far, we’re in our second week, and it has already been an unbelievable experience. It’s that thing I was telling the kids, ‘Run towards that thing.’ This is that thing that I ran towards and chased the challenge, and this was a challenge for me. I love Benny, he’s one of my best friends and most embraced collaborators, so I can’t wait for you to see it,” said Johnson.
As Deadline exclusively announced the film based on Daniel Pinkwater’s novel, Safdie told us us that Lizard Music is about “a kid who discovers an island of lizards that are sentient, and they play music, they have broadcast TV. And they want him to come and see them. And he teams up with the Chicken Man, who Dwayne plays, and they go on this adventure to find the land of the lizards.”
“[Johnson] was just talking about how he was slimming down,” said Safdie, after the actor revealed at Toronto International Film Festival that he was undergoing another transformation for the role.
Last October, Amazon MGM Studios’ United Artists scooped up Lizard Music, which is written and directed by Safdie, following his and Johnson’s work together on A24’s The Smashing Machine last year.

Ennore fisherfolk held a demonstration on Sunday after large quantities of fish were found dead and floating in the Kosasthalaiyar river near the Ennore estuary. Officials from the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board (TNPCB) collected water and fish samples from the affected areas for analysis.
Thousands of fish and other aquatic life, including madavai, kizhangan, oodan, karuva and kelathi, besides prawns and crabs, were found dead in the river. The fish were seen floating across large stretches of the water. Scores had accumulated along the banks and near mangroves.
Fisherfolk from Ennore said the incident was an unprecedented disaster as they had never witnessed fish dying and washing ashore on such a scale. They alleged that the fish deaths could be linked to the discharge of chemical effluents into the river and raised concerns over the impact on their livelihoods.
Fisherfolk from eight fishing villages resorted to a road blockade on Thazhankuppam main road. Following this, Tiruvallur MLA T. Arunkumar, the Tahsildar, TNPCB officials, and an Assistant Engineer from the Fisheries Department arrived to hold talks.
The incident comes amidst longstanding concerns over pollution in the Ennore estuary and the Kosasthalaiyar River. The area has been affected by industrial effluents, sewage, coolant water, and fly ash from the concentration of industries and thermal power plants around the estuary.
Yellow chemical covers waters of Ennore Creek; fishermen want government to step in
Fisherfolk sought a detailed report on the nature of the effluents that had entered the waterbody, including whether they were toxic and which industries or companies were responsible for the discharge. “Such kind of effluent release has become a regular incident now. How can we make a livelihood by fishing if this is the case,” said Madhanagopal.
They also sought compensation for the loss of livelihood. The fisherfolk said the estuary was an important fish-breeding area and that thousands of fish had died in the incident. They demanded compensation equivalent to one year’s livelihood, saying they had never witnessed a fish kill on this scale.
Their third demand was for employment opportunities in the industries and thermal power plants in the area. Vishanth, a local fisher, said the community had been promised jobs when the thermal power plants were established, but only around 500 people were provided employment initially. “Our livelihoods have already been damaged by fly ash and hot coolant water,” he said. 'Pressure will follow him' - Rocky Flintoff faces up to tests ahead
- Published
It is not just the name on Rocky Flintoff's shirt that is familiar.
It is the stride to the crease with his helmet in one hand and the way he hits sixes over straight mid-wicket.
Even the way he leans on his bat at the non-striker's end is a throwback to his father.
After a headline-snatching first senior century on Tuesday, the 18-year-old's One-Day Cup drew to a close with 22 in Lancashire's defeat by Durham in the knockout stage on Friday.
Eight matches, 315 runs and an average of 63.
"Naturally pressure will follow him, unfortunately, because of his surname, but he has been up to the task so far," Lancashire coach Steven Croft told BBC Sport.
"The way he has carried himself in this competition has been brilliant."
Given the name - his father Andrew, or 'Freddie', as he is best known, played 227 times for England and had an iconic role in their 2005 Ashes win - and the talent, excitement around Flintoff is inevitable.
David 'Bumble' Lloyd, who played for and coached England and Lancashire and was an early mentor to Flintoff senior, did little to dampen the talk this week, calling for the teenager to be "fast tracked" into the full international set-up after his brutal 123 against Somerset.
"He's got everything," Lloyd said, external. "I think he's an international cricketer.
"England have been pretty good in recent years in identifying talent and stretching and pushing them forward, and I think they can do that with Flintoff."
The hype is not unfounded.
Aged 16, Flintoff became Lancashire's youngest player and England Under-19s' and England Lions' youngest centurion - the latter feat achieved against a Cricket Australia XI featuring players more than 10 years his senior as he took the Lions record from his father.
But, even at this early point, Flintoff's career has not been straightforward.
Injuries, plus a preference for him to play England Under-19 matches last summer, meant he did not feature for Lancashire's first team at all in 2025.
He has not played in the County Championship since averaging 12.42 across four matches in Lancashire's 2024 relegation season.
And he is yet to feature in The Hundred - in which he was a wildcard pick at Northern Superchargers, where his father was coach last summer - or the T20 Blast.
This good form, which also included 61 not out against Warwickshire and contributions of 33 or more against Leicestershire, Kent and Northamptonshire, has been timely.
"That first hundred for him [against Somerset] is massive," Croft said.
"To get his first one... I won't say out of the way... but now he knows he can do it at this level.
"The next for him is to do it at first-class level. He is a very fast learner."
Croft suggested a return to Lancashire's County Championship XI, where he would face higher quality bowlers compared to the Hundred-depleted One-Day Cup attacks, may not be far away.
"He has put himself in a great position," Croft said.
"The way he is striking the ball. He has stuck to what he is good at."
Lancashire host Northamptonshire when the red-ball competition restarts on Thursday and travel to Worcestershire the week after.
There are also five youth one-day internationals between England and Pakistan from 2 September, placing another decision is on the horizon.
His parents are known to play a big role in that decision-making.
And Flintoff is - like his father and 20-year-old older brother Corey, currently in Kent's second XI ranks - an all-rounder at heart.
Bone stress issues in his back and pelvis have prevented him bowling his lively seam in a competitive match since his Under-16 days, but there remains careful quiet hope that could change by next summer, if the teenager comes through the rest of this season and the winter injury-free.
Friday's knock at Old Trafford came against a Durham side featuring Ben Stokes.
The prospect of a Flintoff succeeding Stokes, after Stokes succeeded a Flintoff, as England's all-rounder is tantalising if, at this point, a long way off.
In truth, other England Under-19 contemporaries caught up while Flintoff struggled for first-team action and fitness.
His superb innings at Taunton was ended by a catch from spin-bowling all-rounder Archie Vaughan - a Somerset regular at 20 and son of former England captain Michael.
Elsewhere, Flintoff's Lancashire team-mate Joe Moores, Somerset wicketkeeper Thomas Rew, Middlesex's all-rounder Caleb Falconer and Hampshire pace bowler Manny Lumsden all featured in The Hundred in recent weeks.
And batters Ben Dawkins and Ben Mayes, of Kent and Hampshire respectively, plus Surrey's spin bowling all-rounder Ralphie Albert - another with famous family heritage - have all featured this season's County Championship.
With Rew, Dawkins and Mayes having already scored first-class centuries, it is a youth cohort some regard as England's best for a generation.
You may think Flintoff would benefit from the flying under the radar, however unlikely that may be, but Croft does not appear overly concerned by the attention that comes.
"I don't think he is one of them that will do some mindless scrolling," he said.
"He is level-headed really.
"It is always going to be a bit of a challenge, it is the way of the world these days.
"But he has a good head on his shoulders, is a level kid and hopefully takes it all in his stride."
