Capital, SBI Capital Markets, DAM Capital Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026 Amagi Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services. The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price. Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr. Aye Finance Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO. In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. Fractal Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn. In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X, with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900. On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. Kissht Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property. The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast. The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X. Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. Klassroom Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country. The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr. Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X. Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170, a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25. LEAP India A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON. LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures. The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility. Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025. In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer. Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE. Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25. SEDEMAC Founded in 2007 by IIT-Bombay professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Amit Dixit, and Manish Sharma, SEDMAC designs electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications. The deeptech company produces motor control units, integrated starter generators, fuel injection systems, genset controllers, and small industrial powertrains. Backed by Xponentia Capital Partners, A91 Partners, and 360 ONE Asset, SEDMAC has raised over $107 Mn to date. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the deeptech company filed its DRHP with SEBI in November 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in February 2026. Its public issue comprised solely an OFS component of up to 80.43 Lakh shares. The IPO was oversubscribed 2.68X, with investors cumulatively bidding for 1.51 Cr shares against 56.32 Lakh shares on offer. Shares of the company made a stellar debut on the exchanges on March 11, listing at a premium of 13.5% on the NSE. The stock opened at ₹1,535 as against the issue price of ₹1,352 per share. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹1,510, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price. SEDEMAC reported a net profit of ₹71.4 Cr in the first nine months of FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹770.66 Cr during the period under review. Shadowfax Founded in 2015 by Vaibhav Khandelwal and Abhishek Bansal, Shadowfax is a logistics company that offers hyperlocal and on-demand delivery solutions for businesses. Competing with the likes of Delhivery, LoadShare and Pickrr, the logistics major is backed by names such as Flipkart, Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India), IFC, Nokia Growth Partners, Qualcomm and Trifecta Capital. Shadowfax pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 for an IPO, and received markets regulator's nod in October 2025. It filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in November 2025. The company’s IPO comprised a fresh issue worth ₹1,000 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹907 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.72X, receiving total bids for 24.23 Cr shares against 8.9 Cr on offer. Subsequently, shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on January 28. The stock listed at ₹112.60 apiece on the NSE, a discount of 9.19% to the issue price of ₹124. On the BSE, shares of the logistics unicorn debuted at ₹113, down 8.87% below the issue price. In H1 FY26, the logistics unicorn’s net profit more than doubled to ₹21 Cr from ₹9.8 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue surged 68.4% YoY to ₹1,805.6 Cr during the period. Turtlemint Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurtech platform that enables financial advisors to distribute car, bike, health, and term life insurance to their customer networks. It claims to serve over 3 Lakh advisors nationwide. The startup has raised more than $197 Mn to date from investors such as Amansa Capital, Jungle Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Vitruvian Partners, and Nexus Venture Partners. In September 2025, Turtlemint pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI, and secured market regulator’s approval three months later in December. Subsequently, the insurtech unicorn filed its RHP in June 2026. The IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹660.7 Cr and an OFS of 1.46 Cr shares. Its public issue opened on June 19 and closed on June 23, with an oversubscription of 1.2X. Despite this, the startup made a muted debut on the bourses on June 29. Shares of the insurtech startup listed at ₹134.90 on the NSE, a discount of 11.25% to the issue price of ₹152. On the BSe, the stock listed at ₹136.2 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 10.4% to the issue price. The insurtech company’s net loss rose 19% to ₹184.7 Cr in the first nine months (9M) of FY26 as against a net loss of ₹154.7 Cr in the year-ago period. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 80% to ₹741.1 Cr from ₹411.1 Cr in 9M FY25. The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut. A month later at the fag end of the year, AceVector filed its updated DRHP, which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹300 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 6.39 Cr shares. On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue leapt nearly 35% to ₹244.4 Cr in the first half (H1) of the financial year 2025-26 (FY26) from ₹181.1 Cr the year ago period. Meanwhile, losses also shrank almost 80% to ₹22.4 Cr versus ₹110.3 Cr in H1 FY25. C5i Founded in 2000 by Ashwin Mittal, C5i (formerly known as Course5 Intelligence) is an enterprise AI company that helps large businesses automate tasks and turn data into actionable insights. Reigniting its IPO ambitions, the startup once again filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in July 2026. C5i is now looking to raise about ₹1,000-1,200 Cr via the public issue. On the financial front, C5i’s consolidated net profit declined 15% to ₹48.3 Cr in FY25 as against ₹56.7 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Curefoods Founded in 2020 by Ankit Nagori, Curefoods is a cloud kitchen unicorn that manages brands like EatFit, CakeZone, Nomad Pizza, Sharief Bhai Biryani, and Frozen Bottle. It claims to operate over 200 cloud kitchens and offline outlets across 70 Indian cities. The startup has raised over $175 Mn from backers including Iron Pillar, Accel, Three State Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, and ASK Finance. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Curefoods filed its DRHP with SEBI in late June 2025 and received markets regulator’s approval in late October. As per the DRHP, the proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to ₹800 Cr and an offer-for-sale of up to 4.85 Cr equity shares. However, in June 2026, the startup took a U-turn and put its IPO plans on hold amid the turmoil in the Indian equities market and concerns over its potential valuation. On the financial front, Curefoods' net loss remained steady at ₹169.9 Cr in FY25 as against ₹172.6 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 27.4% to ₹745.8 Cr compared to ₹585.1 Cr in FY24. Fibe Founded in 2015 by Akshay Mehrotra and Ashish Goyal as EarlySalary, Fibe initially offered salary advances and small-ticket personal loans to young working professionals. Since then, it has evolved into a diversified consumer finance platform. Today, it offers personal loans and purpose-driven financing solutions across sectors such as education, insurance, healthcare, rooftop solar and travel. It claims to operate a merchant network spanning 10,387 touchpoints across India, and claims to have ₹8,603 Cr in assets under management as of March 2026. It has raised more than $266 Mn from a host of marquee names such as TPG, Norwest Venture Partners, Eight Roads Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, TR Capital, and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). In June 2026, the lending tech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of up to ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of over 4 Cr shares. On the financial front, Fibe saw its net profit more than double to ₹257.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹113.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue surged 31% to ₹1,584.6 Cr from ₹1,208.9 Cr in FY25. Garuda Aerospace Founded in 2015 by Agnishwar Jayaprakash and Rithika Mohann, Garuda Aerospace manufactures over 30 types of drones, while also offering drone-as-a-service (DaaS) solutions. It claims to have trained over 1 Lakh drone pilots, serving more than 100 government agencies along with over 500 enterprises. The startup currently operates a fleet of over 400 drones and has a manufacturing capacity of up to 15,000 units annually. Backed by cricketer MS Dhoni, Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle and Ocgrow Ventures, Garuda Aerospace has raised more than $37.1 Mn in funding to date. It was last pegged at a post-money valuation of $250 Mn during its last fundraise last year. The company first signalled its intent to go public in 2023. At the time, Jayaprakash told Inc42 that the company would list on the bourses within two years. Eventually in April 2026, the Chennai-based dronetech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. While the exact size of the IPO is yet to be determined, the company’s board, in March, approved a proposal to raise up to ₹750 Cr via fresh issue of shares and an undisclosed OFS component. The startup bagged SEBI’s approval for its IPO in August 2026. On the financial front, Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹11 Cr in H1 FY26 against an operating revenue of ₹41.2 Cr. InCred Holdings Founded in 2016 by Bhupinder Singh, InCred Group runs three distinct business verticals. InCred Finance handles lending, InCred Capital is focussed on wealth and asset management, while InCred Money specialises in retail bonds and alternative investments. The company boasts backing from heavyweights like Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), OAKS, Investcorp, Moore Capital, and Elevar Equity, among others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in September 2025, InCred Holdings, the parent of InCred Financial Services, sought shareholder approval to raise up to ₹ 1,500 Cr through a fresh issue of shares. By November 2025, InCred Holdings filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. The startup received the markets regulator's nod for its IPO in February 2026. In May 2026, the company filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a public issue, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,250 Cr and an OFS of up to 9.9 Cr equity shares. InCred Holdings reported a 5.3% jump in net profit to ₹290 Cr in 9M FY26 from ₹275.5 Cr during the same period last fiscal. Operating revenue also surged 38.6% to ₹1,848.9 Cr from ₹1,333.9 Cr in 9M FY25. Infra.Market Founded in 2016 by Souvik Sengupta and Aaditya Sharda, Infra.Market runs a B2B marketplace that helps customers procure construction materials like concrete, steel, pipes, fittings, and chemicals. The startup has raised over $415 Mn till date from investors such as Tiger Global, Accel, and Nexus Ventures. In October 2025, Infra.Market confidentially pre-filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI for a nearly ₹5,000 Cr ($563.3 Mn) listing. It received SEBI’s go-ahead in January 2026. However, the platform now appears to have ditched plans for a standalone IPO and is exploring a reverse-listing route via its listed subsidiary Shalimar Paints. In August 2026, the paint manufacturing giant proposed that it would acquire shares and CCPS of Infra.Market through a swap, involving securities worth around ₹10,545 Cr. The two companies are also exploring a potential “unification” at a later stage, subject to applicable laws and requisite approvals. Infra.Market’s net profit dwindled 42% to ₹219.7 Cr in FY25 from ₹378 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, revenue from operations rose 27% to ₹18,472 Cr versus ₹14,530.2 Cr in FY24. Kuku Founded in 2018 by Lal Chand Bisu,Vikas Goyal and Vinod Kumar Meena, Kuku is an audio-centric OTT platform that hosts audiobooks, podcasts, and original shows under Kuku FM in multiple Indian languages. It also operates a vernacular short-video app under Kuku TV brand and a microlearning platform Guru. The startup claims to have raised more than $156 Mn in funding to date and is backed by marquee names such as Vertex Ventures, Krafton, IFC and Paramark Ventures. In December 2025, reports first emerged that the OTT soonicorn was looking to list on the bourses. The company is said to have appointed Kotak Mahindra Capital, Axis Bank and Morgan Stanley as bankers to helm its potential IPO. In June 2026, Inc42 reported that Kuku filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr to ₹3,500 Cr (about $261 Mn to $366 Mn) through its IPO. The startup is targeting a valuation of up to ₹15,000 Cr (about $1.8 Bn) for the public listing. The IPO will comprise both a fresh issue of shares and an offer-for-sale component. Kuku FM’s net losses soared 59% to ₹153 Cr in FY25 from ₹96 Cr the prior fiscal, while operating revenue soared 175% to ₹242 Cr from ₹88 Cr in FY24. MakeMyTrip Launched in 2000 by Keyur Joshi, Rajesh Magow, and Deep Kalra, MakeMyTrip is an online travel aggregator (OTA) that operates an end-to-end platform for booking flights, hotels and holiday packages. It also offers ancillary services such as forex cards and travel insurance. Over the years, it acquired rivals such as Goibibo and redBus to complement its primary business of air ticketing and hotels. More recently, it also acquired a minority stake in Visa processing platform Atlys and holiday packages business Flamingo Transworld. Since its inception, the company claims to have processed over 8.7 Cr transactions for retail consumers and onboarded 77,000 SME and large corporate customers. It was also one of the first Indian startups to list on Nasdaq in 2010. After Nasdaq, the travel tech major is now eyeing an Indian IPO. A hot day could be expected to have an extra four hours of extreme heat by the end of the century if the planet continues to warm under a high-emissions scenario, a study has found.
Researchers, including those from China's Sun Yat-sen University and Southern Marine Science and Engineering Guangdong Laboratory, also projected that days not categorised as 'hot days' -- having a heat exceeding 90 per cent of those on previously measured days -- could potentially gain a further three hot hours.
Low and middle-income countries are likely to be the worst hit, findings published in the journal Nature Climate Change show.
Extreme heat events are typically assessed using daily mean average, maximum, or minimum temperatures. However, the measures can neglect shorter but potentially important periods of extreme heat, the researchers said.
The modelling study shows that hourly assessments can capture heat exposure overlooked by daily metrics and could support a more effective heat risk management and public health planning, they said.
Global hourly data, combining weather observations and model estimates during 1981-2023 and coupled with future climate projections to the end of the 21st century, was analysed.
Land areas around the world experience an average of approximately 269 hours of extreme heat each summer, the analysis found.
An hourly heat event was defined as temperature exceeding 90 per cent of previous measurements of that hour during the baseline of 1981-2010.
More than 80% of the world's land area showed an increase in heat, with an average of 62 additional hours per decade of extreme heat between 1981 and 2023 -- 28 per cent of the events were also found to occur on days not identified as heat extremes by daily metrics.
"HHEs (hourly heat extremes) are emerging worldwide and exhibit marked unequal exposure across regions and generations," the authors wrote.
By late century, hourly heat extreme events could be expected to increase fourfold with a sixfold increase in population exposed to such instances under a high-emissions scenario, they found.
"Each hot day will gain about four hot hours, and a further three hot hours will occur on non-hot days, which daily metrics overlook," they wrote.
Low and middle-income countries were found to account for more than three-quarters of both current and projected heat exposure and face the largest increases in lifetime exposure across generations.
The researchers said future research should focus on mechanisms causing hourly heat extremes, such as heat bursts or flash heat events.
An improved understanding of short-term heat events on an hourly scale could improve early warning systems, potential health risk assessments, and adaptation to a warming climate, they said.

The former governor of Guerrero state in Mexico has been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.
Ángel Aguirre, who was arrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.
On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.
A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”
Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.
The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.
On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.
But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.
The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.
Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”
Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formed an investigative unit to dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.

Trump’s Latest Vaccine Order Is Making Things More Confusing
Americans have been stuck in a state of vaccine whiplash.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
In January, the Trump administration attempted to fundamentally change the way the United States handles childhood immunizations. Following a memo from the Department of Health and Human Services, the CDC updated its vaccine schedule to recommend that some shots no longer be given to all children. A federal court undid the effort in March. In an executive order in May, Donald Trump called on states to adopt the narrower schedule anyway. On Monday, Trump issued a new executive order on the same subject, focused on lowering the number of vaccines that the government recommends for all children. As I wrote earlier this week, this White House has a habit of doubling down when it doesn’t get its way. But only states have the power to put these proposals into practice—and many state policy makers, concerned that the White House is contradicting existing research, aren’t keen to follow its guidance.
According to the new executive order, preventive shots for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, dengue, and other diseases should be recommended for “high-risk” groups only. The order also calls to split up vaccinations for measles, mumps, and rubella—the two-dose MMR shot that has been a standard recommendation for U.S. children for decades—into three separate stages, and directs the attorney general to pursue legal action against states that don’t respect “parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations, and equal protection under the law.” (The order says it will align U.S. policy with the best practices of other countries, such as Denmark, but the experts I spoke with highlighted that what works in one country won’t necessarily work in another.)
The mandate may not have any legal authority to compel states to change their guidelines in the near term, although the invocation of the attorney general suggests that litigation may be on the horizon. And the single-disease vaccines that the executive order encourages aren’t yet available in the U.S. But this week’s order risks creating even more uncertainty about vaccines than already exists. “If you set out to write a policy that confuses people, it would look a lot like this one,” Jake Scott, an infectious-disease specialist at Stanford, told me.
Between the policy priorities of the Trump administration and the guidance of public-health experts, Americans have been stuck in a state of vaccine whiplash. When the American Academy of Pediatrics broke with the government earlier this year over its proposed vaccine schedule, the chair of the organization’s committee on infectious diseases told reporters that the recommendations are a “strong departure from the medical evidence and no longer offer the optimal way to prevent illness in children.” Some state lawmakers have been fighting over how best to adapt to the CDC’s changing guidelines; Kansas’s GOP-dominated legislature tried to bring the state’s vaccine rules into alignment with the CDC’s, only for its Democratic governor to veto the effort in April. And many other states have publicly said that they will reject the guidelines.
Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has questioned vaccines’ safety in the past, has been driving the discussions of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee, as my colleagues Tom Bartlett and Katherine J. Wu reported. And although the secretary has moved away from explicit anti-vax rhetoric in recent months (following a reported White House push for health officials to stick to messages with broad public support), vaccine skepticism clearly lingers within the administration. During the press conference for Monday’s executive order, Trump suggested that the MMR vaccine could be “quite lethal.” There is no evidence for this. Measles, though, can kill: Last year, the U.S. saw its first deaths from measles in a decade.
Rethinking MMR at this moment poses extreme logistical challenges. Even if pharmaceutical companies opted to invest the time and money to introduce these shots to the American market, splitting up the doses would create new problems for caregivers. “We are essentially tripling the operational labor required of the parent or guardian (who must now schedule three separate appointments for their child),” Maimuna Majumder, a Harvard epidemiologist, told me in an email, which is “all but guaranteed to result in missed vaccines.”
In the meantime, the executive order risks misinforming Americans who are already unsure of how they feel about vaccination. The Kaiser Family Foundation released a study in June suggesting that about a third of American adults fall into a “mixed middle group” of vaccine skepticism—they believe some myths and reject others. My colleague Nick Florko, who covers public health, told me that these are the people most likely to be swayed by the administration’s latest push: “Those are the folks that might see this and think, Okay, maybe my belief that I want to delay this vaccine is well founded because the federal guidance now says that we should do that.” Under the White House’s rubric, the Americans who most need clear guidance are those who stand to lose.

By Kevin Sieff
Last Tuesday night, I was eating sushi with a Mexican police chief in downtown Culiacán, a city that had momentarily flickered back to life amid a bloody cartel turf war. At the table next to us was a birthday party. The police chief ordered a salmon roll. Through the window, I could see groups of families and friends walking on the sidewalk, past car dealerships and strip malls, after months of self-imposed lockdown.
Among them were three influencers who pulled up to a KFC down the street. They were dressed as food-delivery workers, carrying insulated bags on their backs, joking with one another and livestreaming everything with their phones. César Gastélum, the group’s front man, had become famous for such innocuous pranks. Even as thousands were murdered by the cartels, Gastélum, a stocky, bearded 24-year-old, posted videos of himself dancing in pajamas, dressing as a priest, sipping iced coffee. He had more than 700,000 followers on TikTok.

A A A A video (here & here) is widely circulating on social media, claiming to show two women thrashing a Muslim man who had allegedly snatched their mobile phone in Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh. Let’s verify the authenticity of this claim. Archived post can be seen here Claim: Visuals show two women apprehending a Muslim man for stealing their phone in Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh. Fact: The accused caught in this incident is named Manpreet Singh. The local Padav police have clarified that he is not a Muslim. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE. A reverse image search on keyframes from the viral video led us to several news reports (here, here & here) covering the incident. According to these reports, on 08 August 2026, two sisters, Harshita Agarwal and Rishita Agarwal, were riding a scooter in Gwalior when a man on a motorcycle snatched their phone. The women chased him down, caught him, and handed him over to the local police. A copy of the FIR can be seen here. The investigation by the local Padav police revealed that the accused, Manpreet Singh, is a native of Punjab. To confirm this, we reached out to the Padav Police Station. SHO Shailendra Bhargava clarified that the accused is Manpreet Singh, son of Jaspal Singh, and stated that they do not belong to the Muslim community. To sum it up, the individual caught stealing the phone in the viral video is not a Muslim.

The Kerala State Drugs Control department has begun acting against medical shops displaying boards that offer arbitrary discounts on drugs.
According to sources, drug inspectors and assistant drug controllers have been authorised to check if the shops are putting up misleading advertisements that can influence the purchasing decisions of consumers. Based on a complaint from the All-Kerala Chemists and Druggists Association (AKCDA), a drug inspector in Alappuzha has reportedly begun an inquiry against a newly opened shop in the district.
This follows a recent circular issued by K. Sujith Kumar, State Drugs Controller, based on the orders of the Kerala High Court. In the circular dated July 17, Mr. Sujith Kumar says that the court had on June 19 upheld the State Drugs Controller’s authority to seek an affidavit from medical shop licencees while applying for or renewing a drug licence, undertaking that they will not display discount boards with misleading or vague claims about drug prices.
The court had also clarified, however, that there is no ban on selling drugs below the maximum retail price, and that it is not illegal to give an actual discount to customers. Exhibiting boards with misleading or vague advertisements offering discounts alone is restricted. Medical shops should not display or install discount boards, banners, posters, hoardings, or digital display systems with misleading or vague claims on the prices or discounted prices of drugs. All announcements related to drug prices should be transparent, honest, clear, and examinable. The existing licensees and those applying for new licences should give the required affidavits in the prescribed manner, the circular says.
The departmental action also comes against the backdrop of a legal dispute between traditional pharmacy shops and new-generation outlets offering discounts between 20% and 80%. A section of such new pharmacies, too, had approached the High Court. Official sources say that concerns have been raised about the quality of drugs coming to Kerala via dealers not directly authorised by pharmaceutical companies.
A.N. Mohan, president, AKCDA, says that the manufacture and sale of drugs are regulated under the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules. He points out that the prices of medicines are directly controlled by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority, under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, wherein the margins fixed are between 8% and 16% for controlled category medicines like insulin drugs and between 10% and 20% for de-controlled products for wholesalers and retailers, respectively. “When retail chemists gets 16% margin on products like insulin, how can new-generation shops offer 25% to 80%? Either it is their calculated attempt to finish off small retail chemists, who have been in this business for years, and monopolise the medicine trade with their money power, or to procure medicines from unauthorised sources with doubtful quality. Also, objectionable advertisements are banned under the Drugs and Magic Remedies [Objectionable Advertisements] Act,” Mr. Mohan says.

In 29-year-old, George Town resident Shaikh Shamsudeen’s mind is lodged a memory that time cannot bleed away. Back in 2016, that memorable day arrived unbidden, and when it ended, a desire Shamsudeen had nursed for years had been fulfilled; the desire to follow in his father Shaikh Sadaqathullah’s footsteps as a selfless blood donor. New College has always had a strong culture of blood donation, supporting government hospitals particularly Royapettah GH. And on that day ten years ago, an urgent request for AB Negative blood rolled into the open doors of Shamsudeen’s classroom in New College; it was required for someone undergoing treatment at Cancer Institute. In a fraction of a second, Shamsudeen’s hand went up.
That hand would keep going up with the same eagerness over the years whenever a need for AB Negative showed up on the horizon. Shamsudeen has registered with Madras Voluntary Blood Bureau (MVBB), based in Gopalapuram and run by TTK Group as a service to society, and whenever he receives a call-up from them, he is in attendance at that address the next moment. In April this year, MVBB celebrated its Golden Jubilee.
Get started
Shamsudeen elaborates: “As I have a rare blood type, I do not donate blood once in three to four months as many donors do, but donate when there is an emergency, an urgent need for AB Negative. MVBB keeps a record of when I donated blood, and in an emergency, they would call me if I am within the date for donating blood again.”
Bookmark this thought: irrespective of whether one’s blood group is rare or common, one would do well to be attached to a blood donation organisation so that one gets tuned in to the idea of donating blood as often as they can by virtue of getting timely reminders and urgent call-ups.
Shamsudeen’s blood donation tally stands at 22.
As he desired, Shamsudeen’s journey as a blood donor has followed the same trajectory as his father’s.
(Before proceeding with the how of it, a snapshot of a recent honour to the father-son duo. Last month, on World Blood Donors Day, Crescent Blood Donors honoured Shaikh Sadaqathullah and his son Shaikh Shamsudeen for their commitment to blood donation at an event organised at Kavikko Convention Centre in Mylapore. The award was jointly presented by noted film director Ameer Sultan and Ahmed Buhari, trustee of B.S. Abdur Rahman Crescent Institute of Science & Technology)
Besides the commitment to donating blood as often they can and the choice to be attached to MVBB, father and son share their blood type, AB Negative. The blood donation tally of Shaikh Sadaqathullah, 56 years old, stands at 53. As Sadaqathullah notes, a tinge of disappointment slipping into his voice for a fleeting moment, he stopped donating blood due to health concerns.
(A trivia: Sadaqathullah is an amateur radio operator and his call sign is VU2SDU)
Sadaqathullah’s blood donation journey was initiated at the Perambur Railway Hospital in 1993 where he donated blood responding to a friend’s call. “It was then I realised that my blood group was rare. Any negative blood type is considered rare, and AB Negative is rare even among the negative blood types. Globally, 2 per cent of the population has this blood type. Given this, I have not donated at blood donation camps, only when there was an emergency need for AB Negative, and MVBB would call me.”
The interviews with the father and son duo were conducted separately, and what struck was the similarity not only in the language they used, but also the sentiments they expressed.
There is a lesson there, and probably hope too, for blood donation champions such as Srivatsa Vema from the Federation of Indian Blood Donors Organisation (FIBDO) who has expressed concern over a decreasing number of blood donors.
Bookmark this thought too: if you gripped by a mission to increase the numbers of blood donors, but do not know where to begin, begin at home. Have conversations with your children about your blood donation journey. It sure works: ask the Shaikhs.
A family tradition
Nanganallur resident R. Ravikumar would not skip certain schedules, some day-based and others occurring every few months, not for all the tea in China. These schedules largely relate to his passion for cycling, running and donating blood. The unwavering commitment to blood donation has put an enviable tally against his name: 106 blood donations, the last donation made on March 17, 2026 at Sunrays Hospital in Ashok Nagar.
Ravikumar, a retired manager from the Oriental Insurance Company Limited, has never viewed blood donation as a mere act of charity. It has been a family legacy, a service that brings him closer to his father’s memory: his father was a blood donor, having donated over 50 times in his lifetime. And Ravikumar traces his iron-clad commitment to blood donation to his late father S. Rengarajan’s example as well as simple philosophy, which drives his world view. “Even if we cannot help someone financially, we can always serve the society through our actions without expecting anything in return,” his father would often say. Inspired by those words, Ravikumar (whose blood type is B Positive) began donating blood at the age of 23 in 1984, the first donation aimed at helping a colleague’s wife who was undergoing surgery. To continue this service, Ravikumar has made staying healthy his top priority through regular marathon runs and long distance cycling, believing physical fitness is the reason that he is still able to answer every call for blood.
Since the age of 56, he has participated in numerous endurance events, earning 85 medals. He is also an active member of several blood donation groups in Chennai, continuing to respond to urgent need for donors.
Among the 106 donations, one will always remain etched in his memory. In 2019, after donating blood for a six-year-old cancer patient from Odisha, the child’s parents insisted on meeting him. “I told them I had done nothing special, but they still wanted to thank me,” he recalls. The scene that followed will make anyone go teary-eyed. They bowed in gratitude, a gesture that deeply moved him and reaffirmed his belief that compassion knows no language.
While Ravikumar’s father donated blood over 50 times, and today his brother R. Ramesh has crossed 60 donations.
What began as one man’s quiet belief in selfless service has now grown into a powerful family tradition.
The list of hospitals Ravikumar has donated blood to include Apollo Hospital in Greams Road, Nandanam Apollo Cancer Speciality Hospital, Vijaya Hospital, Miot Hospital, Egmore Children’s Hospital, Adyar Cancer Institute, VHS Blood Bank, various Rotary Club camps, Railway Hospital in Perambur, Sevalaya in Thirunindravoor, SIMS Hospital, Chrompet Government Hospital, Rajaji Government Hospital, Sunrays Hospital and WCCG blood donation camps.
Ravikumar is 65 years old now, usually considered the maximum age at which one could donate blood. Exceptions to that rule do exist; and Ravikumar seems set to be an exception.

IPO-bound consumer appliances startup Atomberg has joined hands with Tata-owned Voltas to manufacture compressors for room air conditioners (ACs) in India. In a statement, Voltas said that it has signed a binding term sheet with Atomberg’s B2B subsidiary, Atomberg Innovation Private Limited (AIPL), to form a joint venture (JV) to develop, manufacture and supply room AC compressors and other allied parts. “The proposed joint venture is intended to undertake the development, manufacturing, and supply of air conditioner compressors, with a strong emphasis on high energy efficiency, operational reliability, cost competitiveness, and progressive localisation,” said Voltas in a statement. The partnership will look to leverage Voltas’ 30,000 touch points and expertise in areas such as manufacturing, product and supply chain. On the other hand, Atomberg Innovation will bring to the table its capabilities in compressor technology, engineering and product design. In a statement, Voltas also said that it will be the anchor customer of the JV and will provide a “stable demand base”. The AC manufacturer also added that the venture will have the flexibility to supply compressors to other customers, “enabling broader market participation, scale, and long-term competitiveness”. “Atomberg has developed deep-tech capabilities in efficient motors, control drives and advance engineering. This partnership gives us the opportunity to combine our technology strengths with Voltas’ extensive air conditioning expertise, manufacturing capability and market scale…,” said Atomberg cofounder Manoj Meena. The JV is still subject to the completion of due diligence and receipt of applicable approvals from relevant authorities. Founded in 2012 by IIT Bombay alumni Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg initially operated on a B2B model and sold energy-efficient BLDC fans. It entered the consumer market in 2016. Today, it sells a range of appliances such as mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. It entered the B2B manufacturing business via AIPL in March this year to build motors and controllers for home appliances. Backed by the likes of Inflexor Ventures, Trifecta Capital Advisors, Steadview Capital and Temasek, atomberg has raised nearly $126.5 Mn to date. On the financial front, the appliance startup managed to narrow its net losses by 41% YoY to ₹117 Cr in FY25, while operating revenue rose over 20% YoY to ₹958.4 Cr during the fiscal under review. The partnership comes as Atomberg is looking to list on the bourses. Last month, the startup took its first step towards an IPO after it converted into a public entity. It is looking to raise ₹1,500 Cr to ₹2,000 Cr ($165 Mn to $220 Mn) via its public offering, which will comprise both fresh issue of shares (25-35%) and an offer for sale (OFS) by existing investors.

Maguire wants 'huge threat' Rashford to stay at Man Utd
- Published
Manchester United defender Harry Maguire says he hopes Marcus Rashford will stay at Old Trafford because he can improve the team.
Rashford came on as a second-half substitute in his first game for United since December 2024 in the 4-2 pre-season defeat by AC Milan in Wroclaw.
He produced one moment of skill by the corner flag and also came close to scoring after being given the number nine shirt by Michael Carrick.
United officials have stressed the number is not regarded as permanent on a day when striker Benjamin Sesko - who had been expected to take the nine shirt this season - was not available through injury.
However, even that underlines the uncertainty around Rashford's future before the 1 September transfer deadline.
Carrick could not say last week whether the England forward will stay, and Maguire is equally unsure of his team-mate's future. However, he wants him to remain at Old Trafford.
"Obviously the transfer window is still open," said Maguire.
"As players, we hope he stays because if he does, he is a big asset to have. He can improve us for sure.
"You saw when he came on, he threatened the backline really well. He could have scored. He's a huge threat.
"I've played with Marcus for numerous years and I know that playing against him and playing with him in training is going to help us."
The disappointment was Rashford's return coincided with what Maguire accepted was Manchester United's "worst" pre-season performance, a week before their Premier League opener at Hull.
Skipper Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second game running, which would have made it 2-1 at half-time, although there were encouraging signs in his link-up play with Youri Tielemans as both completed the full 90 minutes for the first time.
"We're wanting to play much further up the pitch, be more aggressive and more on the front foot," said Maguire.
"This was the only game where I didn't feel we did ourselves justice in that aspect. We had a lot of high regains and created a lot of chances from that, but we didn't sustain our pressure anywhere close to enough."
In a long, five-week, six-match pre-season, Maguire took on the captain's duties in the early games, when Fernandes was missing. That is an indicator he could be the vice-captain this season, although that is yet to be confirmed.
He also had some warm words for former boss Ruben Amorim.
Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo, who both fell out with Amorim, were on the other side of the pitch acknowledging supporters when the Portuguese saw some of his old players as they left the field post-presentation.
There were plenty of warm embraces for Amorim and his coaching staff.
Speaking to Gazzetta dello Sport after the game, Amorim said: "I'm proud to have been at Manchester United and I still love Manchester United."
He embraced journalists he remembered from his time in England, joked "do you miss me guys" and laughed that press conferences "are more boring" without him.
Maguire has nothing negative to say about Amorim's 14 months in charge either.
"It was great to see him and all his staff," he said.
"I got on with Ruben really well and all his staff. I am happy he has another chance to impress and show everyone what a great manager he is. I'm sure he's going to be a success.
"I have nothing bad to say about Ruben. It just didn't work out at Manchester United.
"But he's got a massive club now. I'll be following them and hope they have an amazing season."

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a Muslim woman throwing slippers at a statue of Shivaji Maharaj and being detained by police for the alleged act. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a Muslim woman throwing slippers at a statue of Shivaji Maharaj.
Fact: The video does show a woman throwing slippers at a statue of Shivaji Maharaj in Sasane Nagar, Pune, on 10 August 2026. The woman has been identified as Ashwini Dagde and is a Hindu. Media reports and Girisha Nimbalkar, Senior Police Inspector at Kalepadal Police Station, confirmed that the woman involved in the incident is not Muslim. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple social media posts (here, here, and here) by media outlets featuring the same visuals. According to these posts, the incident took place in Sasane Nagar, Pune, Maharashtra, on 10 August 2026. In one of the posts, we also noticed the woman seen in the viral video, surrounded by several individuals, with ink smeared on her face, and with female police officers. We also learned that the Kalepadal Police Station had filed a case against the woman, who was identified as Ashwini Dagde (here, here).
We then contacted Girisha Nimbalkar, Senior Police Inspector at Kalepadal Police Station. She refuted the viral claim and clarified that the woman involved in the incident is not Muslim and is identified as Ashwini Dagde. She also confirmed that the police filed a case against her on 10 August 2026 and arrested her. The police are investigating the reason behind her throwing slippers at the statue of Shivaji Maharaj.
To sum up, the woman who threw slippers at the Shivaji Maharaj statue in Sasane Nagar, Pune, is not Muslim.

Maharashtra FDA suspends Parle Agro's licence after expired Frooti, Appy found in Chembur godown
The action comes as a part of FDA's wider statewide campaign against restaurants, hotels, dhabas, bakeries, online food platforms and other food businesses.
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) suspended the licence of M/s Parle Agro after finding expired stocks of Frooti, Appy and Apple Fizz at its Chembur godown. Stocks worth ₹99,970 were seized from the Velocity Express Warehouse near Chembur Naka.
The action comes as a part of the agency's wider statewide campaign against restaurants, hotels, dhabas, bakeries, online food platforms and other food businesses under its commissioner Tukaram Mundhe. Mundhe took over as the Maharashtra FDA chief in May, 2025.
The FDA, as of August 13, had inspected 109 hotels, restaurants and dhabas, issuing 49 improvement notices and suspended four food-business licences. It had, a few days ago, also found dirty cooking utensils, significant fly infestation, wastewater and food residue in the kitchen at Bollywood Cafe in Film City, Goregaon East.
FDA crackdown on quick-commerce outlets: Cockroaches, rats and expired chicken found
The FDA, during its special inspection drive targeting quick-commerce food delivery outlets across Mumbai, found several hygiene lapses. These included cockroaches crawling through food storage areas, expired chicken lying in refrigerators, rotten vegetables, rodent droppings and food packets kept directly on dirty floors.
Earlier this week on Friday, the agency suspended the licences of 10 food delivery chains, including Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. The action followed inspections of 86 outlets on Thursday. Of these, 60 were served improvement notices, 14 had their licences suspended, while one outlet was ordered to stop business operations immediately.
The officials found cockroaches moving through the storage area, along with rodent and pest droppings near food packets, at an Instamart facility on the first floor of Gitaneel Arcade on Hill Road, Bandra. Dust, cobwebs and food waste were also found across the warehouse, with the facility also lacking adequate pest-proofing. It had an ant infestation, rusted racks, chipped flooring and poor housekeeping.
Another Instamart facility in Andheri West, near Azad Nagar Metro station, was found storing curry-cut chicken that had expired on August 12.
SRK, Ajay Devgn, Tiger Shroff get FDA notices over Vimal ad
The Maharashtra FDA also recently issued show-cause notices to Bollywood stars Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff for their participation as brand endorsers in an advertisement for Vimal Elaichi, allegedly a tobacco product.
The show-cause notice gives them a period of 15 days from the date of receipt to submit a written explanation. The agency says the campaign could be a surrogate or indirect promotion of prohibited pan masala/tobacco-related products. The agency has warned that if no explanation is received, or if it is found to be unsatisfactory, further action may be initiated under applicable law.

‘I’m a little sad over my KFC’: Bear bursts into Kentucky woman’s home and steals her dinner
A Kentucky woman is warning neighbors to secure their doors after a large bear shattered her glass table and snatched her dinner while she slept
A Kentucky woman woke up to a broken table and a missing dinner early Thursday morning after a bear broke into her home, likely lured by her leftover fast food.
Kendra North was asleep when the animal entered her house, but her sister, who lives next door, witnessed the bear leaving the premises around 5 a.m., as reported by FOX 56 News.
“My sister started calling me, like, five in the morning, and I declined her at least twice, and she just kept calling,” North told the local news station.
Upon answering, North learned what had occurred.
“I answered the call, and she was like, ‘Bro, there’s a bear, and it just walked out of your house, and it came down your steps,” North said. “It came and looked at me, dead in the eyes, on my side of the yard.’”
The force of the bear's entry broke a heavy piece of furniture inside the home.
“My table is really thick glass, and it completely shattered it. She said she actually heard the table shatter from inside her house, and she thought that it was a car wreck outside,” North said, adding that she believed the animal was large.
North said she suspected the bear was drawn inside by food left out in the open.
“I’m a little sad over my KFC,” North said.
Wildlife officials advise residents to take precautions to prevent wild animals from approaching homes in search of food. John Hast, Kentucky Fish and Wildlife Bear Program Coordinator, noted that outdoor food sources are a primary driver of these interactions.
“If you store pet food or if you feed your dogs outside, just think about that,” Hast told FOX 56. “Make sure you’re not leaving any out on the porch, and that’ll keep the bear from just coming right in and getting an easy meal.”
Hast added that residents should evaluate other potential attractants if bears are reported in the area.
“If you’ve got reports right there close to the house, just think about where your garbage is,” he said.
North said the incident prompted her to change her routine moving forward.
“Definitely don’t leave your leftover KFC on the kitchen table and make sure the door is shut very well,” she said.

Several countries on Sunday condemned Israel's decision to reject the latest US proposal for the next stage of the Gaza peace process.
Egypt, Jordan, the UAE, Qatar, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan issued a joint statement, saying the move "seriously undermines collective efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace."
"The roadmap, which has been accepted by the Palestinian factions, is the culmination of intensive efforts by the mediators - Egypt, Qatar, Turkey and the United States, as well as the High Representative for Gaza and the Board of Peace," the statement read.
"It represents a crucial step towards the confinement of weapons alongside the withdrawal of Israeli forces, the deployment of an International Stabilisation Force, the transfer of administrative authority to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, and the reconstruction of Gaza, as set out in the comprehensive plan," it added.
The countries also urged the US to "compel Israel" to fully comply with the commitments and arrangements set out in the comprehensive plan and its roadmap.
"Rejecting the roadmap is an explicit refusal to move forward with the implementation of the comprehensive plan and directly threatens to derail the intensive efforts undertaken by US President Donald Trump to end the war in Gaza and create the conditions necessary for lasting peace. 
In this regard, the ministers stress the importance of continued active US engagement to ensure and compel Israel to fully comply with the commitments and arrangements set out in the comprehensive plan and its roadmap, and to prevent any further obstruction of their implementation," the statement said.
Last Sunday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the proposal and insisted that Hamas must be fully disarmed before Israeli forces withdraw.
"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at the beginning of a cabinet meeting.
He said the Israeli military would "not withdraw at all until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens."
"And when I say disarm Hamas, that means heavy weapons, less-heavy weapons, all weapons. And we are talking about real disarmament, not a fictitious disarmament," Netanyahu added.
US President Donald Trump had announced at the end of July what he described as a historic agreement aimed at securing the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
The announcement came months after Trump first unveiled a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas. Hamas, however, has said it would agree to the next stage only if Israel stops its strikes in Gaza and withdraws its troops to the "yellow line" set out under the October ceasefire agreement.

Taking a safe bet here that most of you who have heard of Louise Joy Brown have not heard at all of Jean Purdy, or her role in the birth of Baby Brown. Louise Brown was the first baby born of an IVF procedure on July 25, 1978. But this might not have been a joyful story, but for Jean Purdy.
Like all the heroines in this column, Jean Marian Purdy, a clinical embryologist and a critical part of the development of in vitro fertilisation, remained uncredited for a long while. Born in Cambridge, U.K., she went to work with physiologist Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. They were working on a high-risk experiment and taking medical science where it had never been before – who would have thought babies could be created in test tubes before the trio managed to show that it is possible.
Purdy trained as a nurse in Addenbrooke Hopsital in Cambridge, and joined Edwards in 1968 as a research nurse and quickly became indispensable to the team. Going back to study the records later, scientists established that it was Purdy who managed the laboratory, prepared and tested culture media, and recorded and organised the data of the early IVF work in the lab. Besides this, the records also put her at the centre of patient care, in this case, supporting women who volunteered their eggs and wombs at a time when public sentiment was entirely against it.
Purdy was the first to recognise and describe the formation of the early human blastocyst – the cluster of cells that forms five or six days after a sperm fertilises an egg, in the culture, a key milestone in pre-implantation development. It represents the early stage of embryonic development, where the embryo implants itself into the wall of the uterus to establish a pregnancy. Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells successfully dividing in the lab, soon these cells would go on to become on 25 July 1978, she was the first to see the embryonic cells that would become Louise Brown. This moment is significant, because it was the first indication that their pioneering technique had worked.
That was not all; between 1970 and 1985, until her death, she co-authored 26 academic papers with Edwards and others in leading journals, including Nature, documenting methods, outcomes and sophistication that made IVF safe and more reliable.
After NHS funding for IVF was withdrawn following early successes, Purdy helped establish the world’s first dedicated IVF clinic, Bourn Hall Clinic near Cambridge in 1980, and served as its technical director. Again, she helped standardise medical protocols for IVF and scale up treatment, overseeing the birth of more than 500 IVF babies before her death from cancer at just 39 years, in 1985.
In their article The Oldham Notebooks: an analysis of the development of IVF 1969–1978. V. The role of Jean Purdy reassessed, archived in PubMed, Martin H. Johnson and Kay Elder, look at her body of work in early fertility care. The authors pored over the Oldham Notebooks - 21 handwritten laboratory notebooks and loose records kept primarily by Purdy between 1969 and 1978. They concluded that: “Purdy’s interests were clearly focused on the research and development aspects, especially those exploring viable embryo development and improved transfer procedures. For example, in a film made in 1980 (Williams, 1980), she talks about a modification to the transfer cannula that she was trying. Thus, whilst Edwards provided the ideas and the intellectual stimulation and Steptoe the authoritative clinical skills, it is arguable that without Purdy’s systematic approach and dedicated contributions, the project at Oldham may have faltered.”
Despite all this, centuries of sexism weighing in on the scientific community, a classic example of the Matilda Effect, her role was minimised in public memory for decades. Even though Edwards and other colleagues objected to it, Purdy’s name was omitted from a commemorative plaque installed at Oldham Hopsitals, associated with IVF’s breakthrough. Correspondence from Edwards archived at Cambridge later described Purdy as “crucial” to their work, underscoring how her erasure contradicted the team’s own view of her importance. In fact, Edwards’ own records state his growing confidence in her and her essentiality in the team: Purdy was “being ‘particularly good with the patients’, and her ‘cooperation had become crucial. It was no longer just Patrick and me. We had become a threesome’.
However, only Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for IVF. While recognition for the work that Purdy did, has grown only recently, thanks in good measure to the research of Johnson and Elder, some things cannot be corrected any more. Now, some museums and clinics cite Purdy as the first clinical embryologist, and other institutions have begun naming awards and exhibitions after her. Sidelined again, this time, though her collaborators acknowledged her work, Purdy’s contributions were callously and credit consistently denied.
Though belated, it’s now time to undo the wrongs. It is time to say her name! Say Jean Purdy, shout it out from the rooftops!

Cristiano Ronaldo has said the 2026-27 season could be the final year of his playing career, offering his clearest indication yet that retirement is approaching. The 41-year-old has spent more than two decades at the highest level and, with his contract at Al Nassr running until June 2027, has now begun speaking openly about what he wants his life to look like once football is over.
“This is probably my last year of football, and I want to leave a spectacular legacy,” Ronaldo told 
Vogue
 in an interview published on Sunday.
Ronaldo opens up about life after football
Ronaldo has previously spoken about retirement without committing to a particular date. In November, he said he expected to continue playing for “one or two years” and confirmed that the 2026 World Cup would be his final tournament.
Portugal were eliminated by Spain in the round of 16 last month. Ronaldo scored three goals at the tournament and became the first player to score at six different World Cups, finishing his World Cup career with 11 goals from 27 appearances.
He was less specific about his overall playing future after Portugal's exit. His comments to 
Vogue
 are the closest he has come to putting a timeframe on it.
Ronaldo said he has already planned for the period after football and expects to spend more time with his family, travel and play and watch padel.
“I have my future all mapped out,” he said. “I have so many things to keep me busy that to tell you just one thing is hard.
“Because football could leave a big hole, you have to fill your time in various ways, not just one. And also have more fun, travel more, watch and play padel, which I really like, and continue to enjoy what I've earned -- what we've earned.
“Because after all it's been 25 years with a lot of sacrifice.”
A final season with Al Nassr and Portugal still ahead
Ronaldo remains contracted to Al Nassr until June 2027 and has continued to play for Portugal after the World Cup.
He is also 24 senior goals short of reaching 1,000, a milestone he has spoken about wanting to achieve during the latter stages of his career.
Portugal's new manager, Jorge Jesus, described Ronaldo as a “symbol of Portuguese football” after taking the job in July and said he would continue selecting him while the forward remains fit and playing.
Ronaldo's three goals at the 2026 World Cup took his international total to 146, the highest in men's international football.
His club career has continued alongside those international records. He began at Sporting CP before moving to Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus and Al Nassr. His most prolific spell came in Madrid, where he scored 450 goals in 438 appearances, becoming the club's all-time leading scorer.
The career Ronaldo is preparing to leave behind
Ronaldo has won five Ballon d'Ors and five Champions League titles, along with league championships in England, Spain and Italy. With Portugal, he won the European Championship and Nations League.
His career has also produced records across club and international football, including his position as men's international football's leading goalscorer and his six World Cup appearances.
The 2026 tournament was already established as the end of his World Cup career. Now, with the new domestic season beginning, Ronaldo has indicated that the wider playing career could have only one more season left.
His comments came in an interview conducted five days before his marriage to Georgina Rodríguez in Cascais, Portugal. The couple had been together for nearly a decade before announcing their marriage with a photograph of their wedding rings.
Ronaldo has also spoken about wanting to spend more time with his family after football and about the interests he intends to pursue away from the sport.
Messi has also raised questions about his future
Ronaldo's comments came shortly after 
Lionel Messi expressed uncertainty over how much longer he would continue playing following the death of his father, Jorge.
The pair have spent much of the past two decades at the centre of football's defining individual rivalry, collecting major individual awards and setting scoring records while playing for Barcelona, Real Madrid and their respective national teams.
Both are now 39 or older, with Ronaldo at 41 and Messi at 39, and both have recently spoken about circumstances that could bring their playing careers towards an end.
For Ronaldo, there is still football to play, goals to chase and a contract that extends into 2027. But for the first time, he has put the possibility of retirement at the end of the current season into his own words.

500 PLA summer camp cadets battle heat as they step out of their comfort zone
Combined camp brought together around 350 school pupils and 150 university students for two weeks of military training
Wilson Hui Chau-yuen, a 22-year-old final-year student at Hong Kong Metropolitan University, recalls that the scorching heat was the biggest enemy during an annual two-week summer camp organised by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) garrison.
“Even on the city’s hottest day, our training continued without pause including martial arts, bayonet practice and marching drills,” Hui said on Sunday, adding that he hoped to join Hong Kong’s disciplined services in the future.
The Hong Kong Observatory recorded a maximum temperature of 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) last Sunday, the highest since records began in 1884.
Hui was among about 500 local students who spent two weeks building resilience and self-reliance at the PLA camp at San Wai Barracks in Fanling.
Form Three student Lewis Wong Lok-hei, from Methodist College, recalled his biggest takeaway from the experience.
“It was very tough, but if it wasn’t tough, why would I even come here? … We came to step out of our comfort zone, train ourselves and persevere.”

Rajeev Shrivastava, General Manager, Central Railway hoisted the National flag on the occasion of 80th Independence Day at the Central Railway headquarters, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, Mumbai on 15.8.2026.
The General Manager reviewed the RPF Parade and addressed the gathering.
Conveying his warmest greetings to all railway personnel, their families and esteemed users, the General Manager in his Independence Day address shared his thoughts with pride, on the significant contributions of Central Railway towards the progress and development of our Nation.
Acknowledging the efforts of the employees, the General Manager said “Thanks to the tireless efforts of our railway employees over the past year, Central Railway has achieved numerous milestones. Working day and night in remote areas and under challenging conditions, our railway staff keep our system safe and make invaluable contributions to operations. Giving highest priority to Customer services, the General Manager said that punctuality remains a key challenge and ensuring safety and security under all circumstances is the foremost objective of Central Railway.
Indian Railway has a crucial role in the Nation’s progress and the remarkable progress achieved in railway electrification over the past decade has proved invaluable in helping the Nation overcome the challenges that rose from the recent disruptions in Oil imports.
The General Manager in his address also congratulated Shankar Shivswami Edle, Head Constable, RPF Zonal Cyber Cell, Central Railway, for having received the President’s Medal for Meritorious Service (MSM) from the President of India, on the occasion of 80th Independence Day at New Delhi.
On the occasion the General Manager expressed gratitude to the Central Railway Women’s Welfare Organisation (CRWWO) for their various welfare activities, thanked the employees for their dedication and commitment towards their duties, and also thanked the media for effectively highlighting and presenting the achievements of Central Railway.

Smt. Snigdha Srivastava President, CRWWO, with executive members of CRWWO, Prateek Goswami, Additional General Manager, Principal Heads of Department, Divisional Railway Manager, Mumbai Division and other officials were also present on the occasion.

I Tested the Best Cat Water Fountains—These Are Worth Buying
Featured in this article
As seen with the rise of automatic litter boxes, automatic feeders, pet trackers, and now cat water fountains, technology has made it so that we can take care of our pets without having to do as much of the manual labor.
These fancy fountains don't just make our lives easier. They can also help cats stay hydrated and live healthier. Ever wonder why your cat can't resist a dripping faucet but ignores its water bowl? In the wild, cats are drawn to moving water, since stagnant puddles can house bacteria. A water fountain plays into this natural instinct, encouraging cats to drink more. These techy fountains are also often connected to an app, which sends reminders and tracks drinking habits.
After prolonged testing, I now look for these three things when shopping for an automatic cat water fountain: a wireless pump for easier cleaning, stainless steel (or glass) construction so it's more hygienic, and a window to monitor water levels (especially if it's not connected to an app). I think the Petkit EverSweet Ultra with AI Camera Pet Water Fountain ($250) is the overall best cat water fountain, and the cheaper Oneisall 3.5L Cord-Free Pet Water Fountain ($40) is the best choice for most people who are on a budget.

This fountain had Bissell's signature sleek aesthetic, but there were several design features that reminded me that Bissell is still used to designing cleaning tools.
